# tcp scanning [← reference index](../../readme.md) · [previous: path and discovery](01-path-and-host-discovery.md) · [next: service identification](03-service-identification.md) | [strategy map](../../notes/attack_strategy_map.md) | study methods: [discover attack surfaces](../../notes/methods/discovery.md) > **purpose:** get quick leads, complete tcp coverage, and adapt scan type, discovery handling, timing and output to the access path. ## 2. get initial tcp results ```bash sudo nmap -ss -n -oa scans/tcp-initial target ``` > **coverage:** 1,000 common tcp ports. review `scans/tcp-initial.nmap` in a text editor.
variants — host list, connect scan or selected ports ### initial view: 1,000 common ports **assigned host list, syn scan:** ```bash sudo nmap -ss -n -il targets.txt -oa scans/tcp-initial-list ``` **one host, connect scan without raw-packet privileges:** ```bash nmap -st -n -oa scans/tcp-connect target ``` default coverage is the common-port selection, not ports 1-1000. ### selected ports or a range **one host:** replace ports with, for example, `25,43` or `1-1024`. ```bash sudo nmap -ss -n -p ports -oa scans/tcp-selected target ``` **find relevant services across assigned hosts:** ```bash sudo nmap -ss -n -p ports -il targets.txt -oa scans/tcp-service-sweep ``` a focused service sweep is not a full port map.
## 3. complete tcp coverage ```bash sudo nmap -ss -n -p- -oa scans/tcp-all target ``` > **coverage:** tcp 1-65535. investigate useful initial results while this runs.
variants — connect scan, blocked discovery, timing and progress ### all tcp ports: 1-65535 **connect scan:** ```bash nmap -st -n -p- -oa scans/tcp-all-connect target ``` inspect additional endpoints before narrowing the investigation. tcp coverage says nothing about udp. ### discovery skips a running target **recheck relevant ports with response reasons:** ```bash sudo nmap -ss -n -pn --reason -p ports -oa scans/tcp-recheck target ``` **proceed with full tcp coverage despite failed discovery:** ```bash sudo nmap -ss -n -pn -p- -oa scans/tcp-all-no-discovery target ``` `-pn` assumes online status; inspect actual responses. it does not fix routing. use `-st` without sudo if ordinary tcp connections are needed. ### timing and progress **full tcp with normal timing and periodic progress:** ```bash sudo nmap -ss -n -p- -t3 --stats-every 30s -oa scans/tcp-normal target ``` **faster timing on a stable path:** ```bash sudo nmap -ss -n -p- -t4 --stats-every 30s -oa scans/tcp-faster target ``` `-t3` is normal timing; `-t4` is more aggressive. periodic progress changes display, not coverage. recheck decisive results if loss or filtering makes observations uncertain. ### tcp-only access through a socks proxy use ordinary connect calls when a previously established proxy is the only route. this is a bounded first view, not complete tcp coverage: ```bash proxychains nmap -st -pn -n --top-ports 100 -oa scans/tcp-proxy-top100 target ``` `proxychains` cannot turn syn probes or udp into proxied tcp connections. `-pn` avoids discovery probes that may not traverse the proxy. confirm the proxy route first, preserve the 100-port limit, and expand with another connect scan only when scope and path permit it.

# service identification [← reference index](../../readme.md) · [previous: tcp scanning](02-tcp-scanning.md) · [next: udp scanning](04-udp-scanning.md) | [strategy map](../../notes/attack_strategy_map.md) | study methods: [discover attack surfaces](../../notes/methods/discovery.md) > **purpose:** identify applications on discovered ports and choose only the probing needed for the next decision. ## 4. identify discovered applications ```bash nmap -st -n -sv -p ports -oa scans/tcp-services target ``` > **next:** choose service-specific enumeration from application evidence. a version match alone does not establish exploitability.
variants — default scripts, named scripts and os fingerprints ### identify applications on discovered ports **version probing plus the default nse script set:** use when those scripts answer relevant enumeration questions. ```bash nmap -st -n -sv -sc -p ports -oa scans/tcp-services-default target ``` read the application evidence and script results. default scripts add interactions; they do not complete service enumeration or prove exploitability. **lighter version probing when time or fragile service behavior matters:** ```bash nmap -st -n -sv --version-light -p ports -oa scans/tcp-services-light target ``` light mode tries fewer uncommon probes and can miss an identity that the default intensity finds. use the default first unless a concrete constraint justifies the tradeoff. ### select a named script **inspect behavior locally:** ```bash nmap --script-help http-headers ``` **after identifying http, inspect its relevant port(s):** ```bash nmap -st -n -p ports --script http-headers -oa scans/http-headers target ``` returned headers are clues. choose scripts for the question they answer and their behavior. ### os fingerprinting and bundled probing **estimate os from network-stack behavior:** ```bash sudo nmap -n -o -oa scans/os target ``` **request more tentative os guesses:** ```bash sudo nmap -n -o --osscan-guess -oa scans/os-guesses target ``` **bundle os/version detection, default scripts and traceroute:** ```bash sudo nmap -ss -n -a -oa scans/combined-detail target ``` os guesses are hypotheses. these use default tcp coverage; `-a` does not mean all ports. choose this bundle only when its additional probing is useful.

# Service Identification [← Reference index](../../README.md) · [Previous: TCP scanning](02-tcp-scanning.md) · [Next: UDP scanning](04-udp-scanning.md) | [Strategy map](../../notes/Attack_Strategy_Map.md) | Study methods: [Discover attack surfaces](../../notes/methods/discovery.md) > **Purpose:** Identify applications on discovered ports and choose only the probing needed for the next decision. ## 4. Identify discovered applications ```bash nmap -sT -n -sV -p PORTS -oA scans/tcp-services TARGET ``` > **Next:** choose service-specific enumeration from application evidence. A version match alone does not establish exploitability.
Variants — default scripts, named scripts and OS fingerprints ### Identify applications on discovered ports **Version probing plus the default NSE script set:** use when those scripts answer relevant enumeration questions. ```bash nmap -sT -n -sV -sC -p PORTS -oA scans/tcp-services-default TARGET ``` Read the application evidence and script results. Default scripts add interactions; they do not complete service enumeration or prove exploitability. **Lighter version probing when time or fragile service behavior matters:** ```bash nmap -sT -n -sV --version-light -p PORTS -oA scans/tcp-services-light TARGET ``` Light mode tries fewer uncommon probes and can miss an identity that the default intensity finds. Use the default first unless a concrete constraint justifies the tradeoff. ### Select a named script **Inspect behavior locally:** ```bash nmap --script-help http-headers ``` **After identifying HTTP, inspect its relevant port(s):** ```bash nmap -sT -n -p PORTS --script http-headers -oA scans/http-headers TARGET ``` Returned headers are clues. Choose scripts for the question they answer and their behavior. ### OS fingerprinting and bundled probing **Estimate OS from network-stack behavior:** ```bash sudo nmap -n -O -oA scans/os TARGET ``` **Request more tentative OS guesses:** ```bash sudo nmap -n -O --osscan-guess -oA scans/os-guesses TARGET ``` **Bundle OS/version detection, default scripts and traceroute:** ```bash sudo nmap -sS -n -A -oA scans/combined-detail TARGET ``` OS guesses are hypotheses. These use default TCP coverage; `-A` does not mean all ports. Choose this bundle only when its additional probing is useful.

# udp scanning [← reference index](../../readme.md) · [previous: service identification](03-service-identification.md) · [next: results and next actions](05-results-and-next-actions.md) | [strategy map](../../notes/attack_strategy_map.md) | study methods: [discover attack surfaces](../../notes/methods/discovery.md) > **purpose:** sample udp separately, preserve ambiguous states, and expand only when the objective or evidence warrants it. ## 5. check udp separately ```bash sudo nmap -su -n --top-ports 20 -oa scans/udp-top20 target ``` > **limit:** this is a sample. `open|filtered` remains inconclusive; expand when evidence or the objective warrants it.
variants — larger sample, selected ports, application probes and tcp + udp ### common-port samples **expand to 100 common ports when more coverage is warranted:** ```bash sudo nmap -su -n --top-ports 100 -oa scans/udp-top100 target ``` these are samples. `open|filtered` is inconclusive; tcp results cannot fill udp gaps. ### selected ports **check a relevant udp port/list:** ```bash sudo nmap -su -n -p ports -oa scans/udp-selected target ``` **add application probes to resolve a useful candidate:** ```bash sudo nmap -su -n -sv -p ports -oa scans/udp-detail target ``` a reply can resolve ambiguity; no reply can leave it inconclusive. if discovery skips an assigned running host, add `-pn` with the same limitations as tcp. ### full udp coverage when the objective justifies the cost ```bash sudo nmap -su -n -p- --stats-every 60s -oa scans/udp-all target ``` this selects udp ports 1-65535 and may take a long time because silence requires waiting and icmp errors may be rate-limited. it is the coverage-expansion option, not a universal first command. continue service work in parallel and preserve the result if the scan cannot finish. ### combined tcp/udp selection **example selection:** change the tcp (`t:`) and udp (`u:`) lists for the actual question. ```bash sudo nmap -ss -su -n -p t:22,80,445,u:53,123,161 -oa scans/tcp-udp target ``` the port lists are examples, not complete coverage. udp waiting can extend the combined scan.

# UDP Scanning [← Reference index](../../README.md) · [Previous: Service identification](03-service-identification.md) · [Next: Results and next actions](05-results-and-next-actions.md) | [Strategy map](../../notes/Attack_Strategy_Map.md) | Study methods: [Discover attack surfaces](../../notes/methods/discovery.md) > **Purpose:** Sample UDP separately, preserve ambiguous states, and expand only when the objective or evidence warrants it. ## 5. Check UDP separately ```bash sudo nmap -sU -n --top-ports 20 -oA scans/udp-top20 TARGET ``` > **Limit:** this is a sample. `open|filtered` remains inconclusive; expand when evidence or the objective warrants it.
Variants — larger sample, selected ports, application probes and TCP + UDP ### Common-port samples **Expand to 100 common ports when more coverage is warranted:** ```bash sudo nmap -sU -n --top-ports 100 -oA scans/udp-top100 TARGET ``` These are samples. `open|filtered` is inconclusive; TCP results cannot fill UDP gaps. ### Selected ports **Check a relevant UDP port/list:** ```bash sudo nmap -sU -n -p PORTS -oA scans/udp-selected TARGET ``` **Add application probes to resolve a useful candidate:** ```bash sudo nmap -sU -n -sV -p PORTS -oA scans/udp-detail TARGET ``` A reply can resolve ambiguity; no reply can leave it inconclusive. If discovery skips an assigned running host, add `-Pn` with the same limitations as TCP. ### Full UDP coverage when the objective justifies the cost ```bash sudo nmap -sU -n -p- --stats-every 60s -oA scans/udp-all TARGET ``` This selects UDP ports 1-65535 and may take a long time because silence requires waiting and ICMP errors may be rate-limited. It is the coverage-expansion option, not a universal first command. Continue service work in parallel and preserve the result if the scan cannot finish. ### Combined TCP/UDP selection **Example selection:** change the TCP (`T:`) and UDP (`U:`) lists for the actual question. ```bash sudo nmap -sS -sU -n -p T:22,80,445,U:53,123,161 -oA scans/tcp-udp TARGET ``` The port lists are examples, not complete coverage. UDP waiting can extend the combined scan.

# scan results and next actions [← reference index](../../readme.md) · [previous: udp scanning](04-udp-scanning.md) · [next: windows network checks](06-windows-network-checks.md) | [strategy map](../../notes/attack_strategy_map.md) | study methods: [discover attack surfaces](../../notes/methods/discovery.md) > **purpose:** resolve uncertainty that affects a decision, preserve coverage limits, and turn scan output into a service-enumeration queue. ## 6. resolve a result that changes your next action keep source, destination, transport and port consistent when comparing results. revisit relevant checks after a new route, foothold or identity changes access.
variants — netcat verification, response reasons and readable output ### netcat connection check **one tcp port:** replace ports with one number. ```bash nc -nv -w 3 -z target ports ``` **short port range:** replace ports with a range such as `3388-3390`. ```bash nc -nvv -w 3 -z target ports ``` success establishes tcp connection acceptance; refusal and timeout differ. the second form gives more verbose output. a three-second wait may be insufficient on a slow path. ### output and diagnostics **readable text only, with verbose output and port-state reasons:** ```bash sudo nmap -ss -n -v --reason -p ports -on scans/tcp-check.txt target ``` open saved `.nmap` or `.txt` output in a text editor. `-oa` writes `.nmap`, `.gnmap` and `.xml`; `-on` writes only normal text. use a different output prefix when retaining another run.
## 7. build the service queue open the saved `.nmap` files in a text editor. for every useful endpoint, capture one line with this structure: ```text source -> target | tcp/udp port | observed state | application evidence | coverage limit | next test ``` > **next:** carry the complete endpoint tuple into [stage 02 service enumeration](../02-service-enumeration/readme.md) and choose the cheapest protocol-aware test that can change your understanding or access. keep an explicit return item for incomplete tcp, udp or application coverage.
interpretation cues — preserve what the scan actually established - `open` establishes a reachable endpoint from the scan source; it does not establish a vulnerability or usable authentication. - `closed` records an explicit rejection in that context. move on unless later evidence changes the route, source or target state. - `filtered` leaves the listener state unresolved because filtering, loss or the path prevented classification. - `unfiltered` means the selected probe reached the port but could not determine whether it was open or closed; use a scan type that can answer the required question. - udp `open|filtered` is inconclusive. a useful protocol probe may reduce uncertainty, but another silence can remain inconclusive. - `closed|filtered` is also an explicit ambiguity. preserve it unless resolving the distinction changes the next action. - a port-based service label is a clue. use application evidence before treating product, version, operating system or machine role as confirmed. - record the exact target, transport, selected ports and source position. a successful narrow scan does not cover untested ports, the other transport or another network position.
## 8. prioritize and know when to rescan rank candidates by the cheapest test likely to produce access, credentials, sensitive information or a decisive prerequisite. prefer observed application behavior over conventional port numbers. keep at least one return item for incomplete coverage so an attractive early service does not erase the rest of the map. re-run network discovery after a new source host, route, tunnel or target restart. re-enumerate a service after a new credential or identity. inspect local listeners after a foothold. recheck a previous result when the source, target state, port selection or network conditions changed—not simply because the first attack failed.

# windows network checks [← reference index](../../readme.md) · [previous: results and next actions](05-results-and-next-actions.md) · [next: rdp access](../03-initial-access/01-rdp-access.md) | [strategy map](../../notes/attack_strategy_map.md) | study methods: [discover attack surfaces](../../notes/methods/discovery.md) > **purpose:** test tcp reachability from a windows host when source position or available tooling matters. test one tcp port from the windows source host: ```powershell test-netconnection -computername target -port ports ``` > **read:** `tcptestsucceeded`, source and destination addresses. use one number for ports. failure does not distinguish a closed port, filtering or a path problem.
variants — scan ports 1-1024 or a selected port list ### scan a low-port range ```powershell 1..1024 | % {echo ((new-object net.sockets.tcpclient).connect("dc_ip", $_)) "tcp port $_ is open"} 2>$null ``` ### check a selected port list the example list can be changed to the endpoints of interest. ```powershell 22,80,443,445,3389 | % {echo ((new-object net.sockets.tcpclient).connect("target", $_)) "tcp port $_ is open"} 2>$null ``` `$_` is the current port; errors are hidden. no printed result does not prove every port is closed. results reflect the windows host's access and the stated port selection.

# scanner alternatives and web baseline checks [← stage index](readme.md) | [discovery cheatsheet](../../cheatsheets/discovery-scanning.md) | [master notes](../../notes/master_notes.md) | [strategy map](../../notes/attack_strategy_map.md) | study methods: [discover attack surfaces](../../notes/methods/discovery.md) > **use when:** nmap remains the interpretation baseline, but a faster tcp discovery pass or a bounded web-server check is useful. these tools generate candidates; nmap/manual protocol checks confirm them. ## rustscan: fast tcp discovery, nmap interpretation > **prerequisite:** rustscan and nmap on kali; direct tcp reachability. **coverage:** only the explicit tcp range. **decisive output:** a discovered port that nmap can reproduce and identify. ```bash rustscan -a target -r 1-65535 --ulimit 5000 -- \ -pn -sv -sc -oa rustscan-followup ``` if the target or network becomes unstable, lower concurrency rather than trusting an empty result. rustscan does not replace udp work and does not prove that closed/filtered ports were tested with the same semantics as nmap.
bounded first 1,000 tcp ports ```bash rustscan -a target -r 1-1000 --ulimit 5000 -- \ -pn -sv -sc -oa rustscan-1000 ``` > use only for a quick selection. it is not full tcp coverage and is not equivalent to nmap's default top-1,000 selection.
## masscan: raw-packet discovery, then validation > **prerequisite:** root/raw-packet access and a directly routed target. **choose it:** for a large authorized address/port space where discovery speed matters. **failure cue:** high loss or inconsistent results at the chosen rate. ```bash sudo masscan target -p1-65535 --rate 500 -ol masscan-open.txt ``` treat each hit as a candidate and recheck with nmap: ```bash ports=$(awk '$1 == "open" && $2 == "tcp" {print $3}' masscan-open.txt \ | sort -nu | paste -sd,) test -n "$ports" && sudo nmap -pn -sv -sc -p "$ports" target -oa masscan-verified ``` masscan's raw-packet model is not suitable through a tcp socks proxy. a rate that overwhelms the path can create false negatives and disrupt the lab; record the rate with the result. ## unknown-port discrimination start passively or with protocol-appropriate probes. do not spray arbitrary strings at a stateful or destructive service. ```bash nmap -pn -sv --version-all -p port target -on port-port-version.txt nmap --script-help banner nmap -pn --script=banner -p port target -on port-port-banner.txt nc -nv target port openssl s_client -connect target:port -servername hostname curl -vk --max-time 10 https://target:port/ ``` > **next action:** route application evidence to the matching stage 02 page. if tls succeeds but http does not, preserve the certificate names and protocol evidence instead of labelling it https. ## nse candidate checks inspect a script before selecting it: ```bash nmap --script-help script_name grep -i 'script_name' /usr/share/nmap/scripts/script.db ``` run a named script against a confirmed service/port: ```bash nmap -pn -sv --script script_name -p port target -on nse-script_name.txt ``` the broad `vuln` category is candidate generation and can be intrusive or misleading. if its use is justified in the authorized lab, restrict it to identified ports and manually validate every result: ```bash nmap -pn -sv --script vuln -p ports target -on nse-vuln-candidates.txt ``` avoid `*brute*` categories as a default; first establish exact service, known test identities, lockout/rate limits and explicit authorization. ## nikto: bounded web-server candidate generation > **prerequisite:** an identified http(s) endpoint. **choose it:** after manual baselining to identify common files, headers and server misconfiguration candidates. **decisive output:** a finding manually reproduced with the same host, path and authentication context. ```bash nikto -h http://target:port -output nikto-target-port.txt ```
https, host name and tuning variants ```bash nikto -h https://hostname:port -output nikto-hostname-port.txt nikto -h http://target:port -vhost hostname -output nikto-vhost.txt nikto -h http://target:port -tuning 123b -output nikto-focused.txt ``` > tuning codes are version-sensitive. inspect `nikto -h` / local documentation before relying on a copied code set.
nikto is explicitly listed as allowed by the current offsec exam guide, but its findings remain scanner candidates. recheck the guide before an exam and manually validate anything that affects an attack decision. ## sources - [getsh scan route](https://lizajose.github.io/getsh/scan), reviewed at source commit [`e1f62dd`](https://github.com/lizajose/getsh/commit/e1f62dd351bd061b59e2573beea741f6c5bb4f98) - [nmap service/version detection](https://nmap.org/book/man-version-detection.html) - [rustscan usage](https://github.com/bee-san/rustscan) - [masscan readme](https://github.com/robertdavidgraham/masscan) - [nikto documentation](https://github.com/sullo/nikto/wiki) - [current oscp+ exam guide](https://help.offsec.com/hc/en-us/articles/360040165632-oscp-exam-guide)

## masscan: raw-packet discovery, then validation

> **prerequisite:** root/raw-packet access and a directly routed target. **choose it:** for a large authorized address/port space where discovery speed matters. **failure cue:** high loss or inconsistent results at the chosen rate.

```bash
sudo masscan target -p1-65535 --rate 500 -ol masscan-open.txt
```

treat each hit as a candidate and recheck with nmap:

```bash
ports=$(awk '$1 == "open" && $2 == "tcp" {print $3}' masscan-open.txt \
  | sort -nu | paste -sd,)
test -n "$ports" && sudo nmap -pn -sv -sc -p "$ports" target -oa masscan-verified
```

masscan's raw-packet model is not suitable through a tcp socks proxy. a rate that overwhelms the path can create false negatives and disrupt the lab; record the rate with the result.

sections.title: Unknown-port discrimination
sections.search:
## unknown-port discrimination

start passively or with protocol-appropriate probes. do not spray arbitrary strings at a stateful or destructive service.

```bash
nmap -pn -sv --version-all -p port target -on port-port-version.txt
nmap --script-help banner
nmap -pn --script=banner -p port target -on port-port-banner.txt
nc -nv target port
openssl s_client -connect target:port -servername hostname
curl -vk --max-time 10 https://target:port/
```

> **next action:** route application evidence to the matching stage 02 page. if tls succeeds but http does not, preserve the certificate names and protocol evidence instead of labelling it https.

sections.title: NSE candidate checks
sections.search:
## nse candidate checks

inspect a script before selecting it:

```bash
nmap --script-help script_name
grep -i 'script_name' /usr/share/nmap/scripts/script.db
```

run a named script against a confirmed service/port:

```bash
nmap -pn -sv --script script_name -p port target -on nse-script_name.txt
```

the broad `vuln` category is candidate generation and can be intrusive or misleading. if its use is justified in the authorized lab, restrict it to identified ports and manually validate every result:

```bash
nmap -pn -sv --script vuln -p ports target -on nse-vuln-candidates.txt
```

avoid `*brute*` categories as a default; first establish exact service, known test identities, lockout/rate limits and explicit authorization.

https, host name and tuning variants ```bash nikto -h https://hostname:port -output nikto-hostname-port.txt nikto -h http://target:port -vhost hostname -output nikto-vhost.txt nikto -h http://target:port -tuning 123b -output nikto-focused.txt ``` > tuning codes are version-sensitive. inspect `nikto -h` / local documentation before relying on a copied code set.

HTTPS, host name and tuning variants ```bash nikto -h https://HOSTNAME:PORT -output nikto-HOSTNAME-PORT.txt nikto -h http://TARGET:PORT -vhost HOSTNAME -output nikto-vhost.txt nikto -h http://TARGET:PORT -Tuning 123b -output nikto-focused.txt ``` > Tuning codes are version-sensitive. Inspect `nikto -H` / local documentation before relying on a copied code set.
Nikto is explicitly listed as allowed by the current OffSec exam guide, but its findings remain scanner candidates. Recheck the guide before an exam and manually validate anything that affects an attack decision. ## Sources - [getSH Scan route](https://lizajose.github.io/getSH/scan), reviewed at source commit [`e1f62dd`](https://github.com/lizajose/getSH/commit/e1f62dd351bd061b59e2573beea741f6c5bb4f98) - [Nmap service/version detection](https://nmap.org/book/man-version-detection.html) - [RustScan usage](https://github.com/bee-san/RustScan) - [Masscan README](https://github.com/robertdavidgraham/masscan) - [Nikto documentation](https://github.com/sullo/nikto/wiki) - [Current OSCP+ exam guide](https://help.offsec.com/hc/en-us/articles/360040165632-OSCP-Exam-Guide)

# ftp enumeration [← stage index](readme.md) · [cheatsheet](../../cheatsheets/service-opportunities.md#ftp) | [strategy map](../../notes/attack_strategy_map.md) | study methods: [extract opportunities from services](../../notes/methods/services.md) > **recognize:** ftp usually appears on tcp/21, but trust an ftp banner or protocol response on any port. **goal:** determine authentication, listable/readable content and effective write locations. ## baseline: anonymous access ```bash ftp target ``` at the prompts, try user `anonymous` and an email-like password. then: ```text status pwd ls -la binary get file quit ``` if login succeeds but listing/transfer fails, use the client's `passive` command to toggle data-channel mode and retry once before changing credentials. > **decisive output:** code `230` accepts the login; directory listings and successful `retr` establish read access. inspect downloaded backups, configuration, keys and source locally. store target artifacts outside this public repository.
variant — authenticated ftp ```bash ftp target ``` enter `user` and the password when prompted. enumerate from the authenticated root again; it may expose a different namespace than anonymous access.
variant — curl listing, download and bounded write test ```bash curl --list-only ftp://target/ curl -o file ftp://target/path/file curl --user user ftp://target/ curl --user user -o file ftp://target/path/file curl --user user --upload-file ./probe.txt ftp://target/path/probe.txt ``` omit `--user` for anonymous access. let curl prompt for an authenticated password instead of placing it in shell history. upload only a harmless uniquely named probe when write validation is necessary and authorized; remove it through the ftp client after the test.
variant — focused nmap helpers ```bash nmap -sv -p port --script ftp-anon,ftp-syst target ``` `ftp-anon` checks anonymous login and may flag writable entries; `ftp-syst` asks for server/system information. manually confirm useful access with a protocol client.
> **failure cues:** `530` means that login was rejected, not that ftp has no other usable identity. a listing failure after `230` may be a data-channel/passive-mode or authorization problem. a successful upload proves write access only; it does not prove that a web server, scheduled task or privileged process consumes that file. > **next action:** inspect recovered files; record exact read/write boundaries; validate any new credential once against its likely service; send a writable-consumer hypothesis to the appropriate web, execution or privilege-escalation block.

sections.title: SSH Enumeration and Access Validation
sections.search:
# ssh enumeration and access validation [← stage index](readme.md) · [cheatsheet](../../cheatsheets/service-opportunities.md#ssh) | [strategy map](../../notes/attack_strategy_map.md) | study methods: [extract opportunities from services](../../notes/methods/services.md) > **recognize:** ssh commonly uses tcp/22. **prerequisite for access:** an accepted authentication method plus a permitted account/session context. ## baseline: validate one known identity ```bash ssh -v -p port user@target ``` > **decisive output:** the debug trace separates connection, host-key negotiation, offered authentication methods and account acceptance. a shell prompt establishes session access as that identity.
variant — private key ```bash chmod 600 key ssh -v -i key -p port user@target ``` the key must correspond to an authorized public key for that account. `permission denied (publickey)` can mean wrong user, wrong key, server policy or account restrictions.
variant — discover methods for a known username ```bash nmap -p port --script ssh-auth-methods --script-args "ssh.user=user" target ``` this starts an authentication exchange and is logged; nmap classifies it as intrusive. use it only when the supported methods change the next decision.
variant — non-interactive key check ```bash ssh -o batchmode=yes -o connecttimeout=5 -i key -p port user@target 'id' ``` batch mode will not prompt for passwords or key passphrases. it is useful only when the key is already usable non-interactively.
> **failure cues:** timeout suggests route/filtering/service issues; refusal means no accepting listener in that context; host-key failure occurs before user authentication; `permission denied` proves that the attempted method/context failed, not that every credential is invalid. a valid account may still have no shell or be restricted by server policy. > **next action:** after a shell, verify `whoami`, groups, hostname and addresses, then re-enumerate locally. password spraying and key-passphrase cracking belong to the credential-attack block, not this procedure.

# smtp enumeration [← stage index](readme.md) · [cheatsheet](../../cheatsheets/service-opportunities.md#smtp) | [strategy map](../../notes/attack_strategy_map.md) | study methods: [extract opportunities from services](../../notes/methods/services.md) > **recognize:** smtp commonly uses tcp/25, submission uses 587, and implicit tls commonly uses 465. **goal:** collect banner/capabilities, mail-domain clues and only defensible user evidence. ## baseline: banner and capabilities ```bash nc -nv target port ``` then enter: ```text ehlo example.invalid help vrfy user expn postmaster quit ``` > **decisive output:** `250-` capability lines reveal extensions such as starttls or auth. `250` after `vrfy` may support a valid mailbox; `550` commonly rejects or denies it; `252` explicitly means the server will not verify and is not proof that the user exists.
variant — starttls or implicit tls ```bash openssl s_client -connect target:587 -starttls smtp -crlf -quiet openssl s_client -connect target:465 -crlf -quiet ``` run `ehlo example.invalid` after tls negotiation. certificate names and capabilities can yield host/domain clues; authentication still requires a supported identity and mechanism.
variant — focused automated user checks ```bash smtp-user-enum -m vrfy -u users.txt -t target -p port smtp-user-enum -m rcpt -u users.txt -t target -p port ``` `rcpt` testing requires an smtp transaction and servers may deliberately normalize responses. treat automation as candidate generation and manually compare decisive responses.
variant — windows source position ```powershell test-netconnection -computername target -port port ``` this verifies tcp reachability only. use an available netcat/ncat or openssl client for protocol dialogue.
> **failure cues:** multiline replies begin with `nnn-` and finish with `nnn `; read the final line. `503` often means the command sequence is wrong. uniform `252` or `550` responses make enumeration inconclusive. a visible auth method does not mean anonymous relay or valid credentials. > **next action:** add confirmed/candidate names and domains to the private evidence ledger; test new names only in the later credential block. do not send real mail or run relay checks unless the objective requires it. ## pop3 and imap handoff mail-access services expose mailbox capabilities and, with legitimate credentials, stored messages that may contain workflow or reset links. ```bash openssl s_client -connect target:995 -crlf -quiet # pop3s openssl s_client -connect target:993 -crlf -quiet # imaps ``` pop3 dialogue: ```text capa user user pass password stat list quit ``` imap dialogue: ```text a1 capability a2 login user password a3 list "" "*" a4 logout ``` > test one legitimately acquired credential. capability output is not authentication; avoid brute-force nse scripts until lockout/authorization is explicitly understood. source supplement: reviewed getsh nmap mail blocks.

## pop3 and imap handoff

mail-access services expose mailbox capabilities and, with legitimate credentials, stored messages that may contain workflow or reset links.

```bash
openssl s_client -connect target:995 -crlf -quiet   # pop3s
openssl s_client -connect target:993 -crlf -quiet   # imaps
```

pop3 dialogue:

```text
capa
user user
pass password
stat
list
quit
```

imap dialogue:

```text
a1 capability
a2 login user password
a3 list "" "*"
a4 logout
```

> test one legitimately acquired credential. capability output is not authentication; avoid brute-force nse scripts until lockout/authorization is explicitly understood. source supplement: reviewed getsh nmap mail blocks.

# dns enumeration [← stage index](readme.md) · [cheatsheet](../../cheatsheets/service-opportunities.md#dns) | [strategy map](../../notes/attack_strategy_map.md) | study methods: [extract opportunities from services](../../notes/methods/services.md) > **recognize:** dns uses udp/53 for most queries and tcp/53 for operations including conventional zone transfers and oversized responses. **prerequisite:** a known or inferred domain for meaningful record and name enumeration. ## baseline: query the target dns server directly ```bash dig @target domain soa dig @target domain ns dig @target domain a dig @target domain mx dig @target domain txt ``` > **decisive output:** `answer` records disclose names, addresses, mail exchangers or text. the `aa` flag supports an authoritative answer. record `status` separately from the answer count.
variant — reverse lookup and zone transfer ```bash dig @target -x ip dig @target domain axfr ``` a successful axfr returns the zone records and closing soa. `transfer failed`, `refused` or `notauth` only disproves an unauthenticated transfer from this source; continue ordinary queries.
variant — name guessing after the domain is known ```bash dnsrecon -d domain -n target -t std dnsrecon -d domain -n target -d wordlist -t brt dnsenum --dnsserver target domain ``` check wildcard behavior before trusting large result sets. every resolved in-scope name becomes a new discovery/service-enumeration input.
variant — reverse sweep of an explicitly assigned range ```bash dnsrecon -r subnet -n target ``` use this only when the entire `subnet` is assigned. ptr names are clues; resolve/scan only in-scope results.
variant — host and windows nslookup ```bash host -t mx domain target host -t txt domain target ``` ```powershell nslookup host.domain target nslookup -type=txt host.domain target nslookup -type=mx domain target ```
> **failure cues:** `nxdomain` means that queried name does not exist in that view; `noerror` with no answer can mean the name exists but lacks that record type. timeout can be filtering, loss or a silent/unreachable server. a recursive answer does not establish that the server is authoritative. > **next action:** add new hostnames/ips to the scoped queue, correlate naming roles with observed services, and repeat discovery/service identification for those in-scope endpoints.

# nfs and unix rpc enumeration [← stage index](readme.md) · [cheatsheet](../../cheatsheets/service-opportunities.md#nfs-and-unix-rpc) | [strategy map](../../notes/attack_strategy_map.md) | study methods: [extract opportunities from services](../../notes/methods/services.md) > **recognize:** rpcbind commonly appears on tcp/udp 111 and nfs on tcp/udp 2049, with additional dynamically assigned rpc ports. **goal:** find exports, allowed client ranges and effective uid/gid-based permissions. ## baseline: list rpc services and exports ```bash rpcinfo -p target showmount -e target ``` > **decisive output:** `rpcinfo` maps rpc programs to versions/transports/ports. `showmount -e` returns exports and apparent allowed clients, but nfsv4-only servers may not expose the mount service and `showmount` completeness varies by implementation.
variant — nmap without mounting ```bash nmap -sv -p 111,2049 --script nfs-showmount,nfs-ls,nfs-statfs target ``` the scripts can list exports, file attributes and access flags. confirm access manually when a finding matters.
variant — mount read-only first ```bash sudo mkdir -p /mnt/nfs-audit sudo mount -t nfs -o ro,vers=3,nolock target:/export /mnt/nfs-audit find /mnt/nfs-audit -maxdepth 3 -ls sudo umount /mnt/nfs-audit ``` if version 3 fails and version 4 is advertised, retry with `-o ro,vers=4`. nfsv4 may present a pseudo-filesystem whose export path differs from `showmount` output.
variant — inspect numeric ownership ```bash ls -lan /mnt/nfs-audit find /mnt/nfs-audit -maxdepth 3 -type f -readable -ls ``` nfs commonly authorizes unix identities by numeric uid/gid. a matching local username is irrelevant if its number differs. `root_squash` usually maps remote uid 0 to an unprivileged identity; `no_root_squash` is dangerous but still requires a useful writable object and privileged consumption path.
variant — bounded write verification ```bash sudo mount -t nfs -o rw,vers=3,nolock target:/export /mnt/nfs-audit touch /mnt/nfs-audit/probe-file ls -ln /mnt/nfs-audit/probe-file rm /mnt/nfs-audit/probe-file sudo umount /mnt/nfs-audit ``` use a unique harmless name only when write validation is needed and authorized. record the resulting numeric owner/group. success proves write in that directory, not execution or privileged ownership.
> **failure cues:** `showmount` failure does not rule out nfsv4. `access denied by server` can mean export client restrictions or wrong path/version. `permission denied` after mounting is file authorization, not network failure. do not change local uids or write to an export during concept study. > **next action:** inspect readable backups, home data, keys and configuration; record numeric ownership and actual write boundaries; send a writable/privileged-consumer hypothesis to the escalation block.

# smb and ms-rpc enumeration [← stage index](readme.md) · [cheatsheet](../../cheatsheets/service-opportunities.md#smb-and-ms-rpc) | [strategy map](../../notes/attack_strategy_map.md) | study methods: [extract opportunities from services](../../notes/methods/services.md) > **recognize:** direct-hosted smb commonly uses tcp/445; netbios session service commonly uses tcp/139; ms-rpc endpoint mapping commonly uses tcp/135. they are related windows surfaces but not interchangeable. **goal:** distinguish null, guest and authenticated contexts; enumerate shares, files, users, groups, domain/workgroup clues and actual permissions. ## baseline: list shares without credentials ```bash smbclient -n -l //target ``` > **decisive output:** a share list proves that this access context can enumerate names. it does not prove access to share contents. `nt_status_access_denied` means this context was denied; repeat after obtaining a legitimate credential.
variant — authenticated share listing and connection ```bash smbclient -l //target -u 'domain/user' smbclient //target/share -u 'domain/user' smbclient -l //target -u 'target/user' smbclient -l //target -u 'guest%' ``` the first two forms use a domain identity, the third makes a local target account explicit, and the fourth tests a guest account with an empty password. let the client prompt for non-empty passwords. inside the share: ```text pwd ls allinfo file get file mkdir probe-dir rmdir probe-dir exit ``` use a harmless uniquely named directory only when write permission must be verified. a successful create/remove establishes share-level write access, not code execution.
variant — recursive retrieval ```bash smbclient //target/share -u 'domain/user' -c 'recurse on;prompt off;mget *' ``` run from a dedicated local evidence directory and review expected volume first. search downloaded configuration, scripts, backups, keys and unattended-install files locally; never publish recovered data.
variant — rpc null or authenticated session ```bash rpcclient -u '' -n target rpcclient -u 'domain/user' target ``` useful interactive queries: ```text srvinfo enumdomains enumdomusers enumdomgroups queryuser rid netshareenumall quit ``` null-session denial is common on modern systems. authenticated output must be labelled with the identity that produced it.
variant — fast permission summary and consolidated candidates ```bash nxc smb target -u user -p password --shares enum4linux-ng -a target ``` netexec (`nxc`) is the current command name on recent kali releases; older material may use `crackmapexec`. these tools consolidate candidates. confirm useful shares and files with `smbclient` or native access.
variant — protocol, signing and time clues ```bash nmap -p 139,445 --script smb-protocols,smb2-security-mode,smb2-time target ``` signing and dialect results affect later relay/exploit decisions but are not vulnerabilities by themselves. the older `smb-os-discovery` script depends on smbv1 behavior and may not identify modern hosts reliably.
variant — windows built-ins ```powershell net view \\target /all get-childitem \\target\share get-content \\target\share\file ``` these use the current windows logon context unless alternate credentials or mappings are established. an existing connection to the same server under another identity can cause credential-conflict errors.
smbmap — map rights, then read one useful file use from kali when smb is reachable. choose the same domain/local identity that worked with smbclient. suppress write probes when inventorying reads; this means a writable label is not being tested here. ```bash # known domain account: enumerate share access without creating a probe file smbmap -h target -d domain -u user -p 'password' --no-write-check # inspect the selected share to a bounded depth smbmap -h target -d domain -u user -p 'password' -r 'share' --depth 2 --no-write-check # download the specific file found above smbmap -h target -d domain -u user -p 'password' --download 'share\path\file' --no-write-check ``` > **read:** a listed file must still be readable under this identity. a downloaded config/backup → classify its credential material, then test only the relevant account/service. a denied share → try another listed share or a newly obtained identity; do not infer a host-wide denial. [smbmap upstream](https://github.com/shawndevans/smbmap). for broader smb/rpc collection, use the existing enum4linux-ng baseline; authenticate explicitly when credentials exist: ```bash # no credentials: anonymous rpc/smb candidates enum4linux-ng -a target # known identity: domain objects visible to this account enum4linux-ng -a -w domain -u user -p 'password' target ``` > **next:** validate returned users/groups/shares with rpcclient or smbclient. a collector can return partial data despite a successful login.
> **failure cues:** distinguish connection failure, authentication failure, share enumeration denial and file authorization denial. a share named `ipc$` is not a general file share. guest acceptance may look like success while returning a restricted namespace. a share marked writable still needs a consumer/trigger before it becomes an execution path. > **next action:** inspect readable content, record per-share rights, validate names/domain clues, and re-run authenticated enumeration whenever identity changes. move file-consumer hypotheses to web/execution/escalation and signing/relay hypotheses to the later credential/ad blocks. ## netbios names before smb enumeration use when udp/137 or smb suggests windows names but dns/domain identity is unclear. ```bash # ask the assigned host for its netbios names nbtscan target nmblookup -a target ``` read: a machine name and group/domain label are leads. a workgroup label does not prove ad membership. resolve the returned name and use the smb/ldap checks with the accepted identity. no reply can mean filtering or disabled netbios while tcp/445 still works. sources: [upstream 1](https://www.kali.org/tools/nbtscan/). ## smb/rpc rid lookups when a normal user listing is denied use when the accepted identity can translate sids but cannot list the directory directly. keep the queried host/domain and a bounded rid range explicit. ```bash nxc smb target -d domain -u user -p 'password' --rid-brute 4000 ``` read: classify returned sid types—users, groups and machine accounts are different objects. the upper bound is coverage, not proof that higher rids contain nothing. a resolved name is not a password, service authorization or successful logon. prefer the existing native directory/rpc listing when it is available; do not infer no accounts from a single denied enumeration method. sources: [upstream 1](https://www.netexec.wiki/smb-protocol/enumeration/enumerate-users-by-bruteforcing-rid).

## netbios names before smb enumeration

use when udp/137 or smb suggests windows names but dns/domain identity is unclear.

```bash
# ask the assigned host for its netbios names
nbtscan target
nmblookup -a target
```

read: a machine name and group/domain label are leads. a workgroup label does not prove ad membership. resolve the returned name and use the smb/ldap checks with the accepted identity. no reply can mean filtering or disabled netbios while tcp/445 still works.

# snmp enumeration [← stage index](readme.md) · [cheatsheet](../../cheatsheets/service-opportunities.md#snmp) | [strategy map](../../notes/attack_strategy_map.md) | study methods: [extract opportunities from services](../../notes/methods/services.md) > **recognize:** snmp queries commonly use udp/161. versions 1 and 2c authenticate with a community string sent without modern transport protection; version 3 can provide user-based authentication and privacy. **goal:** turn a valid read context into host, interface, route, process, software, user and listener clues. ## baseline: find a read community, then walk ```bash onesixtyone -c community_file target snmpwalk -v2c -c community target 1.3.6.1.2.1 ``` use `-v1` instead when version 1 is indicated. start with the standard system tree before a huge full walk. > **decisive output:** returned oid/value pairs prove that the selected version/community can read those objects. hostnames, interfaces, routes, users, processes and locally listening ports become new hypotheses to validate through the appropriate service or post-access path.
variant — efficient v2c bulk walk ```bash snmpbulkwalk -v2c -c community target 1.3.6.1.2.1 ``` bulk requests reduce round trips but require snmpv2c or later. if the agent rejects them, fall back to `snmpwalk` with the verified version.
variant — high-value windows oids ```bash snmpwalk -v1 -c community target 1.3.6.1.4.1.77.1.2.25 snmpwalk -v1 -c community target 1.3.6.1.2.1.25.4.2.1.2 snmpwalk -v1 -c community target 1.3.6.1.2.1.25.6.3.1.2 snmpwalk -v1 -c community target 1.3.6.1.2.1.6.13.1.3 ``` these target user names, running process names, installed software and tcp listener ports. availability depends on the agent and exposed mib view.
variant — snmpv3 authenticated and private walk ```bash snmpwalk -v3 -l authpriv -u user -a sha -a auth_password -x aes -x priv_password target 1.3.6.1.2.1 ``` the security level, authentication algorithm, privacy algorithm and credentials must match the configured snmpv3 user. `authnopriv` authenticates without encryption; `noauthnopriv` supplies neither and should be used only when that exact configuration is observed.
variant — focused udp verification ```bash sudo nmap -su -sv -p 161 --script snmp-info target ``` `snmp-info` extracts basic snmpv3 engine information without proving a usable v1/v2c community.
> **failure cues:** udp silence can remain `open|filtered`; it does not prove that the community is wrong. `timeout: no response` can be version mismatch, wrong community, filtering, loss or an unavailable oid view. `no such object` means the queried oid is absent/not exposed, not that the whole service failed. do not use a discovered write community to change configuration during enumeration. > **next action:** translate output into exact host/service/user hypotheses, scan newly disclosed in-scope addresses/listeners from the proper source position, and keep configuration-changing snmp actions outside this stage.

variant — efficient v2c bulk walk ```bash snmpbulkwalk -v2c -c community target 1.3.6.1.2.1 ``` bulk requests reduce round trips but require snmpv2c or later. if the agent rejects them, fall back to `snmpwalk` with the verified version.
variant — high-value windows oids ```bash snmpwalk -v1 -c community target 1.3.6.1.4.1.77.1.2.25 snmpwalk -v1 -c community target 1.3.6.1.2.1.25.4.2.1.2 snmpwalk -v1 -c community target 1.3.6.1.2.1.25.6.3.1.2 snmpwalk -v1 -c community target 1.3.6.1.2.1.6.13.1.3 ``` these target user names, running process names, installed software and tcp listener ports. availability depends on the agent and exposed mib view.
variant — snmpv3 authenticated and private walk ```bash snmpwalk -v3 -l authpriv -u user -a sha -a auth_password -x aes -x priv_password target 1.3.6.1.2.1 ``` the security level, authentication algorithm, privacy algorithm and credentials must match the configured snmpv3 user. `authnopriv` authenticates without encryption; `noauthnopriv` supplies neither and should be used only when that exact configuration is observed.
variant — focused udp verification ```bash sudo nmap -su -sv -p 161 --script snmp-info target ``` `snmp-info` extracts basic snmpv3 engine information without proving a usable v1/v2c community.
> **failure cues:** udp silence can remain `open|filtered`; it does not prove that the community is wrong. `timeout: no response` can be version mismatch, wrong community, filtering, loss or an unavailable oid view. `no such object` means the queried oid is absent/not exposed, not that the whole service failed. do not use a discovered write community to change configuration during enumeration. > **next action:** translate output into exact host/service/user hypotheses, scan newly disclosed in-scope addresses/listeners from the proper source position, and keep configuration-changing snmp actions outside this stage.

# SNMP Enumeration [← Stage index](README.md) · [Cheatsheet](../../cheatsheets/service-opportunities.md#snmp) | [Strategy map](../../notes/Attack_Strategy_Map.md) | Study methods: [Extract opportunities from services](../../notes/methods/services.md) > **Recognize:** SNMP queries commonly use UDP/161. Versions 1 and 2c authenticate with a community string sent without modern transport protection; version 3 can provide user-based authentication and privacy. **Goal:** turn a valid read context into host, interface, route, process, software, user and listener clues. ## Baseline: find a read community, then walk ```bash onesixtyone -c COMMUNITY_FILE TARGET snmpwalk -v2c -c COMMUNITY TARGET 1.3.6.1.2.1 ``` Use `-v1` instead when version 1 is indicated. Start with the standard system tree before a huge full walk. > **Decisive output:** returned OID/value pairs prove that the selected version/community can read those objects. Hostnames, interfaces, routes, users, processes and locally listening ports become new hypotheses to validate through the appropriate service or post-access path.
Variant — efficient v2c bulk walk ```bash snmpbulkwalk -v2c -c COMMUNITY TARGET 1.3.6.1.2.1 ``` Bulk requests reduce round trips but require SNMPv2c or later. If the agent rejects them, fall back to `snmpwalk` with the verified version.
Variant — high-value Windows OIDs ```bash snmpwalk -v1 -c COMMUNITY TARGET 1.3.6.1.4.1.77.1.2.25 snmpwalk -v1 -c COMMUNITY TARGET 1.3.6.1.2.1.25.4.2.1.2 snmpwalk -v1 -c COMMUNITY TARGET 1.3.6.1.2.1.25.6.3.1.2 snmpwalk -v1 -c COMMUNITY TARGET 1.3.6.1.2.1.6.13.1.3 ``` These target user names, running process names, installed software and TCP listener ports. Availability depends on the agent and exposed MIB view.
Variant — SNMPv3 authenticated and private walk ```bash snmpwalk -v3 -l authPriv -u USER -a SHA -A AUTH_PASSWORD -x AES -X PRIV_PASSWORD TARGET 1.3.6.1.2.1 ``` The security level, authentication algorithm, privacy algorithm and credentials must match the configured SNMPv3 user. `authNoPriv` authenticates without encryption; `noAuthNoPriv` supplies neither and should be used only when that exact configuration is observed.
Variant — focused UDP verification ```bash sudo nmap -sU -sV -p 161 --script snmp-info TARGET ``` `snmp-info` extracts basic SNMPv3 engine information without proving a usable v1/v2c community.
> **Failure cues:** UDP silence can remain `open|filtered`; it does not prove that the community is wrong. `Timeout: No Response` can be version mismatch, wrong community, filtering, loss or an unavailable OID view. `No Such Object` means the queried OID is absent/not exposed, not that the whole service failed. Do not use a discovered write community to change configuration during enumeration. > **Next action:** translate output into exact host/service/user hypotheses, scan newly disclosed in-scope addresses/listeners from the proper source position, and keep configuration-changing SNMP actions outside this stage.

# database enumeration and privilege boundaries [← stage index](readme.md) · [cheatsheet](../../cheatsheets/service-opportunities.md#databases) | [strategy map](../../notes/attack_strategy_map.md) | study methods: [extract opportunities from services](../../notes/methods/services.md) > **recognize:** common ports include mssql 1433, mysql/mariadb 3306 and postgresql 5432, but instances can use other ports. **goal:** establish database identity, authentication context, databases/schemas/tables, granted rights, useful data, server-side file access and command execution only where explicit privileges permit it. database administrator and operating-system administrator are different identities. server-side file/program features act in the database server's filesystem and service-account context, not kali's. ## mysql / mariadb ```bash mysql -h target -p port -u user -p ``` ```sql select version(), user(), current_user(); show databases; show grants; use database; show tables; describe table; select * from table limit 20; select @@secure_file_priv; ``` > **interpret:** `user()` shows the presented client identity; `current_user()` shows the account used for privilege checking. `secure_file_priv` restricts server-side import/export: a directory constrains it, an empty value is unrestricted by that variable, and `null` disables these operations. the `file` privilege is still required.
mysql variant — validate server-side file read/write prerequisites ```sql select load_file('/path/on/database/server'); select 'probe' into outfile '/allowed/server/path/probe.txt'; ``` use only an authorized harmless path. `load_file` returning `null` is ambiguous among missing file, permissions, size, file privilege and `secure_file_priv`. `into outfile` will not overwrite an existing file. a written file becomes execution only if another privileged component consumes it.
## microsoft sql server ```bash impacket-mssqlclient 'user@target' impacket-mssqlclient 'domain/user@target' -windows-auth ``` let the tool prompt for the password. at the sql prompt: ```sql select @@version; select system_user; select is_srvrolemember('sysadmin'); select name from sys.databases; use database; select table_schema, table_name from information_schema.tables; select top 20 * from schema.table; ``` > **interpret:** `is_srvrolemember('sysadmin')` returns `1`, `0` or `null`; `null` is not success. impacket also exposes helpers such as `enum_impersonate` and `xp_cmdshell` depending on version and rights.
mssql variant — command-execution boundary ```sql exec xp_cmdshell 'whoami'; ``` `xp_cmdshell` is disabled by default on new installations. enabling it generally requires high privilege and changes server configuration; do not enable it merely to enumerate. when available, a sysadmin's child process normally runs as the sql server service account; an authorized non-sysadmin may use a configured proxy. verify returned identity before choosing the next action.
## postgresql ```bash psql -h target -p port -u user -d postgres ``` ```text \conninfo \l \du \dn \dt *.* ``` ```sql select version(), current_user, session_user; select rolname, rolsuper, rolcreaterole, rolcreatedb from pg_roles; ```
postgresql variant — server file/program privilege boundary ```sql select pg_has_role(current_user, 'pg_read_server_files', 'member'); select pg_has_role(current_user, 'pg_write_server_files', 'member'); select pg_has_role(current_user, 'pg_execute_server_program', 'member'); ``` server-side `copy ... from/to 'file'` uses the postgresql server's filesystem and service identity. `copy ... program` executes on the server and requires superuser or the corresponding predefined role. client-side `\copy` reads/writes the client filesystem and is not the same primitive.
> **failure cues:** connection refusal/timeout is network or listener context; login rejection is authentication/context; an empty database list may be visibility limits; object denial is authorization. query only bounded rows first. never assume that reading application credentials or obtaining database admin implies os execution. > **next action:** identify application accounts, hashes/credentials, paths and linked systems; record the precise grant enabling any file or execution primitive; validate recovered credentials in the later credential block and re-enumerate after any identity change. ## redis ```bash nmap -pn -sv --script redis-info -p port target redis-cli -h target -p port ping redis-cli -h target -p port info redis-cli -h target -p port acl whoami redis-cli -h target -p port acl list ``` authenticated when a password is legitimately known: ```bash redis-cli -h target -p port --askpass ``` > `pong` proves an accessible redis command surface, not write/file/execution permission. check acls, mode, bind/protected-mode and persistence/module configuration before reasoning about an effect. do not run `config set`, write keys or load modules during enumeration. ## oracle tns/sid triage ```bash nmap -pn -sv --script oracle-tns-version -p 1521 target nmap -pn --script oracle-sid-brute -p 1521 target ``` > a discovered sid/service name is a namespace clue, not credentials. continue with an installed oracle client only when a legitimate identity is available; preserve listener/version/sid evidence and do not treat a conventional port as oracle proof. source supplement: reviewed getsh nmap oracle block. ## mongodb — inspect readable databases with mongosh use when the service is mongodb, commonly tcp/27017. current installations use `mongosh`; the old `mongo` binary may be absent. ```bash # reachable service without known credentials mongosh --host target --port port # known account; -p prompts rather than storing the password in the command mongosh --host target --port port -u user -p --authenticationdatabase admin ``` inside mongosh, choose the real database/collection: ```javascript show dbs use database show collections db.getcollection('collection').find().limit(5) db.getcollection('users').findone({username: 'user'}) ``` read: returned documents prove that identity can read those collections. an empty database list can reflect authorization, not an empty server. classify recovered secrets and use the matching service. login/operator injection is an application query issue, distinct from direct db access. do not overwrite account records just because the repo contains an update example. sources: [upstream 1](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/mongodb-shell/). ## sqlite — inspect a recovered application database use when a downloaded/local application file is sqlite. it is a file format, not a remote listener. ```bash file app.db sqlite3 -readonly app.db ``` ```sql .tables .schema users pragma table_info(users); select * from users limit 5; .quit ``` read: identify the schema and credential format before choosing a recovery mode. keep the database's provenance and any required wal/shm companions; a locked/incomplete copy can give misleading results. recovered passwords/hashes → the credential procedure, not an assumption of os or domain access. sources: [upstream 1](https://www.sqlite.org/cli.html).

use when the service is mongodb, commonly tcp/27017. current installations use `mongosh`; the old `mongo` binary may be absent.

# windows remote-access validation [← stage index](readme.md) · [rdp access procedure](../03-initial-access/01-rdp-access.md) · [cheatsheet](../../cheatsheets/service-opportunities.md#windows-remote-access) | [strategy map](../../notes/attack_strategy_map.md) | study methods: [extract opportunities from services](../../notes/methods/services.md) > **recognize:** rdp commonly uses tcp/3389; winrm commonly uses 5985/http and 5986/https. **goal:** determine whether one known credential is accepted in the correct local/domain context and whether it is authorized for a usable session. ## rdp baseline: authentication-only check ```bash xfreerdp3 /v:target /u:user /d:domain /auth-only /cert:ignore ``` some distributions expose the binary as `xfreerdp`. omit `/d:domain` for the intended local-account context; use `/u:target\\user` if needed to make that context explicit. > **decisive output:** successful authentication-only validation supports that the credential is accepted for rdp/nla. it does not prove an interactive desktop will be granted under every policy/session condition.
variant — open an rdp desktop ```bash xfreerdp3 /v:target /u:user /d:domain /dynamic-resolution /cert:ignore ``` let freerdp prompt for the password. `/cert:ignore` suppresses certificate validation and is suitable only in the controlled lab context; it removes server-identity protection.
variant — identify rdp security requirements ```bash nmap -p 3389 --script rdp-enum-encryption,rdp-ntlm-info target ``` this can disclose supported security layers, nla and ntlm host/domain clues. it does not validate a credential.
## winrm baseline: interactive session ```bash evil-winrm -i target -u user ``` ```bash evil-winrm -i target -u 'domain\\user' ``` omitting `-p` makes the established ruby client prompt for the password. > **decisive output:** an interactive powershell prompt establishes winrm authorization. immediately verify identity and host context with `whoami`, `hostname` and `get-netipaddress`.
variant — winrm over https ```bash evil-winrm -i target -u user -s -p 5986 ``` check `evil-winrm -h` because the established ruby client and newer `evil-winrm-py` use different long-option spelling. do not assume a copied command matches the installed implementation.
variant — windows powershell remoting ```powershell $cred = get-credential enter-pssession -computername target -credential $cred ``` powershell remoting uses the configured winrm endpoint. local trusted-host, kerberos/name-resolution and endpoint authorization settings can fail independently of password validity.
> **failure cues:** certificate warnings are different from authentication failure. rdp errors can reflect nla, account context, expired/locked accounts or missing logon rights. winrm `401` supports authentication/authorization failure; `winrm cannot process the request` can be name resolution, trusted-host, listener or transport context. valid smb credentials do not guarantee rdp or winrm rights. > **next action:** after a session, re-enumerate identity, groups, privileges, files, local services/listeners and routes. password spraying, pass-the-hash and ticket use belong to later credential/ad blocks. ## vnc ```bash nmap -pn -sv --script vnc-info -p port target vncviewer target:port ``` > vnc may expose a desktop without windows logon semantics; the vnc server's authentication and the resulting os session identity are separate. use `realvnc-auth-bypass` or password testing only for a confirmed compatible product and explicit authorized objective, then verify the desktop identity. ## telnet ```bash nmap -pn -sv -p port target nc -nv target port telnet target port ``` > telnet is plaintext and may expose a banner/login prompt. validate only legitimately acquired credentials; do not make `telnet-brute` a baseline. after login, verify host and identity because appliance/application shells can differ from an os shell. source supplement: reviewed getsh nmap vnc/telnet blocks. ## gnu inetutils telnetd — conditional authentication-bypass check use only after identifying the affected gnu inetutils telnetd/login chain and its patch status. cve-2026-24061 concerns how a supplied user value reaches login; it does not apply to every telnet server. distribution backports matter. ```bash # client supports sending the autologin user environment value user='-f root' telnet -a target port ``` read: if a shell is obtained, verify hostname and id. a prompt or echoed username is not root access. a different daemon, fixed build, client negotiation mismatch or a rejected user value → return to service identification. the affected upstream range and distribution fixes must be checked against the advisory rather than inferred from port 23. sources: [upstream 1](https://security-tracker.debian.org/tracker/cve-2026-24061).

Omit `/d:DOMAIN` for the intended local-account context; use `/u:TARGET\\USER` if needed to make that context explicit. > **Decisive output:** successful authentication-only validation supports that the credential is accepted for RDP/NLA. It does not prove an interactive desktop will be granted under every policy/session condition.
Variant — open an RDP desktop ```bash xfreerdp3 /v:TARGET /u:USER /d:DOMAIN /dynamic-resolution /cert:ignore ``` Let FreeRDP prompt for the password. `/cert:ignore` suppresses certificate validation and is suitable only in the controlled lab context; it removes server-identity protection.
Variant — identify RDP security requirements ```bash nmap -p 3389 --script rdp-enum-encryption,rdp-ntlm-info TARGET ``` This can disclose supported security layers, NLA and NTLM host/domain clues. It does not validate a credential.
## WinRM baseline: interactive session ```bash evil-winrm -i TARGET -u USER ``` ```bash evil-winrm -i TARGET -u 'DOMAIN\\USER' ``` Omitting `-p` makes the established Ruby client prompt for the password. > **Decisive output:** an interactive PowerShell prompt establishes WinRM authorization. # http and web application mapping [← stage index](readme.md) · [quick sheet](../../cheatsheets/web-mapping.md) · [mechanics](../../notes/master_notes.md#web-behavior-to-access) | [strategy map](../../notes/attack_strategy_map.md) | study methods: [map useful web behavior](../../notes/methods/web-mapping.md) > **use when:** an http(s) endpoint must become a route, request, role, object and input map before exploitation. > **enter with:** `source -> target | tcp port | http/tls evidence | hostname clues | coverage limit`. ## baseline the application identity ```bash curl -skl -d headers.txt -o body.html http://target:port/ curl -sk -o /dev/null -w 'code=%{http_code} bytes=%{size_download} type=%{content_type} redirect=%{redirect_url}\n' http://target:port/ ``` > **decisive output:** record the scheme, hostname/`host` header, port, redirects, page title, certificate names, server/framework clues and whether the view is anonymous or authenticated.
variant — explicit virtual-host candidate ```bash curl -sk -h 'host: candidate.domain' http://target:port/ ``` compare it with a random hostname. a different status alone is weak evidence; compare body, length, title and redirects.
variant — preserve cookies and follow redirects ```bash curl -skl -c cookies.txt -b cookies.txt http://target:port/path ``` use a separate cookie jar per identity. do not mix anonymous, ordinary-user and administrator evidence.
variant — replay through burp community ```bash curl -sk -x http://127.0.0.1:8080 http://target:port/path ``` confirm the proxy listener is active on `127.0.0.1:8080`. use `-k` only for the controlled lab because it disables destination-certificate verification.
## manual behavior map for every visible function, capture one unchanged request in burp proxy history, send it to repeater and record: ```text method path | content-type | access context/role input location + name | baseline value status | length/hash | redirect | marker/error/time object/function selected | next one-variable test ``` check login/registration/reset, profiles/objects, search/filter/pagination, download/export/preview, upload/import, administration and every javascript api call. > **next:** a browser-side restriction is not server authorization. replay the raw request and change one field, object reference, method or access-context element at a time. ## inspect exposed artifacts ```bash curl -sk http://target:port/robots.txt curl -sk http://target:port/sitemap.xml curl -sk http://target:port/.git/head curl -sk http://target:port/openapi.json curl -sk http://target:port/swagger.json ``` also inspect html comments, hidden inputs, form actions, linked javascript, route strings, source-map references, cookies and response headers. > **decisive output:** a path, parameter, api schema, object identifier, component or secret-bearing artifact that creates a specific next request. source disclosure is not command execution. ## discover files and directories request a random nonexistent path first and record its status, length and body marker. ```bash gobuster dir -u http://target:port/ -w /usr/share/wordlists/dirb/common.txt -t 10 -o gobuster-root.txt ``` > **decisive output:** manually verified routes including useful `200`, redirect, `401`, `403` and `405` responses.
variant — technology-aware extensions ```bash gobuster dir -u http://target:port/ -w wordlist -x php,txt,bak,old,zip -t 10 -o gobuster-ext.txt ``` choose extensions from observed stack evidence; do not spray every extension.
variant — authenticated discovery ```bash gobuster dir -u http://target:port/ -w wordlist -c 'session=value' -h 'authorization: bearer token' -t 10 -o gobuster-auth.txt ``` use only the cookie or header that applies. an expired session can turn every result into the same login redirect.
variant — filter a confirmed wildcard body length ```bash gobuster dir -u http://target:port/ -w wordlist --exclude-length noise_length -t 10 -o gobuster-filtered.txt ``` filtering without first confirming the noise response can hide a real path.
## discover virtual hosts ```bash gobuster vhost -u http://domain:port/ --append-domain -w /usr/share/seclists/discovery/dns/subdomains-top1million-5000.txt -o vhosts.txt ``` alternative with automatic calibration: ```bash ffuf -w wordlist -u http://target:port/ -h 'host: fuzz.domain' -ac -o ffuf-vhosts.json ``` > **failure cue:** uniform status/length may be the default vhost. compare each candidate with a random host header before adding it to the application map. ## discover parameters and object values get parameter names: ```bash ffuf -w /usr/share/seclists/discovery/web-content/burp-parameter-names.txt -u 'http://target:port/path?fuzz=test' -ac -o params-get.json ``` post form parameter names: ```bash ffuf -w wordlist -u http://target:port/path -x post -h 'content-type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' -d 'known=value&fuzz=test' -ac -o params-post.json ``` object values with an authenticated api: ```bash ffuf -w numbers -u 'http://target:port/api/objects/fuzz' -h 'authorization: bearer token' -mc all -fc 404 -o object-values.json ``` > **decisive output:** a manually reproduced parameter or value that changes application behavior. tool outliers are candidates, not confirmed access-control flaws.
ffuf — preserve a captured authenticated request save a working raw request from the proxy as request.txt, retain its host/cookie/body, and put fuzz at the single parameter name/value or path being tested. replay it once manually first. the request file does not specify tls: choose the transport explicitly. ```bash # https request, including its original method and session headers ffuf -request request.txt -request-proto https -w wordlist -mc all -ac -t 10 -o request-https.json # plain http request: otherwise ffuf defaults to https ffuf -request request.txt -request-proto http -w wordlist -mc all -ac -t 10 -o request-http.json ``` > **read:** compare an outlier's status/length/body with a known missing value, then replay that exact request. a login redirect for every value → refresh the session before continuing. a one-time csrf token → repair token handling; the saved-request flag does not refresh it automatically. [ffuf request configuration](https://github.com/ffuf/ffuf/wiki/home#request-configuration).
## map api methods, schema and authorization ```bash curl -ski http://target:port/api/v1/path curl -ski -x options http://target:port/api/v1/path curl -ski -x post -h 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"username":"test_user","password":"test_password"}' http://target:port/api/v1/login ``` > **interpretation:** `405` can establish that a route exists but rejects the method. validation errors can reveal required fields. a token establishes only the authorization demonstrated by a later request. build a matrix across anonymous, user a, user b and administrator contexts where available: ```text path | method | identity/role | object/property | result | next ``` ## exit and handoffs > **exit condition:** each interesting function has a baseline request, access context, controllable input, expected result, observed difference and cheapest next test. - file/path selector -> [file handling attacks](../03-initial-access/02-web-file-handling.md); - shell/diagnostic or database-backed input -> [command and sql injection](../03-initial-access/03-command-and-sql-injection.md); - object/role/property or browser-script context -> [access control and xss](../03-initial-access/04-access-control-and-xss.md); - product/plugin/version exploit candidate -> block 6 public-exploit adaptation; - new credential -> block 5 credential handling and authenticated re-enumeration; - verified server command execution -> block 7 session handling. ## wfuzz alternative for paths and form values use when wfuzz is the available/familiar client for the same controlled-response test. choose a nonexistent control first; preserve the actual host and authenticated session. ```bash # paths; hiding 404s is appropriate only after checking the site's failure behavior wfuzz -c -z file,wordlist --hc 404 -u 'http://target:port/fuzz' # a form value in a working authenticated request wfuzz -c -z file,wordlist -b 'session=cookie' \ -d 'name=fuzz' --hc 404 -u 'http://target:port/path' ``` read: status/length/body outliers need manual replay. uniform redirects, wildcard bodies or expired cookies → fix the response/session controls before expanding the list. the presence of an outlier is not a vulnerability result. sources: [upstream 1](https://github.com/xmendez/wfuzz). ## http proxy variables — control which client request goes through burp use when a client honors http proxy environment variables. keeping them on a single invocation avoids accidentally proxying later unrelated traffic. ```bash http_proxy=http://127.0.0.1:8080 https_proxy=http://127.0.0.1:8080 \ curl -i http://target:port/path # explicit proxy and empty bypass list for a request that otherwise skips the proxy curl --proxy http://127.0.0.1:8080 --noproxy '' -i http://target:port/path ``` read: confirm the request in burp history before trusting the replay. http proxy settings do not tunnel arbitrary smb/kerberos traffic. for https, the client's certificate trust still matters; distinguish a local proxy/tls error from an application response. sources: [upstream 1](https://curl.se/docs/manpage.html). ## extract candidate paths from a downloaded javascript file use after reading an actual application js file. this is a quick string candidate pass; it does not execute the script or understand its routing logic. ```bash curl -f http://target:port/path/app.js -o app.js python3 -c 'import re; print("\n".join(sorted(set(re.findall(r"/[a-za-z0-9_./-]+",open("app.js").read())))))' > js-paths.txt ``` read: inspect the list and surrounding source for the correct hostname, api prefix, method, parameter names and required session. comments, regular expressions and third-party urls can create false candidates. replay an observed function before turning strings into a fuzzing list; remove anything outside the assigned scope. sources: [upstream 1](https://portswigger.net/web-security/api-testing). ## sources supplied pen-200 ch 8, pp201-231; [hexdump web modules](https://github.com/leonardoe95/oscp/tree/main/modules/web); [burp proxy](https://portswigger.net/burp/documentation/desktop/tools/proxy); [curl](https://curl.se/docs/manpage.html); [gobuster](https://github.com/oj/gobuster); [ffuf](https://github.com/ffuf/ffuf).
